name: Ida Mercer
home: the blocks north of the port
voice: I bought this place with the settlement from my bus accident. I can refund a wash. I can't refund this morning. I gave him the good jacket I keep behind the till for meetings with the bank.
agenda: To keep an emergency clothes rail behind the till without turning it into charity theater.
appearance: Ida is easy to recognize by a soft fringe that falls across one eyebrow and fine brows over wide-set eyes. Usually dressed in a red windbreaker with a tiny red thread tied through the lowest buttonhole, Ida raises one eyebrow long before saying yes when listening.
life: Before the accident Ida collected fares and knew regulars by the noises they made climbing onto the bus. Running the Wash House lets her keep that skill. A person dropping one sock at a time needs a chair before they need a lecture about the machines. People around Paper & Pine Books know Ida by a small Wednesday habit. Ida starts with the handwritten shelf cards and often leaves with a suggestion for somebody else.
personality: Ida is patient with a person learning and fiercely impatient with somebody pretending to know. A half-finished job left where a beginner can see it is an invitation, as far as Ida is concerned.
family: Bianca Ward is Ida’s second cousin. Ida makes the call. Bianca is free to hang up first. Some of their best calls last less than a minute. A change of tone is sometimes all the news either one needs. Asked about *A widow bids again*, Bianca says, “I sell luxury property. This is the first bidder who asked me the names on the doorbells.”
connections: Rafael Nunes. The jacket from behind the till is the loan between them that makes the ceremony possible.

name: Lev Bellamy
home: the blocks north of the port
voice: My father taught me to turn a ruined cuff inside out. The dye reached the lining this time. I asked the man where he wanted the white stripe to sit and waited for him to choose.
agenda: To give Rafael the option of keeping one visible mark from the morning.
appearance: Lev has a small notch in the left eyebrow. Look for a gray streak running back from the forehead. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a red windbreaker with a fabric zip pull cut from a school scarf. In conversation Lev leans a shoulder against the wall during long conversations.
life: Lev began by cutting down men's coats for children during a bad winter. He still saves the narrow strips from the inside because they show what the cloth looked like new. He hates it when people ask to be made thinner. Sunday often includes a stop at the corner by Juniper Tailor, where Lev looks at the things people actually bring in for repair before looking in the display window.
personality: Lev loves an audience until a private hurt enters the room. Then the performer disappears and someone very good at getting other people through a door takes over.
family: Lennon Wang is Lev’s younger cousin. Lev leaves the first voice message. Lennon calls back when there is finally a little privacy. In their family a missed ring can mean a bus, a customer, a sleeping child or a bad hour. Neither treats it as an answer in itself. Asked about *Three minutes at the bridge*, Lennon says, “I had hoped the shared rides would turn into a friendship.”
connections: Marnie Phelps. They spread the ruined sleeve on the maintenance table to see what can still be saved.

name: Rafael Nunes
voice: My wife pressed that suit on the kitchen table the night before she died. I went to the ceremony in a borrowed jacket. The spoiled one came home with me on its own hanger.
agenda: To get the cuff photograph framed for his daughter before she leaves home.
appearance: Rafael has a crooked front tooth visible when laughing. Look for short copper curls. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is an olive canvas jacket with a pocket notebook shaped by years of sitting on it. In conversation Rafael steadies a cup with both hands while listening. The borrowed jacket is a little broad over Rafael’s shoulders. He keeps the photographs with the bleached cuff showing.
life: Rafael practiced the oath in the shaft between floors because an elevator counterweight makes a forgiving audience. His daughter never heard him make a mistake. That gave her the false impression that the words came easily. People around Studio Boulevard know Rafael by a small Friday habit. Rafael waits by the window where the whole crossing can be seen without leaning into the road.
personality: Rafael enjoys routines and will defend the right of someone else to break one. As a result, Rafael is often everyone's favorite cover for a missed morning.
family: Albert Hsu is Rafael’s second cousin. Rafael chooses the familiar route. Albert can stop the walk at any corner. Walking side by side makes it easier to disagree without turning each disagreement into a contest. Asked about *The school photograph that travels*, Albert says, “I drove the school route. She wrote my bus number on the photo because she never knew my surname.”
connections: Ida Mercer. The jacket from behind the till is the loan between them that makes the ceremony possible. Also in the story is Alma Faye (portraitist).

name: Marnie Phelps
voice: I signed the machine off yesterday because the test towel came back clean. I've put my initials beside the failed test this time. I want the next shift to know exactly who to wake.
agenda: To secure paid time to test machines between overnight and day shifts.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a black overshirt with pearl buttons and a pair of reading glasses in a cloth sleeve. Marnie has heavy brows and an unusually delicate jaw, with short, uneven waves that refuse to lie flat. Marnie listens with the head tilted a little to the left during a conversation.
life: Marnie used to be trusted with a hotel boiler and nothing else. Leaving for a tiny laundry meant a pay cut and a chance to sign a maintenance sheet with her own name. That signature means more to her than the uniform did. People around the foot of Harbor Viaduct know Marnie by a small Thursday habit. Marnie pauses where the machinery overhead makes two people stand close enough to hear each other.
personality: Marnie is cheerful on a bad morning and unexpectedly melancholy after a success. Finishing a hard thing means losing the daily company of the people who worked on it.
family: Stevie Rose is Marnie’s older cousin. Marnie brings the paper and a pen. Stevie decides what stays off the paper. They have helped each other make decisions that were far easier to discuss once the figures could be moved around. The decisions themselves still belong to the person asking. Asked about *A borrowed name*, Stevie says, “I dislike the book and adore the man. I'm organizing a dinner where nobody has to choose.”
connections: Lev Bellamy. They spread the ruined sleeve on the maintenance table to see what can still be saved.

name: Salma Ilyas
home: the western blocks near Ferry Street Rooms
voice: At my own ceremony nobody could pronounce my mother's name. I wrote the pronunciation on his appointment slip and called ahead about the delay while he changed.
agenda: To make the courthouse call a person's chosen name correctly on the first try.
appearance: Salma has fine brows over wide-set eyes. Look for a cropped cut that shows the shape of the ears. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a pale blue work shirt with a printed handkerchief folded into the pocket. In conversation Salma listens with the head tilted a little to the left.
life: As a schoolchild Salma translated every official letter for her family except the one about her own attendance. She makes families tell her which person has asked for the translation before agreeing to speak. On Friday, near the public end of the South Shore boardwalk, Salma checks the shade on the benches before deciding how long to stay.
personality: Salma finds names easy and faces hard on a crowded street. People who assume they have been snubbed usually get a warmer greeting once they speak.
family: Martin Henry is Salma’s second cousin. Salma calls about good news first. Martin is allowed to ask about the bad news afterward. Neither wants every family conversation to begin with a bill, a diagnosis or an apology. Asked about *The guarantee*, Martin says, “My parents owned nothing they could pledge.”

name: Warren Lyle
voice: I used to work on a hotel laundry line. I found three identical claims under three different machine numbers. I want the service company to come and point to each machine in person.
agenda: To settle the failed-valve claim before the Wash House loses its hotel work.
appearance: Warren has two dimples that appear only with a full smile. Look for short sandy hair and a marked widow's peak. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a charcoal zip cardigan with a pen clipped inside the neckline. In conversation Warren gives a little nod before asking a hard question.
life: Warren took an office job after hot linen burned his forearm. He is still quickest to spot a bad laundry claim by looking at the worker's hands. A neat report with no trace of the people who did the work makes him uneasy. People around the crossing outside Verve Nail Studio know Warren by a small Monday habit. Warren notices whose chair is empty and who has stayed talking after an appointment.
personality: Is a careful borrower and a reckless lender. Things leave this person's house with elaborate instructions and very little expectation of ever coming back.

A present that was perfect at sixteen may be completely wrong at forty. They take the trouble of finding out. Asked about *The broken till*, Nadia says, “I wrote everyone's sandwiches in pictures. The cook hung the sheet beside the menu.”

name: Kit Salcedo
voice: I gave the borrowed shoes a polish on the bank steps. He kept offering me a note. I finally took it because he was starting to feel like everybody's charity case.
agenda: To earn enough on ordinary paid shines to keep the stool on the bank steps.
appearance: Kit is easy to recognize by a center part and straight chestnut hair and a flat bridge to the nose and a mobile brow. Usually dressed in a soft blue checked shirt with a replacement button a shade darker than the others, Kit gathers both sleeves neatly before settling in when listening.
life: Kit rented the shoeshine stool after losing a restaurant job. He makes enough on hearing days to skip the humiliating half-shift his old manager still offers him. People tipping too generously put that pride in a difficult place. On Sunday, near Studio Boulevard, Kit waits by the window where the whole crossing can be seen without leaning into the road.
personality: Kit is kind in very practical ways and prickly about being thanked in public. Kit loves being recognized by the people who notice what happens after the guests have left.
family: Shay Lloyd is Kit’s older cousin. A parent had a second job that nobody mentioned at school. Years later the family discovered two sets of friends who thought they knew entirely different people. Kit can usually spot the person covering a double shift. Asked about *The second dog*, Shay says, “I fostered both litters. Their ears fold the same way until somebody says dinner.”

name: Dora Beck
voice: The rinse valve came from a batch I signed for with my brother's pencil. I paid for a new one out of the van money and kept the old part for the supplier to examine.
agenda: To get the supplier to inspect the old valve with the workers present.
appearance: Dora has brown hair pinned away from the temples, a heart-shaped face and prominent ears, and a favorite piece of clothing, a brown corduroy jacket. life: Dora spent her first decade fixing appliances others deemed uneconomic. She can price every part on sight and badly underprices her own time. Her brother has stopped lending her the van unless she puts labor on the bill. On Tuesday, near Maré Coffee, Dora likes the table where people coming off shift stop checking the time.
personality: Likes beautiful, unnecessary things and gets cross with people who mistake poverty for a lack of taste. Dora takes longer choosing a cheap birthday card than an expensive coat.
family: Sonia Lee is Dora’s cousin. Dora puts the kettle on. Sonia chooses the music. The cups come out before either brings up the reason for the visit. They trust a difficult conversation more if it has had an ordinary beginning. Asked about *The sandwich board*, Sonia says, “I'm the one who wiped off the prices. I wanted people to ask what the cheap lunch actually bought.”
connections: Salma Ilyas. One is waiting for the courthouse to pick up while the other labels the failed valve.

name: Alma Faye
voice: In the photograph you can see one white cuff. His daughter asked me to take it out. He asked me to leave it in. I made him the first print and put the negative away.
agenda: To give Rafael final say over which portrait leaves the studio.
appearance: Alma has thick, tightly coiled hair, heavy brows and an unusually delicate jaw, and a favorite piece of clothing, an old plum windbreaker. It usually goes with a comb in a sleeve sewn into the lining. When somebody else has the floor, Alma starts to lift a hand, then waits to be invited to speak.
life: Alma learned portraits taking passport pictures behind a copy counter. She likes the half-second after a person stops smiling on instruction. Brides pay her bills, but that half-second is what makes her keep the camera. Wednesday often includes a stop at the bank steps, where Alma takes a few minutes to read the public notices, especially the ones written in a hurry.
personality: Alma can be wonderfully decisive about an emergency and maddeningly undecided about a gift. This is because a person can say precisely what hurts and rarely says exactly what they want.
family: Jody Graves is Alma’s cousin. Alma chooses an ordinary story to tell. Jody asks the question the rest of the family avoided. They tend to get further with an important subject when it arrives in the middle of talk about dinner or work. Asked about *The bitter orange*, Jody says, “I remember mustard because she'd send it back if we skimped.”
connections: Kit Salcedo. One finishes the borrowed shoes while the other frames the cuff that won't match them. Also in the story is Rafael Nunes (client).

agenda: To sign a contract that lets the housekeepers reject a bad test load.
appearance: Dee is easy to recognize by a loose dark braid and full cheeks and a mouth that pulls slightly to one side. Usually dressed in a rust-colored canvas coat with a narrow brass watch set a little fast, Dee counts on the side of one finger where hardly anybody notices when listening.
life: Dee once walked into the staff changing room in a skirt stiff with laundry chemicals. The housekeepers laughed and washed it for her. She has asked them to judge every linen sample since. On Wednesday, near the corner by Juniper Tailor, Dee looks at the things people actually bring in for repair before looking in the display window.
personality: Dee can be lavish with time and quite careful with cash. A free afternoon is sometimes the biggest gift Dee can afford to give, and family knows to take it seriously.
family: Jade Hunter is Dee’s half-sibling. Dee checks the date twice. Jade brings something that can still be enjoyed tomorrow. Arrangements do change in their family. Taking a delay seriously without treating it as an insult took both of them years. Asked about *The boy on the corner*, Jade says, “I want to be their foster aunt. My flat is smaller than the official assessor expected and larger than the boys remember.”

voice: My dad marked my height on that chair after every voyage. When my parents split, we thought it went to the dump. I want one last picture of it hanging above the quay, which my supervisor thinks is a terrible idea.
agenda: To bring the chair home with a picture his granddaughter can keep.
appearance: Back on the street, look for a brown corduroy jacket and a small enamel bird on the lapel. Owen has two dimples that appear only with a full smile, with a neat white crop. Owen leans a shoulder against the wall during long conversations during a conversation.

People around Paper & Pine Books know Owen by a small Sunday habit. Owen starts with the handwritten shelf cards and often leaves with a suggestion for somebody else.

name: Bettine Cross
voice: I carried it off a ship because a woman in the crew asked if anyone here repaired cane seats. Now half the port has a claim on it. I still owe that woman an answer.
agenda: To give the seafarer who handed over the chair a straight answer.
appearance: Back on the street, look for a narrow-striped sweater and a comb in a sleeve sewn into the lining. Bettine has a broad nose and a deep dimple on one cheek, with a cropped cut that shows the shape of the ears. Bettine holds eye contact until the other person has finished during a conversation.
life: Bettine goes to sea to visit cousins when holidays permit, so she understands the weight an ordinary object gains after months afloat. The crew member who first entrusted her with the chair worries her more than the people claiming it on shore. People around Tideline Market know Bettine by a small Friday habit. Bettine picks out the bruised fruit first and asks the seller what will ripen by supper.
personality: Bettine tells a better story in a kitchen than at a microphone. Family members sometimes underestimate how far Bettine will go to back a quiet opinion once it is actually challenged.
family: Tristan Collins is Bettine’s half-sibling. Bettine makes the call. Tristan is free to hang up first. Some of their best calls last less than a minute. connections: Willa True. They disagree about moving the chair indoors before the ship's crew gets an answer.

name: Ivor Lake
voice: The lower marks run down instead of up. Somebody measured a child on their knees. I offered to mend the seat and leave the pencil lines exactly where the family put them.
agenda: To make the cane seat sound enough for an adult without disturbing the marks.
appearance: Ivor has short, uneven waves that refuse to lie flat, a long face and high cheekbones, and a favorite piece of clothing, a mustard canvas overshirt. It usually goes with a tiny red thread tied through the lowest buttonhole. When somebody else has the floor, Ivor leans a shoulder against the wall during long conversations.
life: Ivor charges by the finished repair because disability makes his hours unpredictable. Families sometimes mistake the quiet pace of his workshop for leisure. He has been trying to get his apprentice to quote without embarrassment. Tuesday often includes a stop at Ferris Deli, where Ivor asks for the end slice and listens to the names the counter workers use for regulars.
personality: Ivor is fond of ambitious ideas and deeply suspicious of grand openings. The question Ivor asks at any launch is who has the keys for cleaning up a month later.
family: Javier Lai is Ivor’s cousin raised in the same household. Ivor leaves the first voice message. Javier calls back when there is finally a little privacy. In their family a missed ring can mean a bus, a customer, a sleeping child or a bad hour. Neither treats it as an answer in itself. Asked about *No lifeguard at dusk*, Javier says, “I own the cart beside the steps. I can sit for company after the shutters come down, without promising to be a lifeguard.”

name: Tamsin Leung
voice: I put the chair in lost property under freight fittings. That's where I used to sit on breaks during my pregnancy. I'd like the old break room reopened before we give it away.
agenda: To restore a break-room seat for the next worker returning from leave.
appearance: Tamsin is easy to recognize by a soft fringe that falls across one eyebrow and a wide brow and a narrow jaw. Usually dressed in a cream pullover with a stitched row of blue crosses along an old repair, Tamsin touches a knuckle to the chin when searching for a word when listening.
life: After having her first child Tamsin expressed milk in a locked rail office. She has never forgotten the humiliation of asking for a key to a room nobody was using. She makes a fuss about chairs because a chair once mattered that much. Wednesday often includes a stop at the window at Night Shift Donuts, where Tamsin knows when the going-home crowd and the coming-to-work crowd will both be there.
personality: Tamsin is firm about boundaries and unusually forgiving of somebody who admits to crossing one. Demands to act grateful for unwanted help can end a friendship.
family: Cian Ingram is Tamsin’s stepsibling. Tamsin chooses the familiar route. Cian can stop the walk at any corner. Walking side by side makes it easier to disagree without turning each disagreement into a contest. Asked about *The expensive summer*, Cian says, “I brought takeaway chips to the public bench.”
connections: Fen Ellis. A chalk gull lets them test two very different ideas about who used to sit here.

name: Mateo Serrat
voice: I remember carrying that chair up four flights to my first shore flat. I'm sending the family the curry recipe I had to stand on it to reach.
agenda: To cook the old shore-flat supper for both sides of the family.
appearance: Mateo has a thin scattering of white hair over the crown, two dimples that appear only with a full smile, and a favorite piece of clothing, a black overshirt with pearl buttons. It usually goes with a seam let out by a narrow strip of contrasting fabric. When somebody else has the floor, Mateo leans a shoulder against the wall during long conversations.
life: Mateo packed his kitchen into one fish crate when his first shore lease ended. He can cook a week's dinners with the contents of that crate and can still describe the flat by counting the steps to the landing. On Wednesday, near the bank steps, Mateo takes a few minutes to read the public notices, especially the ones written in a hurry.
personality: Mateo loves a well-told anecdote and distrusts the neat ending. The parts Mateo remembers are the interruptions, unfinished jobs and people who had to go back to work halfway through.
family: Briar Poole is Mateo’s younger cousin. Mateo brings the paper and a pen. Briar decides what stays off the paper. They have helped each other make decisions that were far easier to discuss once the figures could be moved around. The decisions themselves still belong to the person asking. Asked about *The first straight paycheck*, Briar says, “I bought from him regularly. Losing his number matters less than losing the only person who asked if I'd eaten.”
connections: Leon Armas. They have undertaken to get a retirement meal and a granddaughter to the same side of the port gate.

name: Willa True
voice: Somebody once took my mother's effects from a loading bay marked free. I moved the chair indoors and made the first person claiming it tell me what was under the seat.
agenda: To establish ownership from a memory somebody could never learn from a photograph.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a pale blue work shirt and a replacement button a shade darker than the others. Willa has two dimples that appear only with a full smile, with a soft fringe that falls across one eyebrow. Willa gathers both sleeves neatly before settling in during a conversation.
life: A night in lost property taught Willa that the people most comfortable claiming a thing often know least about it. She lets quieter owners describe one private detail before she brings anything out from behind the door. People around the approach to Seabright Court know Willa by a small Sunday habit. Willa likes to watch the beach traffic thin enough for workers going the other way.
personality: Willa has excellent recall for voices and a poor memory for official titles. Someone who waited patiently at a counter years ago is more likely to be remembered than the person in charge.
family: Anita Gill is Willa’s stepsibling. Willa calls about good news first. Anita is allowed to ask about the bad news afterward. Neither wants every family conversation to begin with a bill, a diagnosis or an apology. Asked about *The engine lullaby*, Anita says, “I recorded it with my wedding tape by mistake.”
connections: Bettine Cross. They disagree about moving the chair indoors before the ship's crew gets an answer.

name: Fen Ellis
home: the western blocks near Ferry Street Rooms
voice: The chalk gull underneath is mine. I used to draw birds under things at friends' houses. This is the first time one of them has flown back.
agenda: To find one of the other childhood gulls before an old house is sold.
appearance: Fen is easy to recognize by dark brown curls cut close behind the ears and a small notch in the left eyebrow. Usually dressed in an old plum windbreaker with a partly rubbed-away embroidered initial, Fen looks at people's hands before looking at what they carry when listening.
life: Fen drew birds as a child because the family moved too often to keep pets. He signed his first paid shopfront with a tiny gull where only someone opening the shutter could see it. Friday often includes a stop at the crossing outside Verve Nail Studio, where Fen notices whose chair is empty and who has stayed talking after an appointment.
personality: Fen finds it easier to own up to a mistake than to accept praise. The worse the mistake, the more precise the account of exactly when it happened.
family: Hollis Osei is Fen’s older relative by marriage. Fen remembers the birthdays. Hollis asks what the birthday guest would like this year. A present that was perfect at sixteen may be completely wrong at forty. They take the trouble of finding out. Asked about *A tenant who stays*, Hollis says, “I would share the big room for a season. Nobody asked because they thought an old person always wants silence.”
connections: Tamsin Leung. A chalk gull lets them test two very different ideas about who used to sit here. Also in the story is Owen Vale (childhood friend).

name: Leon Armas
voice: Everybody wants a retirement speech. He wants his granddaughter admitted past the gate for ten minutes. I spent the morning finding a quiet place on the public side for the picture.
agenda: To get the granddaughter a place at the farewell within reach of her grandfather.
appearance: Leon is easy to recognize by a high puff tied with plain cord and a long face and high cheekbones. Usually dressed in a boxy denim jacket with a tiny red thread tied through the lowest buttonhole, Leon presses the lips together to keep a smile in when listening.
life: Leon has given fifteen retirement speeches, all of them wrong about one thing. Now he takes the person concerned for tea first and asks which story they would hate to hear repeated at the microphone. On Thursday, near the public road outside the Port of Asphalt, Leon can recognize shift change by the lull between two groups of walkers.
personality: Leon keeps other people's confidences so well that friends sometimes mistake discretion for taking sides. Leon wants to be trusted and resents being asked for proof of it.
family: Briar Patel is Leon’s second cousin. Leon offers the first invitation. Briar gets to change the plan. They learned that a promise to visit is easier to keep when changing a time does not count as letting down the whole family. Asked about *Laundry for a stranger*, Briar says, “My son needs a good shirt for court. I asked the volunteer if the stranger might lend it.”
connections: Mateo Serrat. They have undertaken to get a retirement meal and a granddaughter to the same side of the port gate.

name: Merit Shaw
voice: I offered to pay to ship it to his sister. Then I learned they haven't spoken in eleven years. I gave him the quote in a sealed envelope he can throw away.
agenda: To leave the sister free to decline both the chair and the reconciliation.
appearance: Merit has a long face and high cheekbones. Look for short, uneven waves that refuse to lie flat. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a rust-colored canvas coat with a cloth patch so neatly matched it only shows in strong light. In conversation Merit turns fully toward the person speaking.
life: Merit's first forwarding job was sending home a dead sailor's boots. She learned that a parcel can arrive before a family is ready to open it. Her quotations include a space for the recipient to choose a date. On Thursday, near Juniper Street, Merit knows which of the west-side porches has a seat in the shade.
personality: Merit always notices who paid for the last round. In a group that can be a kindness or a small tyranny, and Merit is trying to tell the difference before the bill arrives.
family: Adriana Arnett is Merit’s half-sibling. Merit puts the kettle on. Adriana chooses the music. The cups come out before either brings up the reason for the visit. They trust a difficult conversation more if it has had an ordinary beginning. Asked about *The second dog*, Adriana says, “I have the delivery photo of both dogs in the same yard.”
connections: Nell Oram. The shipping quote and the recorded recollections are the only things the absent sister can receive without taking ownership.

name: Nell Oram
voice: He told me three versions of who cut the first mark. I asked his permission to record all three. Families ought to be allowed to change their minds on tape.
agenda: To let people listen to the conflicting accounts with their speakers' permission.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a brown corduroy jacket and a replacement button a shade darker than the others. Nell has a straight nose and deep-set eyes, with brown hair pinned away from the temples. Nell presses the lips together to keep a smile in during a conversation.
life: Nell has a splendid memory for voices and a terrible memory for places. She asks interviewees to walk while they talk. It makes the recordings windy and prevents her inventing a street somebody never walked. Tuesday often includes a stop at Tideline Market, where Nell picks out the bruised fruit first and asks the seller what will ripen by supper.
personality: Nell has a talent for getting adversaries to laugh at exactly the same thing. Nell knows better than to expect the laugh to settle what they are arguing about.
family: Terry Sullivan is Nell’s cousin raised in the same household. Nell chooses an ordinary story to tell. Terry asks the question the rest of the family avoided. They tend to get further with an important subject when it arrives in the middle of talk about dinner or work. Asked about *Midnight cinnamon*, Terry says, “I thought it was my grandmother's spice bread.”
connections: Merit Shaw. The shipping quote and the recorded recollections are the only things the absent sister can receive without taking ownership.

name: Vera Rios
voice: For years I bought my crews soup from that cart. I gave the big check because I wanted my late wife's name on a bench. Now the vendor is asking who can actually afford to sit there at lunchtime.
agenda: To put a memorial where her wife would actually have spent a lunch break.
appearance: Vera has a long silver braid, a small notch in the left eyebrow, and a favorite piece of clothing, a dark green knitted vest. It usually goes with a printed handkerchief folded into the pocket. When somebody else has the floor, Vera turns fully toward the person speaking.
life: Vera built her fortune keeping food cold for businesses that couldn't buy their own storage. During the first summer she slept beside a faulty alarm. Today plenty of people call her generous. Very few remember that she used to owe the snack seller lunch money. Friday often includes a stop at Harbour Bakery, where Vera buys one familiar thing and asks who chose the unfamiliar thing in the window.
personality: Vera admires skill and distrusts the idea that skill gives anyone permission to be rude. Vera learns fastest from somebody willing to show how they made a mistake.
family: Emma Davis is Vera’s second cousin. Vera picks the meeting place. Emma sets the time to leave. It lets them stay close without turning a family visit into the loss of an entire day. They have both had stretches when that distinction mattered. Asked about *A room above the dryers*, Emma says, “I live across the landing. I asked for free sittings for the old people nobody photographs unless they're blowing candles out.”
connections: Gil Atwood (former lunch vendor). They knew each other over a cart long before anybody put their names on the same check.

name: Gil Atwood
voice: My eleven dollars were the change regulars left in a jar after a boy broke the chess table. Somebody called me a philanthropist. I still owe those regulars a chess table.
agenda: To replace the children's chess table before the ceremony.
appearance: Gil has short copper curls, a crooked front tooth visible when laughing, and a favorite piece of clothing, a moss-green cardigan. It usually goes with a cloth patch so neatly matched it only shows in strong light. When somebody else has the floor, Gil squares up pieces of paper while thinking.
life: Gil fixes the park cart's smallest wheel with a piece of the chess set the children broke. Repairing the table would let him retire the makeshift axle. He is tired of donors assuming that gratitude pays for spare parts. People around Ferris Deli know Gil by a small Thursday habit. Gil asks for the end slice and listens to the names the counter workers use for regulars.
personality: Gil has a strong competitive streak and a very soft spot for the person finishing last. A prize tastes better when everybody had enough time to enter.
family: Daniel Song is Gil’s second cousin. Gil keeps the photographs. Daniel knows which ones can be shared. They enjoy remembering people in public and also know what it feels like to have a private afternoon turned into an anecdote for strangers. Asked about *Salt in the pockets*, Daniel says, “I need the big coat to keep my knees warm on the early ferry.”
connections: Vera Rios (former lunch customer). They knew each other over a cart long before anybody put their names on the same check.

name: Luz Aranda
voice: I counted the jar twice and kept the bent coin. It's in my drawer because I liked knowing exactly which part of that giant number came from us. I've offered to count the next jar in public.
agenda: To have each little contribution visible in the endowment record.
appearance: Luz has a smooth side part with one rebellious curl, fine brows over wide-set eyes, and a favorite piece of clothing, a soft blue checked shirt. It usually goes with a thin silver ring worn on a cord. When somebody else has the floor, Luz looks toward the door whenever a name is called.
life: Luz counts tips separately from wages because her mother once lost benefits over money somebody only thought she'd earned. She thinks collecting coins deserves as much paper trail as accepting a six-figure transfer. Monday often includes a stop at the courtyard by Ferry Street Rooms, where Luz prefers the bench where the sound of the shop door reaches before the visitor does.
personality: Luz reads little signals of discomfort very accurately and has an unfortunate habit of overruling people for their own good. The friends who say stop are the ones Luz trusts most.
family: Sonia Neal is Luz’s parent’s cousin. Luz makes the call. Sonia is free to hang up first. Some of their best calls last less than a minute. A change of tone is sometimes all the news either one needs. Asked about *The kitchen without a boss*, Sonia says, “I supply eggs and normally ask for the boss.”
connections: Min Calder. They count the little donations against the costs the formal accounts left out.

reactions.asWritten: A traveler asks for the last seat at the bus stop. Luz gives up their own space if possible and asks the passengers who arrived first to choose what happens next.

reactions.asWritten: If told to back off, Luz does so immediately and stays available at a distance the other person chooses.

name: Silas Pike
voice: I wrote the gift restriction in language the vendor couldn't read. My own mother left school at twelve. I owe them a version she could read aloud without stopping.
agenda: To rewrite the gift terms in words a street seller can challenge.
appearance: Silas has a flat bridge to the nose and a mobile brow. Look for a loose dark braid. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a cream pullover with a pair of reading glasses in a cloth sleeve. In conversation Silas holds eye contact until the other person has finished.
life: Silas went into estate law after his mother signed a paper she could not read. He earns most of his money from clients who like difficult clauses. His most interesting work begins when those two facts collide. On Friday, near Harbour Bakery, Silas buys one familiar thing and asks who chose the unfamiliar thing in the window.
personality: Silas has a quick wit and an equally quick sense of shame. A joke is often Silas's way of finding out whether a room is friendly enough for a serious question.
family: Dana Randall is Silas’s stepsibling. Silas leaves the first voice message. Dana calls back when there is finally a little privacy. In their family a missed ring can mean a bus, a customer, a sleeping child or a bad hour. Neither treats it as an answer in itself. Asked about *A closing hour*, Dana says, “I advertised always open before I had a daughter.”
connections: Etta Webb. One drafts the words of the gift. The other has to find out if a child can actually use what those words buy.

reactions.asWritten: If the joke lands badly, Silas seeks out the person it hurt before telling anybody why it was supposed to be funny.

name: Joan Morley
home: the streets inland from Pier Beach
voice: The proposed bench faces straight into the sprinkler. I put a folding chair there and invited the donor out at six in the morning. I want one decision made with wet shoes.
agenda: To move the bench out of the sprinkler's reach.
appearance: Joan has a crooked front tooth visible when laughing. Look for short black hair swept back. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a sand-colored linen shirt with a small enamel bird on the lapel. In conversation Joan leans a shoulder against the wall during long conversations.
life: Joan looks after park soil on a contractor's budget that changes every spring. She distrusts gifts for things that need watering because no donor has ever wanted their name on the water bill. On Monday, near the foot of Harbor Viaduct, Joan pauses where the machinery overhead makes two people stand close enough to hear each other.
personality: Joan listens for the familiar version of a story and then for the one detail that changes it. Friends bring problems here when they want to be heard twice.
family: Martin Rahman is Joan’s cousin raised in the same household. Joan chooses the familiar route. Martin can stop the walk at any corner. Walking side by side makes it easier to disagree without turning each disagreement into a contest. Asked about *The crane shadow*, Martin says, “I painted the gull where the shadow touched on the day I started.”
connections: Sol Lane. They are walking the proposed bench site at the hour when a violin and a sprinkler can both be heard.

reactions.asWritten: The paper wants a photograph with only the biggest donor. Joan asks the vendor where they would like to stand and tells the photographer who paid the eleven dollars.

name: Etta Webb
voice: Our best player can't grip the heavy replacement pieces. I brought along the wooden set my father whittled. The donor played her and lost both rooks.
agenda: To find pieces the club's strongest player can grip.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a narrow-striped sweater and a fabric zip pull cut from a school scarf. Etta has a straight nose and deep-set eyes, with a swept fringe and a closely clipped nape. Etta raises one eyebrow long before saying yes during a conversation.
life: Etta started the chess club so kids could lose at something that wasn't school. She refuses to post rankings. She can, however, recite the first move of every child who has ever beaten her. On Tuesday, near the blocks below Foundry Lofts, Etta checks the little hand-lettered notices around Harbour Supply.
personality: Etta talks very little about private fear and recognizes it quickly in strangers. Offering a choice of seats is one of Etta's ways of saying that it is all right to leave.
family: Elise Cho is Etta’s older cousin. Etta brings the paper and a pen. Elise decides what stays off the paper. They have helped each other make decisions that were far easier to discuss once the figures could be moved around. The decisions themselves still belong to the person asking. Asked about *The first straight paycheck*, Elise says, “I am the mother who always took his gifts. I need to learn to accept a cheaper birthday present without asking why.”
connections: Silas Pike. One drafts the words of the gift. The other has to find out if a child can actually use what those words buy.

name: Perry Han
home: the streets inland from Pier Beach
voice: I was the one who cropped the vendor out of the press picture. I used to sell school photos and hated making children stand at the edge. I called the editor myself.
agenda: To restore the vendor's place in the newspaper photograph.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a cropped bottle-green coat and a fabric zip pull cut from a school scarf. Perry has a small notch in the left eyebrow, with a dark undercut with a longer wave on top. Perry starts to lift a hand, then waits to be invited to speak during a conversation. For a press event Perry brings a square of lens cloth in the same pocket as a carefully folded tie.
life: Perry grew up being moved to the edge of school pictures whenever somebody taller arrived. At work he took the flattering crop before he thought about the person on its edge. He has asked the vendor to choose the replacement. On Friday, near the approach to Seabright Court, Perry likes to watch the beach traffic thin enough for workers going the other way.
personality: Perry prefers exact instructions at work and pleasant surprises at home. The two standards occasionally collide, especially when a relative thinks dropping by counts as notice.
family: Cian Reese is Perry’s first cousin once removed. Perry calls about good news first. Cian is allowed to ask about the bad news afterward. Neither wants every family conversation to begin with a bill, a diagnosis or an apology. Asked about *Hem by hem*, Cian says, “I can't stand long enough for a fitting. The bride carried the mirror to my chair.”
connections: Ava Baptiste. They both worked on the press coverage and have different mistakes to repair.

name: Ava Baptiste
voice: The big check made my deadline easy. Then the vendor asked me to name the eleven people behind the eleven dollars. I gave up my afternoon off to find the first four.
agenda: To identify the regulars who filled the eleven-dollar jar.
appearance: Ava has dark brown curls cut close behind the ears, a flat bridge to the nose and a mobile brow, and a favorite piece of clothing, a dark green knitted vest. It usually goes with a small enamel bird on the lapel. When somebody else has the floor, Ava presses the lips together to keep a smile in.
life: Ava can produce seven hundred words about any ribbon cutting in twenty minutes. She secretly misses the old district desk where every misspelled name brought an angry relative to the office. Sunday often includes a stop at Breakwater Way, where Ava stops on the landward side of the cycle track to watch the first boats turn for home.
personality: Ava never tires of being shown how somebody makes a living. Ava can ask an expert question of a craftsperson and still mishandle a simple emotional cue from a friend.
family: Thomas Sun is Ava’s second cousin. Ava remembers the birthdays. Thomas asks what the birthday guest would like this year. A present that was perfect at sixteen may be completely wrong at forty. They take the trouble of finding out. Asked about *No lifeguard at dusk*, Thomas says, “I thought we had budgeted for coverage until dusk.”
connections: Perry Han. They both worked on the press coverage and have different mistakes to repair.

name: Min Calder
voice: The bank charged more to print the display than the cart raised. I separated those lines on the public statement. It will make our winter appeal awkward, and it ought to.
agenda: To publish the cost of promoting the donation alongside the donation.
appearance: Min is easy to recognize by close-cropped dark curls and a long face and high cheekbones. Usually dressed in a sand-colored linen shirt with a thin silver ring worn on a cord, Min looks at people's hands before looking at what they carry when listening.
life: Min used to balance the books for a dance hall that ran out of money with six weddings still to host. Public accounts make her nervous when they only record what happened to the cash. Monday often includes a stop at the market by Market Flats, where Min often waits until the delivery baskets are stacked before going in.
personality: Min often says yes too quickly out of pride in being useful. The people closest to Min have learned to ask again the next morning, when the answer is more likely to account for sleep.
family: Jesse Arnett is Min’s cousin raised in the same household. Min offers the first invitation. Jesse gets to change the plan. They learned that a promise to visit is easier to keep when changing a time does not count as letting down the whole family. Asked about *Nine unpaid hours*, Jesse says, “I took another job at sea before the meeting.”
connections: Luz Aranda. They count the little donations against the costs the formal accounts left out.

name: Sol Lane
voice: My wife and I used to play chess with bottle caps here. I'm giving the opening concert, but I want the first minute quiet enough to hear the clocks on the tables.
agenda: To play something that will leave the first chess game audible.
appearance: Sol has two white streaks in otherwise dark hair, a scattering of freckles across the bridge of the nose, and a favorite piece of clothing, a soft blue checked shirt. It usually goes with a narrow brass watch set a little fast. When somebody else has the floor, Sol leans a shoulder against the wall during long conversations.
life: Sol's wife played the stronger opening and Sol played the better ending. They passed an entire courtship arguing about the middle game. Playing at a dedication is easy. Hearing chess clocks afterward is the hard part. People around Lighthouse Cove know Sol by a small Thursday habit. Sol takes a few minutes by the low rocks, where conversation sounds different as the tide turns.
personality: Sol thinks best while walking. Sitting beneath someone's office clock makes Sol sound more certain than they feel, an effect close friends have learned to distrust.
family: Beatrice Ko is Sol’s cousin’s child. Sol puts the kettle on. Beatrice chooses the music. The cups come out before either brings up the reason for the visit. They trust a difficult conversation more if it has had an ordinary beginning. Asked about *The fountain score*, Beatrice says, “I chose a saucepan with a dent from my first flat.”
connections: Joan Morley. They are walking the proposed bench site at the hour when a violin and a sprinkler can both be heard.

name: Marisol Vega
voice: My first bicycle belonged to three cousins before me. I thought recognizing a color was enough. I called both families from my own desk so neither would have to queue at the station again.
agenda: To give both riders one uninterrupted chance to identify their property.
appearance: Marisol is easy to recognize by short black hair swept back and a flat bridge to the nose and a mobile brow. Usually dressed in a cream pullover with a knotted piece of sail thread on a key ring, Marisol steadies a cup with both hands while listening when listening.
life: Marisol took a paper route as a kid to pay for punctures. The station has three forms for a bicycle and none asks what it feels like under its rider. She wants the return desk to ask that question before asking for a signature. People around Breakwater Way know Marisol by a small Friday habit. Marisol stops on the landward side of the cycle track to watch the first boats turn for home.
personality: Marisol treats keeping somebody waiting as a serious discourtesy. This can turn a helpful person into an impatient one when everybody else needs a slower conversation.
family: Cory Walker is Marisol’s parent’s cousin. Marisol saves a place. Cory chooses whether to use it. The invitation means something because declining it has never ended the friendship between their households. Asked about *The trust with a typo*, Cory says, “I knew the founder when she couldn't afford the exam.”
connections: Hollis Fry. They meet a second time at the property counter to compare what the wrong saddle cost.

name: Hollis Fry
voice: The taped saddle tips to the left because my hip does. I made it through one delivery on the wrong bike before I began to limp. I want my lost delivery fee as much as my saddle.
agenda: To get the correct saddle back and the lost fee credited.
appearance: Hollis has a flat bridge to the nose and a mobile brow. Look for black hair twisted into a small knot. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a charcoal zip cardigan with a pair of reading glasses in a cloth sleeve. In conversation Hollis rubs a thumb along the edge of the nearest pocket.
life: Hollis learned to ride again after a hip operation by delivering groceries for two neighbors. He remembers every doorway where he could set a bag down and lean for a moment. A delivery penalty can still feel like a verdict on his body. People around Lighthouse Cove know Hollis by a small Saturday habit. Hollis takes a few minutes by the low rocks, where conversation sounds different as the tide turns.
personality: Hollis is patient with a person learning and fiercely impatient with somebody pretending to know. A half-finished job left where a beginner can see it is an invitation, as far as Hollis is concerned.
family: Kate Parra is Hollis’s half-sibling. Hollis picks the meeting place. Kate sets the time to leave. It lets them stay close without turning a family visit into the loss of an entire day. They have both had stretches when that distinction mattered. Asked about *The housecoat commission*, Kate says, “I borrowed the pattern for my dad. He wants pockets large enough for Sunday's newspaper.”
connections: Marisol Vega. They meet a second time at the property counter to compare what the wrong saddle cost. Also in the story is Toby Lin (dispatcher).

name: Opal Finch
voice: I recognized the child's bell by the second ring it never makes. When the officer handed it back I let the kid explain the fault. People have been speaking over her all term.
agenda: To let the child demonstrate the broken bell herself.
appearance: Opal has a heart-shaped face and prominent ears. Look for thick, tightly coiled hair. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a cropped bottle-green coat with a pressed flower kept in the clear back of a phone case. In conversation Opal presses the lips together to keep a smile in.
life: Opal has watched two generations grow tall enough to cross alone. Little children tell her things adults are too busy to hear. She hopes her replacement will wait for the last syllable before lifting the stop sign. People around Maré Coffee know Opal by a small Friday habit. Opal likes the table where people coming off shift stop checking the time.
personality: Opal loves an audience until a private hurt enters the room. Then the performer disappears and someone very good at getting other people through a door takes over.
family: Devin Mills is Opal’s second cousin. Opal keeps the photographs. Devin knows which ones can be shared. They enjoy remembering people in public and also know what it feels like to have a private afternoon turned into an anecdote for strangers. Asked about *An old restaurant debt*, Devin says, “I sold the dead man's plates last month and finally had the money.”

voice: My client had a receipt and no photograph. I found myself asking him for proof I'd never ask my neighbors for. I want our property checklist to fit on the back of a library card.
agenda: To get the property checklist down to something a hurried client can carry.
appearance: Priya has one cheek that creases before the other. Look for a long plait tucked inside the collar. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is an old plum windbreaker with a small enamel bird on the lapel. In conversation Priya takes off the watch before a long conversation.
life: Priya's first case ended with a client getting his wallet back but missing work to do it. She still counts the cost of taking a morning off whenever an official calls a procedure straightforward. People around Ferris Deli know Priya by a small Thursday habit. Priya asks for the end slice and listens to the names the counter workers use for regulars.
personality: Priya enjoys routines and will defend the right of someone else to break one. As a result, Priya is often everyone's favorite cover for a missed morning.

A change of tone is sometimes all the news either one needs. Asked about *The first language*, Peyton says, “I want to read to the shop cat first. It has yet to interrupt anybody's pronunciation.”

name: Jude Wick
voice: Both wheels were built in my shop. I spoke for the wheel I remembered, and the child corrected me. I keep her drawing of the spoke pattern over the truing stand.

personality: Jude is cheerful on a bad morning and unexpectedly melancholy after a success. Finishing a hard thing means losing the daily company of the people who worked on it.

In their family a missed ring can mean a bus, a customer, a sleeping child or a bad hour. Neither treats it as an answer in itself. Asked about *The last light at the harbor*, Samuel says, “I turn ours off from below because my hands no longer reach the switch.”

name: Cleo Penn

voice: I used two identical bags for the keys. I've made a little station where owners can photograph their property with the collection slip. My supervisor wants to know whose idea it was.
agenda: To leave both owners with photographs of what they collected.
appearance: Cleo has a softly rounded chin under sharp cheekbones. Look for dark brown curls cut close behind the ears. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a cropped bottle-green coat with one loose pocket corner secured with green thread. In conversation Cleo takes off the watch before a long conversation.
life: Cleo grew up dividing one dresser drawer with two sisters. She assumed everyone could keep track of their things by memory. The station shelves cured her of that notion within a week. On Sunday, near the steps at Pier Beach, Cleo watches the working part of the waterfront before turning toward the open water.
personality: Cleo finds names easy and faces hard on a crowded street. People who assume they have been snubbed usually get a warmer greeting once they speak.
family: Anita Lund is Cleo’s older relative by marriage. Cleo chooses the familiar route. Anita can stop the walk at any corner. Walking side by side makes it easier to disagree without turning each disagreement into a contest. Asked about *The clean ledger*, Anita says, “I kept the notebook safe through three burglaries.”
connections: Priya Tal. The new collection slip has to satisfy both the counter and the person who will lose wages collecting it.

name: Art Robles
voice: I gave one of those bikes to my grandson and told him it was new. Now the former owner wants to say hello. I have to decide whether a pretty lie is worth another one.
agenda: To tell his grandson where the gift actually came from.
appearance: Art is easy to recognize by steel-colored hair cut square above the collar and a round face with a pronounced chin. Usually dressed in a washed violet jersey with a narrow brass watch set a little fast, Art looks at people's hands before looking at what they carry when listening.
life: Art was a detective long enough to give a persuasive answer even when a less tidy one was true. Retirement has put him in a family full of children who don't accept his first answer. People around the bank steps know Art by a small Monday habit. Art takes a few minutes to read the public notices, especially the ones written in a hurry.
personality: Is a careful borrower and a reckless lender. Things leave this person's house with elaborate instructions and very little expectation of ever coming back.
family: Elena Mehta is Art’s half-sibling. Art brings the paper and a pen. Elena decides what stays off the paper. They have helped each other make decisions that were far easier to discuss once the figures could be moved around. The decisions themselves still belong to the person asking. Asked about *The trust with a typo*, Elena says, “I endowed the second scholarship only after I heard her laugh at the error.”
connections: Alim Ward. They both owe a child an honest account of why adults became so invested in a yellow bicycle.

name: Toby Lin
voice: I docked the courier for arriving late. His customer had watched the entire mix-up. I restored the fee and put a blank line beside the automatic lateness code.
agenda: To restore the courier's pay and hear the next late driver's account.
appearance: Toby has thick, tightly coiled hair, a scattering of freckles across the bridge of the nose, and a favorite piece of clothing, a pale blue work shirt. It usually goes with a pocket notebook shaped by years of sitting on it. When somebody else has the floor, Toby grins on one side while the eyes stay serious.
life: Toby's drivers measure his decisions against a clock they cannot see. He used to think lateness was the only fair measure because everyone got the same seconds. He is discovering what a second costs a courier with a bad hip. On Monday, near Maré Coffee, Toby likes the table where people coming off shift stop checking the time.
personality: Toby is kind in very practical ways and prickly about being thanked in public. Toby loves being recognized by the people who notice what happens after the guests have left.

name: Anton Dove
voice: Window seven is the first place I saw the sea after I moved here. I timed the empty corridor with my watch and asked the patient what counted as sunrise to her.
agenda: To work out a clear route to window seven before sunrise.
appearance: Anton has auburn hair cut square at the nape, a deep crease beside the mouth when smiling, and a favorite piece of clothing, a moss-green cardigan. It usually goes with a pressed flower kept in the clear back of a phone case. When somebody else has the floor, Anton listens with the head tilted a little to the left.
life: Anton knows which ward windows fog first and which patients would rather see streetlights than the sea. His eldest boy thinks he pushes beds for a living. Both descriptions are accurate, which pleases him. Wednesday often includes a stop at the corner outside Coastal Barber, where Anton usually checks the board before the regulars give a more colorful account of the news.
personality: Anton takes a rejection personally for a day and analytically on the second morning. Anton can be generous with a rival once the first night's sleep has intervened.
family: Bruna Morse is Anton’s half-sibling. Anton asks before bringing somebody along. Bruna can always ask for five minutes alone. It keeps a conversation between two people from unexpectedly turning into a family committee. Asked about *Nine unpaid hours*, Bruna says, “I ran payroll. I warned management on Wednesday and told the crews on Friday.”
connections: Lois Fell (ward colleague). The porter knows this window. The chaplain is discovering how much of the morning that knowledge can hold.

reactions.situation: A relative wants the sunrise streamed to a phone
reactions.response: Anton asks the patient whether they want a camera in this particular morning.
reactions.asWritten: A relative wants the sunrise streamed to a phone. Anton asks the patient whether they want a camera in this particular morning.

reactions.response: Anton suggests breakfast together and lets the offer rest until another day.
reactions.asWritten: A neighbor offers to pay for a favor that was meant kindly. Anton suggests breakfast together and lets the offer rest until another day.

reactions.situation: If someone else wins the opportunity
reactions.response: Anton turns up the next morning with the one piece of advice that would have helped either of them.
reactions.asWritten: If someone else wins the opportunity, Anton turns up the next morning with the one piece of advice that would have helped either of them.

name: Nessa Wren
voice: I promised her we'd try. I kept saying try because of the time I promised my father a trip he never got to make. This time I told the family exactly when to arrive.
agenda: To let the patient decide how far to go on the morning.
appearance: Nessa has short sandy hair and a marked widow's peak, a scattering of freckles across the bridge of the nose, and a favorite piece of clothing, a sand-colored linen shirt. It usually goes with a pen clipped inside the neckline. When somebody else has the floor, Nessa grins on one side while the eyes stay serious.
life: Nessa used to promise impossible comforts to people she loved. In nursing school she learned precise language. Her hard days are the ones when precision starts sounding to a family like indifference. On Thursday, near the corner by Juniper Tailor, Nessa looks at the things people actually bring in for repair before looking in the display window.
personality: Nessa admires skill and distrusts the idea that skill gives anyone permission to be rude. Nessa learns fastest from somebody willing to show how they made a mistake.
family: Marc Ramos is Nessa’s cousin’s child. Nessa makes room at the table. Marc brings whatever was actually growing or affordable that week. The meal sometimes produces a solution. Even when it does not, everyone goes away knowing what the other household is up against. Asked about *Saturday keys*, Marc says, “I delivered the missing keys on my skates. It's the first time a grown-up thanked me for using the pavement.”
connections: Cass Pennell. They ask the patient what colors and timing she would want her family to remember.

reactions.situation: A different patient needs the same porter
reactions.response: Nessa checks which part can wait and makes sure the other patient hears about the delay.
reactions.asWritten: A different patient needs the same porter. Nessa checks which part can wait and makes sure the other patient hears about the delay.

reactions.situation: Smoke appears under a shop door after closing
reactions.response: Nessa gets the people at the next doorway away from the smoke and asks a bystander to make the call.

name: Mika Drew
home: the western blocks near Ferry Street Rooms
voice: The rail squealed when I moved it and woke three people. I returned after supper to quiet the other rails too. A day's work can have a different ending from the one on the invoice.
agenda: To quiet the rails on the adjoining beds before the next night shift.
appearance: Mika is easy to recognize by short black hair swept back and an aquiline nose and a square chin. Usually dressed in an old plum windbreaker with a pen clipped inside the neckline, Mika presses the lips together to keep a smile in when listening.
life: Mika charges hospital jobs by the rail and domestic jobs by the hour. A squeak at night feels very different in those two accounts. Mika is collecting real complaints before bidding for the next ward contract. Wednesday often includes a stop at the public end of the South Shore boardwalk, where Mika checks the shade on the benches before deciding how long to stay.
personality: Mika has a strong competitive streak and a very soft spot for the person finishing last. A prize tastes better when everybody had enough time to enter.
family: Greta Hassan is Mika’s second cousin. Mika saves a place. Greta chooses whether to use it. The invitation means something because declining it has never ended the friendship between their households. Asked about *The returned daughter*, Greta says, “I am the half sister born later. Today's visit is the first time anyone explained the family photograph with a cut edge.”
connections: Bea Rial. The last obstacles between the bed and the view are a sticky rail and a pane with an old handprint.

reactions.situation: A relative wants the sunrise streamed to a phone
reactions.response: Mika asks the patient whether they want a camera in this particular morning.
reactions.asWritten: A relative wants the sunrise streamed to a phone. Mika asks the patient whether they want a camera in this particular morning.

reactions.situation: A stranger offers money to cut ahead of an exhausted neighbor
reactions.response: Mika tells the stranger when the next opening is, then stays with the neighbor until their turn comes.
reactions.asWritten: A stranger offers money to cut ahead of an exhausted neighbor. Mika tells the stranger when the next opening is, then stays with the neighbor until their turn comes.

reactions.situation: If accused of favoritism
reactions.response: Mika explains exactly what help was offered and offers the same practical help to the accuser.
reactions.asWritten: If accused of favoritism, Mika explains exactly what help was offered and offers the same practical help to the accuser.

name: Gita Moss
voice: I delivered yellow roses to the wrong bed here once. The woman asked to keep them. Today I stood back until someone told me whose view I might be blocking.
agenda: To bring flowers to the bedside without taking anybody's view.
appearance: Gita is easy to recognize by a blunt cut just below the ears and a broad nose and a deep dimple on one cheek. Usually dressed in a soft blue checked shirt with a stitched row of blue crosses along an old repair, Gita squares up pieces of paper while thinking when listening.
life: Gita learned to wait outside a room until someone made eye contact after walking into a family quarrel carrying congratulations. Her whole flower business depends on reading a doorway in time. Thursday often includes a stop at Ferris Deli, where Gita asks for the end slice and listens to the names the counter workers use for regulars.
personality: Gita reads little signals of discomfort very accurately and has an unfortunate habit of overruling people for their own good. The friends who say stop are the ones Gita trusts most.
family: Cian Khan is Gita’s younger relative by marriage. Gita picks the meeting place. Cian sets the time to leave. It lets them stay close without turning a family visit into the loss of an entire day. They have both had stretches when that distinction mattered. Asked about *Salt in the pockets*, Cian says, “I wanted a scientific name for every crystal until the dockers started giving me better names.”
connections: Anwar Fen. Flowers and toast have to reach the same bedside without getting in anybody's sight line.

reactions.situation: A different patient needs the same porter
reactions.response: Gita checks which part can wait and makes sure the other patient hears about the delay.
reactions.asWritten: A different patient needs the same porter. Gita checks which part can wait and makes sure the other patient hears about the delay.

reactions.situation: An argument on the pavement makes a bystander feel unsafe
reactions.response: Gita walks with the bystander to a staffed doorway and checks whether they want someone called.
reactions.asWritten: An argument on the pavement makes a bystander feel unsafe. Gita walks with the bystander to a staffed doorway and checks whether they want someone called.

reactions.situation: If told to back off
reactions.response: Gita does so immediately and stays available at a distance the other person chooses.
reactions.asWritten: If told to back off, Gita does so immediately and stays available at a distance the other person chooses.

name: Remy Stowe
voice: Those eight minutes belonged to a patient waiting for a scan. I phoned him before moving the slot. He asked if we could send him a picture of what he'd bought.
agenda: To get the waiting scan patient an answer about the changed time.
appearance: Remy has auburn hair cut square at the nape, fine brows over wide-set eyes, and a favorite piece of clothing, a rust-colored canvas coat. It usually goes with a braided bracelet with a single wooden bead. When somebody else has the floor, Remy turns fully toward the person speaking.
life: Remy once shuffled appointments to free a consultant's afternoon and left six patients waiting in gowns. He now writes the name of the person giving up time beside the name of the person gaining it. Wednesday often includes a stop at the entrance to the Wash House, where Remy stops for local notices even on a day without a load to wash.
personality: Remy has a quick wit and an equally quick sense of shame. A joke is often Remy's way of finding out whether a room is friendly enough for a serious question.
family: Elise Kapoor is Remy’s stepsibling. Remy keeps the photographs. Elise knows which ones can be shared. They enjoy remembering people in public and also know what it feels like to have a private afternoon turned into an anecdote for strangers. Asked about *The spare spectacles*, Elise says, “I drew the scene instead of spelling it. The witness moved the desk six inches on paper.”
connections: Ilan Peretz. They are the two people who can get the displaced scan patient his picture and his new time.

reactions.situation: A relative wants the sunrise streamed to a phone
reactions.response: Remy asks the patient whether they want a camera in this particular morning.
reactions.asWritten: A relative wants the sunrise streamed to a phone. Remy asks the patient whether they want a camera in this particular morning.

reactions.situation: A power cut leaves two neighbors waiting on the stairs
reactions.response: Remy stays where both neighbors can hear a familiar voice and gets news from the caretaker.
reactions.asWritten: A power cut leaves two neighbors waiting on the stairs. Remy stays where both neighbors can hear a familiar voice and gets news from the caretaker.

reactions.situation: If the joke lands badly
reactions.response: Remy seeks out the person it hurt before telling anybody why it was supposed to be funny.
reactions.asWritten: If the joke lands badly, Remy seeks out the person it hurt before telling anybody why it was supposed to be funny.

performance.situation: A relative wants the sunrise streamed to a phone

name: Bea Rial
home: the western blocks near Ferry Street Rooms
voice: You can see an old handprint when the sun catches that pane. My daughter left it on a visit years ago. I cleaned the rest and asked the patient whether she minded the hand.
agenda: To leave or remove the little handprint according to the patient's wishes.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a cropped bottle-green coat and a pair of reading glasses in a cloth sleeve. Bea has one cheek that creases before the other, with a cropped cut that shows the shape of the ears. Bea draws breath as if to speak and lets someone else go first during a conversation.
life: Bea has cleaned most city landmarks without ever being invited to an opening. She likes the ward because somebody always notices when the sea suddenly becomes clearer. Saturday often includes a stop at Ferris Deli, where Bea asks for the end slice and listens to the names the counter workers use for regulars.
personality: Bea listens for the familiar version of a story and then for the one detail that changes it. Friends bring problems here when they want to be heard twice.
family: Denise Ho is Bea’s half-sibling. Bea makes the call. Denise is free to hang up first. Some of their best calls last less than a minute. A change of tone is sometimes all the news either one needs. Asked about *The late crossing*, Denise says, “I lost my license and kept quiet. I contribute by watching the driver's children for the round trip.”
connections: Mika Drew. The last obstacles between the bed and the view are a sticky rail and a pane with an old handprint.

reactions.situation: A different patient needs the same porter
reactions.response: Bea checks which part can wait and makes sure the other patient hears about the delay.
reactions.asWritten: A different patient needs the same porter. Bea checks which part can wait and makes sure the other patient hears about the delay.

reactions.situation: The last bus leaves while an elderly stranger is still crossing toward it
reactions.response: Bea offers to walk to the next staffed place together, at the stranger's pace, to ask about another ride.
reactions.asWritten: The last bus leaves while an elderly stranger is still crossing toward it. Bea offers to walk to the next staffed place together, at the stranger's pace, to ask about another ride.

reactions.situation: When a second witness disagrees
reactions.response: Bea keeps the accounts separate until the witnesses have had a chance to meet.
reactions.asWritten: When a second witness disagrees, Bea keeps the accounts separate until the witnesses have had a chance to meet.

performance.situation: A different patient needs the same porter
