name: Cass Pennell
voice: She used her breath to name the colors instead of answering my questions. I wrote them down in order for her granddaughter. It's the only clinical note I've ever copied in orange pencil.
agenda: To pass the sequence of colors to the granddaughter in the patient's own words.
appearance: Cass has thick, tightly coiled hair, full cheeks and a mouth that pulls slightly to one side, and a favorite piece of clothing, a cream pullover. It usually goes with a little coil of soft measuring tape. When somebody else has the floor, Cass folds a paper napkin into quarters without noticing.
life: Cass keeps a collection of patient descriptions of breath, from tight shirts to small rooms. Those ordinary comparisons have done more for her bedside manner than any of her examination answers. Thursday often includes a stop at Ferris Deli, where Cass asks for the end slice and listens to the names the counter workers use for regulars.
personality: Cass talks very little about private fear and recognizes it quickly in strangers. Offering a choice of seats is one of Cass's ways of saying that it is all right to leave.
family: Zachary Teo is Cass’s cousin. Cass leaves the first voice message. Zachary calls back when there is finally a little privacy. In their family a missed ring can mean a bus, a customer, a sleeping child or a bad hour. Neither treats it as an answer in itself. Asked about *The crane shadow*, Zachary says, “I drew the wrong crane in my design portfolio.”
connections: Nessa Wren. They ask the patient what colors and timing she would want her family to remember.

reactions.situation: A relative wants the sunrise streamed to a phone
reactions.response: Cass asks the patient whether they want a camera in this particular morning.
reactions.asWritten: A relative wants the sunrise streamed to a phone. Cass asks the patient whether they want a camera in this particular morning.

reactions.situation: A traveler asks for the last seat at the bus stop
reactions.response: Cass asks the person already using it whether they can comfortably stand, rather than presuming who needs it most.
reactions.asWritten: A traveler asks for the last seat at the bus stop. Cass asks the person already using it whether they can comfortably stand, rather than presuming who needs it most.

reactions.situation: When pressed to explain someone else's silence
reactions.response: Cass says only what happened and lets the absent person keep their reasons.
reactions.asWritten: When pressed to explain someone else's silence, Cass says only what happened and lets the absent person keep their reasons.

performance.situation: A relative wants the sunrise streamed to a phone
performance.response: Cass asks the patient whether they want a camera in this particular morning.

name: Anwar Fen
voice: I brought breakfast in a cup because her hands shook. She wanted to smell toast. I burned a corner the way my mother used to and let it cool on the sill.
agenda: To make a hospital breakfast smell recognizably like the patient's kitchen.
appearance: Away from the heat of the kitchen, look for a sand-colored linen shirt and a knotted piece of sail thread on a key ring. Anwar has a heart-shaped face and prominent ears, with gray hair trimmed very close behind the ears. Anwar grins on one side while the eyes stay serious during a conversation.
life: Anwar makes twelve kinds of toast from the same tin loaf. It is the job he kept after the hotel laid off cooks with better certificates. He has no ambition to serve important people unless they are hungry. Tuesday often includes a stop at the corner by Juniper Tailor, where Anwar looks at the things people actually bring in for repair before looking in the display window.
personality: Anwar prefers exact instructions at work and pleasant surprises at home. The two standards occasionally collide, especially when a relative thinks dropping by counts as notice.
family: Briar Mann is Anwar’s cousin. Anwar chooses the familiar route. Briar can stop the walk at any corner. Walking side by side makes it easier to disagree without turning each disagreement into a contest. Asked about *Hem by hem*, Briar says, “I moved the seam that once hid a pregnancy.”
connections: Gita Moss. Flowers and toast have to reach the same bedside without getting in anybody's sight line.

reactions.situation: A different patient needs the same porter
reactions.response: Anwar checks which part can wait and makes sure the other patient hears about the delay.
reactions.asWritten: A different patient needs the same porter. Anwar checks which part can wait and makes sure the other patient hears about the delay.

reactions.situation: A neighbor offers to pay for a favor that was meant kindly
reactions.response: Anwar accepts a small agreed amount if paying lets the neighbor keep their pride.
reactions.asWritten: A neighbor offers to pay for a favor that was meant kindly. Anwar accepts a small agreed amount if paying lets the neighbor keep their pride.

reactions.situation: When a visitor arrives unexpectedly
reactions.response: Anwar clears one chair and says honestly how long the visit can last.
reactions.asWritten: When a visitor arrives unexpectedly, Anwar clears one chair and says honestly how long the visit can last.

performance.situation: A different patient needs the same porter
performance.response: Anwar checks which part can wait and makes sure the other patient hears about the delay.

name: Lois Fell
voice: I had a reading ready. At the window she asked me to tell her the names of the ships. I didn't know any and had to let the porter be the expert.
agenda: To learn the names of the ships in time for the next good morning.
appearance: Lois is easy to recognize by a soft fringe that falls across one eyebrow and a crooked front tooth visible when laughing. Usually dressed in a pale blue work shirt with a seam let out by a narrow strip of contrasting fabric, Lois touches a knuckle to the chin when searching for a word when listening.
life: Lois trained to fill silences on radio before she became a chaplain. At the hospital the hardest part of the job has been learning to let somebody else's unsteady voice finish a sentence. Thursday often includes a stop at the foot of Harbor Viaduct, where Lois pauses where the machinery overhead makes two people stand close enough to hear each other.
personality: Lois never tires of being shown how somebody makes a living. Lois can ask an expert question of a craftsperson and still mishandle a simple emotional cue from a friend.
family: Cory Mann is Lois’s cousin. Lois brings the paper and a pen. Cory decides what stays off the paper. They have helped each other make decisions that were far easier to discuss once the figures could be moved around. The decisions themselves still belong to the person asking. Asked about *The savings club*, Cory says, “I broke the jar years ago and replaced it with one from my wedding.”
connections: Anton Dove (ward colleague). The porter knows this window. The chaplain is discovering how much of the morning that knowledge can hold.

reactions.situation: A relative wants the sunrise streamed to a phone
reactions.response: Lois asks the patient whether they want a camera in this particular morning.
reactions.asWritten: A relative wants the sunrise streamed to a phone. Lois asks the patient whether they want a camera in this particular morning.

reactions.situation: A diner goes silent in the middle of a noisy family celebration
reactions.response: Lois asks one close relative to check in privately instead of stopping the party for a public inquiry.
reactions.asWritten: A diner goes silent in the middle of a noisy family celebration. Lois asks one close relative to check in privately instead of stopping the party for a public inquiry.

reactions.situation: When a relative hints at needing company
reactions.response: Lois may initially offer a repair, but sits down as soon as the request becomes clear.
reactions.asWritten: When a relative hints at needing company, Lois may initially offer a repair, but sits down as soon as the request becomes clear.

performance.situation: A relative wants the sunrise streamed to a phone
performance.response: Lois asks the patient whether they want a camera in this particular morning.

name: Ilan Peretz
home: the western blocks near Ferry Street Rooms
voice: I took the picture for the man whose scan moved. My own scans always made me feel as if the city had carried on without me. I printed him one with the ward reflected in the glass.
agenda: To put a printed sunrise photograph into the waiting patient's hand.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a cropped bottle-green coat and a stitched row of blue crosses along an old repair. Ilan has a crooked front tooth visible when laughing, with a high puff tied with plain cord. Ilan gives a little nod before asking a hard question during a conversation.
life: Ilan kept counting windows from his treatment bed to remind himself there was a street outside. The liaison badge lets him offer people company in a waiting room he used to know by its ceiling. People around the foot of Harbor Viaduct know Ilan by a small Friday habit. Ilan pauses where the machinery overhead makes two people stand close enough to hear each other.
personality: Ilan often says yes too quickly out of pride in being useful. The people closest to Ilan have learned to ask again the next morning, when the answer is more likely to account for sleep.
family: Dora Iyer is Ilan’s older relative by marriage. Ilan calls about good news first. Dora is allowed to ask about the bad news afterward. Neither wants every family conversation to begin with a bill, a diagnosis or an apology. Asked about *The hair after illness*, Dora says, “I had the same change years ago. I kept my advice in my pocket until she asked.”
connections: Remy Stowe. They are the two people who can get the displaced scan patient his picture and his new time.

reactions.situation: A different patient needs the same porter
reactions.response: Ilan checks which part can wait and makes sure the other patient hears about the delay.
reactions.asWritten: A different patient needs the same porter. Ilan checks which part can wait and makes sure the other patient hears about the delay.

reactions.situation: A coworker arrives late after a night at the hospital
reactions.response: Ilan takes one immediate task off their hands and asks when they want to tell the supervisor.
reactions.asWritten: A coworker arrives late after a night at the hospital. Ilan takes one immediate task off their hands and asks when they want to tell the supervisor.

reactions.situation: When two people ask for the same hour
reactions.response: Ilan rings both of them before quietly counting on somebody else to fill in.
reactions.asWritten: When two people ask for the same hour, Ilan rings both of them before quietly counting on somebody else to fill in.

performance.situation: A different patient needs the same porter
performance.response: Ilan checks which part can wait and makes sure the other patient hears about the delay.

name: Mavis Yeo
voice: I priced the atlas at four dollars before I saw the paste. My parents used to disagree about the name of that street. I pulled the price off and invited them separately to identify it.
agenda: To hear both parents identify the street before committing a label.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a long navy raincoat and a train token tied to a zipper pull. Mavis has two dimples that appear only with a full smile, with a high puff tied with plain cord. Mavis draws breath as if to speak and lets someone else go first during a conversation.
life: Mavis bought the bookshop's old stock, including four boxes nobody had opened in ten years. She pays the rent selling new books and keeps the boxes under her desk for days when rent feels like the entire point. On Wednesday, near Harbour Bakery, Mavis buys one familiar thing and asks who chose the unfamiliar thing in the window.
personality: Mavis feels a room through sound. A door slammed in high spirits can produce the same instant startle as an angry one, and it takes a little while to hear what actually follows.
family: Audrey Mason is Mavis’s cousin. Mavis brings a spare shopping bag. Audrey chooses whether they walk home or sit a while. That small arrangement gives both a reason to see each other on weeks when asking for company outright feels difficult. Asked about *A red mitten*, Audrey says, “I used the mitten to warm the metal armrest for a man in a thin shirt.”
connections: Carl Reeve. The clearing worker brought the atlas to the shop, and the bookseller must now decide what a fair return means. Also in the story is Cal Esmond (research visitor).

reactions.situation: A collector offers cash for the unexamined atlas
reactions.response: Mavis asks the bookseller to put the atlas somewhere safe while its ownership is checked.
reactions.asWritten: A collector offers cash for the unexamined atlas. Mavis asks the bookseller to put the atlas somewhere safe while its ownership is checked.

reactions.situation: Somebody finds a lost wallet outside the bank
reactions.response: Mavis asks the counter staff for a receipt so its return can be traced even after their shift changes.
reactions.asWritten: Somebody finds a lost wallet outside the bank. Mavis asks the counter staff for a receipt so its return can be traced even after their shift changes.

reactions.situation: If an argument gets loud at home
reactions.response: Mavis lowers their own voice and asks for one thought at a time.
reactions.asWritten: If an argument gets loud at home, Mavis lowers their own voice and asks for one thought at a time.

performance.situation: A collector offers cash for the unexamined atlas
performance.response: Mavis asks the bookseller to put the atlas somewhere safe while its ownership is checked.

name: Rene Mott
voice: My hand shook the day I ruined a school register with too much water. I can lift this page, but the paste itself tells us when it was made. I want photographs before anyone reaches for a brush.
agenda: To document both sides of the handmade page before lifting anything.
appearance: Rene is easy to recognize by short, uneven waves that refuse to lie flat and a long face and high cheekbones. Usually dressed in a pale blue work shirt with a partly rubbed-away embroidered initial, Rene takes off the watch before a long conversation when listening.
life: Rene spent a year repairing flood-damaged school papers, most of which nobody famous had touched. He developed a tenderness for cheap glue. It is often the only signature a child leaves on a map. People around the blocks below Foundry Lofts know Rene by a small Monday habit. Rene checks the little hand-lettered notices around Harbour Supply.
personality: Rene treats keeping somebody waiting as a serious discourtesy. This can turn a helpful person into an impatient one when everybody else needs a slower conversation.
family: Charlie Starr is Rene’s cousin. Rene asks before bringing somebody along. Charlie can always ask for five minutes alone. It keeps a conversation between two people from unexpectedly turning into a family committee. Asked about *A room for a father*, Charlie says, “I painted the spare room blue. He called it a color for a nursery and I nearly sent him packing.”
connections: Ona Voss. They compare the age of the paste with the direction of a child's hand stitches.

reactions.situation: A family member disputes the penciled street
reactions.response: Rene marks the disputed piece of street in pencil and keeps the alternative name beside it.
reactions.asWritten: A family member disputes the penciled street. Rene marks the disputed piece of street in pencil and keeps the alternative name beside it.

reactions.situation: A traveler asks for the last seat at the bus stop
reactions.response: Rene gives up their own space if possible and asks the passengers who arrived first to choose what happens next.
reactions.asWritten: A traveler asks for the last seat at the bus stop. Rene gives up their own space if possible and asks the passengers who arrived first to choose what happens next.

reactions.situation: If a frightened person needs longer
reactions.response: Rene changes the plan openly and takes responsibility for the delay.
reactions.asWritten: If a frightened person needs longer, Rene changes the plan openly and takes responsibility for the delay.

performance.situation: A family member disputes the penciled street
performance.response: Rene marks the disputed piece of street in pencil and keeps the alternative name beside it.

name: Elsa Venn
voice: I drove that lane on my first night shift. It dead-ended at a woman selling coffee from a thermos. I'm trying to remember her name before the map gets a label.
agenda: To recover the coffee seller's name while the old route can still be walked.
appearance: Elsa is easy to recognize by a long silver braid and a wide brow and a narrow jaw. Usually dressed in a brown corduroy jacket with a square of clean cloth for polishing smudges, Elsa leans a shoulder against the wall during long conversations when listening.
life: Elsa knows the town by what a passenger might smell with the window open. Street names have changed twice on her old taxi route. The woman with the coffee always stood in the same breeze. People around the blocks below Foundry Lofts know Elsa by a small Saturday habit. Elsa checks the little hand-lettered notices around Harbour Supply.
personality: Elsa is patient with a person learning and fiercely impatient with somebody pretending to know. A half-finished job left where a beginner can see it is an invitation, as far as Elsa is concerned.
family: Patricia Ryan is Elsa’s younger cousin. Elsa makes room at the table. Patricia brings whatever was actually growing or affordable that week. The meal sometimes produces a solution. Even when it does not, everyone goes away knowing what the other household is up against. Asked about *The guarantee*, Patricia says, “I can pay the interest for six months if the family stops calling it a rescue every time we eat.”
connections: Melle Juric. They walk the likely street with somebody who remembers a face more easily than a name.

name: Noam Booth
voice: The blue isn't sea. We used that ink for drains because it was free from the shipyard. I want the caption to say who paid for the original plate.
agenda: To credit the crew that supplied the salvaged blue ink.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a dark green knitted vest and a little coil of soft measuring tape. Noam has a round face with a pronounced chin, with short copper curls. Noam rubs a thumb along the edge of the nearest pocket during a conversation.
life: Noam ran a print studio on discarded industrial ink. A well-funded art school once attributed his distinctive blue to taste. He wants the port cleaners who saved the leftovers to see their part in his work. On Sunday, near the corner by Juniper Tailor, Noam looks at the things people actually bring in for repair before looking in the display window.
personality: Noam loves an audience until a private hurt enters the room. Then the performer disappears and someone very good at getting other people through a door takes over.
family: Daria Singh is Noam’s cousin. Noam saves a place. Daria chooses whether to use it. The invitation means something because declining it has never ended the friendship between their households. Asked about *The widow's razor*, Daria says, “I keep the spare handle. It belonged to a matched pair we bought the day we opened separate shops.”

name: Una Vida
voice: One of my students can read the tiny block letters upside down. He learned setting type. I asked him to teach Thursday's class and chose a seat at the back.
agenda: To give the former typesetter an evening at the front of the class.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a boxy denim jacket and a stitched row of blue crosses along an old repair. Una has a crooked front tooth visible when laughing, with short black hair swept back. Una steadies a cup with both hands while listening during a conversation.
life: Una learned to read at the same table where she now tutors. She deliberately leaves the teacher's chair empty on Thursday evenings so a student with another kind of knowledge can use it first. Monday often includes a stop at the foot of Harbor Viaduct, where Una pauses where the machinery overhead makes two people stand close enough to hear each other.
personality: Una enjoys routines and will defend the right of someone else to break one. As a result, Una is often everyone's favorite cover for a missed morning.
family: Dina Hooper is Una’s half-sibling. Una picks the meeting place. Dina sets the time to leave. It lets them stay close without turning a family visit into the loss of an entire day. name: Carl Reeve
voice: I saved the atlas from the paper skip because its spine matched my coat. Now the family wants it back. I'll tell them where it is once the shop agrees to keep the tracing.
agenda: To return the family's atlas and keep a lawful tracing at the shop.
appearance: Carl is easy to recognize by a high puff tied with plain cord and a strong profile and a little space between the front teeth. life: Carl clears estates for relatives who are sometimes four countries away. He dislikes deciding which ordinary things count as effects. A book with a folded leaf is more difficult than a cabinet of costly china. On Tuesday, near Tideline Market, Carl picks out the bruised fruit first and asks the seller what will ripen by supper.
personality: Carl is cheerful on a bad morning and unexpectedly melancholy after a success. Finishing a hard thing means losing the daily company of the people who worked on it.
family: Lina Barrett is Carl’s cousin raised in the same household. Carl keeps the photographs. Lina knows which ones can be shared. They enjoy remembering people in public and also know what it feels like to have a private afternoon turned into an anecdote for strangers. Asked about *The new language at dinner*, Lina says, “I was ashamed my language sounded provincial when I moved here.”

name: Fara Bloom

She wants the pupils to see the old city in the paintwork without letting visitors turn a working school into a personal museum. Wednesday often includes a stop at Harbour Bakery, where Fara buys one familiar thing and asks who chose the unfamiliar thing in the window.

They have helped each other make decisions that were far easier to discuss once the figures could be moved around. The decisions themselves still belong to the person asking. name: Paz Harrow
voice: My little brother still thinks his castle was disqualified because I didn't like it. I moved the flags to dry ground and asked every builder to walk me to their front door.
agenda: To let every young builder be judged from a reachable patch of sand.
appearance: Paz has a broad nose and a deep dimple on one cheek. Look for short sandy hair and a marked widow's peak. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a plum-colored cardigan with a watch on a cracked leather band. In conversation Paz steadies a cup with both hands while listening.
life: Paz saves a little sand from the first day of each season in old film canisters. Her younger brother considers the collection proof of excessive seriousness. She privately suspects he's right. Sunday often includes a stop at Breakwater Way, where Paz stops on the landward side of the cycle track to watch the first boats turn for home.
personality: Paz often says yes too quickly out of pride in being useful. The people closest to Paz have learned to ask again the next morning, when the answer is more likely to account for sleep.
family: Selena Roberts is Paz’s stepsibling. Paz checks the date twice. Selena brings something that can still be enjoyed tomorrow. Arrangements do change in their family. Taking a delay seriously without treating it as an insult took both of them years. Asked about *A ship without postcards*, Selena says, “I work nights and never see a blue sky here.”
connections: Lia Banks (beach colleague). They move the judging line together and discover there are two different meanings of a reachable castle.

name: Dario Flint
voice: I let children freeze the turrets in my cart. They kept opening the lid and my stock softened. I sold the soft ones cheap and put their names on the receipts as architects.
agenda: To replace the softened stock without charging the children for their turrets.
appearance: Dario has a center part and straight chestnut hair, a round face with a pronounced chin, and a favorite piece of clothing, a cream pullover. It usually goes with one loose pocket corner secured with green thread. When somebody else has the floor, Dario leans a shoulder against the wall during long conversations.
life: Dario's cart is the second business he has owned. The first failed because he never charged friends. He has devised elaborate small jobs children can do in return for treats, a system nobody mistakes for sound accounting. On Sunday, near the public end of the South Shore boardwalk, Dario checks the shade on the benches before deciding how long to stay.
personality: Dario thinks best while walking. Sitting beneath someone's office clock makes Dario sound more certain than they feel, an effect close friends have learned to distrust.
family: Stella Hull is Dario’s second cousin. A relative kept reporting household news on postcards long after everybody could afford to phone. Reading one takes the family back to an ordinary morning rather than a big event. Dario prefers an ordinary request to a grand declaration of affection. Asked about *The sheltered corner*, Stella says, “My wheelchair fits the new turn. I brought the planners cake and asked them to hear the old riders too.”

name: Lia Banks
voice: The judging route crossed a soft patch I knew wouldn't hold a wheel. I borrowed three boards from the marina and made the judges take the long route with everyone else.
agenda: To keep the wheelchair route open through the entire judging session.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a brown corduroy jacket and a square of clean cloth for polishing smudges. Lia has a crooked front tooth visible when laughing, with black hair twisted into a small knot. Lia folds a paper napkin into quarters without noticing during a conversation.
life: Lia learned to read sand density pushing her father's chair. A photograph of an accessible beach usually shows the clean path. She wants people to photograph what happens when the path ends. Sunday often includes a stop at Lighthouse Cove, where Lia takes a few minutes by the low rocks, where conversation sounds different as the tide turns.
personality: Lia treats keeping somebody waiting as a serious discourtesy. This can turn a helpful person into an impatient one when everybody else needs a slower conversation.
family: Clyde Darzi is Lia’s cousin raised in the same household. Lia picks the meeting place. Clyde sets the time to leave. It lets them stay close without turning a family visit into the loss of an entire day. They have both had stretches when that distinction mattered. Asked about *The pawned trumpet*, Clyde says, “I repair brass at night. I can give the player a different instrument but I can't transfer those teeth marks.”
connections: Paz Harrow (beach colleague). They move the judging line together and discover there are two different meanings of a reachable castle.

reactions.situation: The judges ask the fastest builder to speak for everyone
reactions.response: Lia asks each child how they would enter their own castle.
reactions.asWritten: The judges ask the fastest builder to speak for everyone. Lia asks each child how they would enter their own castle.

reactions.situation: A coworker arrives late after a night at the hospital
reactions.response: Lia asks them privately what can be shared about the delay and respects the answer.
reactions.asWritten: A coworker arrives late after a night at the hospital. Lia asks them privately what can be shared about the delay and respects the answer.

reactions.response: Lia changes the plan openly and takes responsibility for the delay.

name: Mona Neri
voice: I donated the prize bucket. The winning child was afraid to come near my white shirt. I sat on the sand with my back to her until she came and filled it herself.
agenda: To let the winning child choose when to collect the bucket.
appearance: Mona has two dimples that appear only with a full smile. Look for black hair twisted into a small knot. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a moss-green cardigan with one loose pocket corner secured with green thread. In conversation Mona rubs a thumb along the edge of the nearest pocket.
life: Mona works with children who are often frightened before they reach her room. On the beach she thought she had left that white-shirt authority behind and was startled to discover how easily it followed her outdoors. On Saturday, near Paper & Pine Books, Mona starts with the handwritten shelf cards and often leaves with a suggestion for somebody else.
personality: Mona is patient with a person learning and fiercely impatient with somebody pretending to know. A half-finished job left where a beginner can see it is an invitation, as far as Mona is concerned.
family: Jo Allard is Mona’s cousin’s child. Mona keeps the photographs. Jo knows which ones can be shared. They enjoy remembering people in public and also know what it feels like to have a private afternoon turned into an anecdote for strangers. Asked about *A house divided kindly*, Jo says, “I am the grandchild who expected to inherit this house.”
connections: Ely Kern. They help small visitors find both a dry towel and an unthreatening way to collect their prize.

reactions.situation: The water reaches a child's castle before judging
reactions.response: Mona gives the builder time to show the judges what the water took.
reactions.asWritten: The water reaches a child's castle before judging. Mona gives the builder time to show the judges what the water took.

reactions.response: Mona tells the first helper what they actually saw and makes room for the rider to answer for themself.
reactions.asWritten: A cyclist goes down in a crowded crossing. Mona tells the first helper what they actually saw and makes room for the rider to answer for themself.

name: Cato Hull
voice: On my break I taught three children how water moves around a pier. Their castle vanished first. They want me back next year to show them how to build the same thing again.
agenda: To return next summer to try a new water channel with the children.
appearance: Cato has a blunt cut just below the ears, fine brows over wide-set eyes, and a favorite piece of clothing, a striped cotton shirt. It usually goes with a fabric zip pull cut from a school scarf. When somebody else has the floor, Cato holds eye contact until the other person has finished.
life: Cato worked boats before learning to swim properly. He dislikes stories that make seafarers sound fearless. Changing currents, failed castles and children's honest questions are more interesting to him than brave poses. Sunday often includes a stop at the steps at Pier Beach, where Cato watches the working part of the waterfront before turning toward the open water.
personality: Cato loves an audience until a private hurt enters the room. Then the performer disappears and someone very good at getting other people through a door takes over.
family: Victor Sun is Cato’s older relative by marriage. Cato makes the call. Victor is free to hang up first. Some of their best calls last less than a minute. A change of tone is sometimes all the news either one needs. Asked about *A wall of birthdays*, Victor says, “I want to measure myself again. Chemotherapy stole a little of my height and a lot of my nerve.”
connections: Aster Loy. One knows where the line should have gone. The other knows how the water reached it anyway.

reactions.situation: The judges ask the fastest builder to speak for everyone
reactions.response: Cato asks each child how they would enter their own castle.
reactions.asWritten: The judges ask the fastest builder to speak for everyone. Cato asks each child how they would enter their own castle.

name: Ada Firth
voice: I found the old finish flag under the new tide. My husband sewed the sleeve on it the year our twins competed. I loaned it for the photo and brought it home.
agenda: To get the family flag home after the closing picture.
appearance: Ada has silver temples and a dark fringe, a wide brow and a narrow jaw, and a favorite piece of clothing, an unlined tan jacket. It usually goes with one loose pocket corner secured with green thread. When somebody else has the floor, Ada raises one eyebrow long before saying yes.
life: Ada associates every beach flag with the summer somebody mended it. She cannot remember who won most years. She can remember whose child was learning to knot a thread when the wind turned. Tuesday often includes a stop at the foot of Harbor Viaduct, where Ada pauses where the machinery overhead makes two people stand close enough to hear each other.
personality: Ada enjoys routines and will defend the right of someone else to break one. As a result, Ada is often everyone's favorite cover for a missed morning.
family: Briar Henry is Ada’s younger relative by marriage. Ada leaves the first voice message. Briar calls back when there is finally a little privacy. In their family a missed ring can mean a bus, a customer, a sleeping child or a bad hour. Neither treats it as an answer in itself. Asked about *The split visit*, Briar says, “I was coming to fix the porch rail and ended up assembling a folding lunch table for three.”
connections: Dario Flint. Turrets from the ice cart and flags from the old competition meet in the families' photograph.

name: Pip Arlen
home: the western blocks near Ferry Street Rooms
voice: I budgeted for one trophy and found myself facing thirty-two mayors of imaginary towns. I paid the photographer for contact sheets and let every mayor sign their own municipal record.
agenda: To give every young mayor a signed copy of a town photograph.
appearance: Pip has a scattering of freckles across the bridge of the nose. Look for a loose dark braid. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a pale blue work shirt with a braided bracelet with a single wooden bead. In conversation Pip counts on the side of one finger where hardly anybody notices.
life: Pip studied accountancy to leave the family souvenir shop and keeps finding ways to spend public budgets on things that fit inside a child's pocket. It is the family habit that proved hardest to leave. Friday often includes a stop at the blocks below Foundry Lofts, where Pip checks the little hand-lettered notices around Harbour Supply.
personality: Pip is cheerful on a bad morning and unexpectedly melancholy after a success. Finishing a hard thing means losing the daily company of the people who worked on it.
family: Taylor Sethi is Pip’s older relative by marriage. Pip chooses the familiar route. Taylor can stop the walk at any corner. Walking side by side makes it easier to disagree without turning each disagreement into a contest. Asked about *The uniform money*, Taylor says, “I wanted to give anonymous money. My niece asked why I was so embarrassed to help someone I knew.”
connections: Nico Salas. They decide what an award ought to recognize after a professional sculptor notices the child's kitchen.

reactions.situation: The judges ask the fastest builder to speak for everyone
reactions.response: Pip asks each child how they would enter their own castle.
reactions.asWritten: The judges ask the fastest builder to speak for everyone. Pip asks each child how they would enter their own castle.

reactions.response: Pip writes down the shift time accurately, then helps them explain the circumstances without having to tell the whole room.
reactions.asWritten: A coworker arrives late after a night at the hospital. Pip writes down the shift time accurately, then helps them explain the circumstances without having to tell the whole room.

reactions.asWritten: When everyone else wants to celebrate immediately, Pip helps set the table, then takes a short turn outside alone.

name: Abel Weaver
voice: My wife left the lamp on for the last nurse walking home from St. Mary. People think it was for me. I'll sell the house if the buyer lets me take the lamp to her sister.
agenda: To deliver the working lamp to his sister-in-law.
appearance: Abel is easy to recognize by soft white hair brushed sideways and a straight nose and deep-set eyes. Usually dressed in an old plum windbreaker with a thin silver ring worn on a cord, Abel gives a little nod before asking a hard question when listening.
life: Abel wired the porch on their first wedding anniversary because he had forgotten to buy a gift. His wife never told the neighbors that part. Losing the house without telling somebody the whole story worries him more than moving. Friday often includes a stop at Harbour Bakery, where Abel buys one familiar thing and asks who chose the unfamiliar thing in the window.
personality: Likes beautiful, unnecessary things and gets cross with people who mistake poverty for a lack of taste. Abel takes longer choosing a cheap birthday card than an expensive coat.
family: Winifred Reese is Abel’s cousin’s child. The family has a birthday plate with a shallow crack. Whoever borrows it is responsible for returning it in person, which has salvaged more than one bad goodbye. Abel insists on washing it by hand. Asked about *Salt in the pockets*, Winifred says, “My mother used to shake out our coats over a blue plate and read the weather in the grains.”
connections: Orla Till (neighbor who works nights). The night route and the porch lamp turn out to have been part of the same marriage without the nurse ever knowing it.

reactions.situation: A buyer offers extra for the porch lamp
reactions.response: Abel asks the owner whether the lamp is even part of the sale before discussing the offer.
reactions.asWritten: A buyer offers extra for the porch lamp. Abel asks the owner whether the lamp is even part of the sale before discussing the offer.

reactions.asWritten: A friend asks for a loan due back before payday. Abel asks which other bill repayment would displace, then offers only what the household can afford to give.

reactions.asWritten: When a relative dismisses a little luxury, Abel asks which ordinary pleasure the relative would give up first.

name: Ruth Eade
voice: I described it as original hardware. When the owner started to cry I crossed the phrase out. I still need the commission to cover my own rent, and I'll earn it with a different sentence.
agenda: To sell the house with terms the owner can sign freely.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a cream pullover and a partly rubbed-away embroidered initial. Ruth has a strong profile and a little space between the front teeth, with a cropped cut that shows the shape of the ears. Ruth counts on the side of one finger where hardly anybody notices during a conversation.
life: Ruth grew up in a house staged for sale every spring. She knows how exhausted a family can become trying to look as if it has never used its own kitchen. She has started scheduling viewings around one untouched family meal. Tuesday often includes a stop at Breakwater Way, where Ruth stops on the landward side of the cycle track to watch the first boats turn for home.
personality: Ruth can be wonderfully decisive about an emergency and maddeningly undecided about a gift. This is because a person can say precisely what hurts and rarely says exactly what they want.
family: Ariel Powell is Ruth’s parent’s cousin. Ruth checks the date twice. Ariel brings something that can still be enjoyed tomorrow. Arrangements do change in their family. Taking a delay seriously without treating it as an insult took both of them years. Asked about *The last home visit*, Ariel says, “I brought sweet tea for years. My oldest client said she'd waited for my last day to admit she liked it bitter.”
connections: Verity Long. The prospective buyer and agent must decide what a lodger means for the old owner's conditions.

reactions.situation: A shift worker turns up after the porch goes dark
reactions.response: Ruth keeps the worker company at the gate and lets the homeowner explain the dark.
reactions.asWritten: A shift worker turns up after the porch goes dark. Ruth keeps the worker company at the gate and lets the homeowner explain the dark.

reactions.situation: Someone begins blaming the youngest worker for a missing item
reactions.response: Ruth brings the worker into the conversation and asks what they remember without feeding them a story.
reactions.asWritten: Someone begins blaming the youngest worker for a missing item. Ruth brings the worker into the conversation and asks what they remember without feeding them a story.

reactions.response: Ruth asks for an afternoon to work out whether accepting it would put someone else in debt.
reactions.asWritten: If a neighbor offers a costly present, Ruth asks for an afternoon to work out whether accepting it would put someone else in debt.

name: Lev Adair
voice: The switch worked. He'd unscrewed the bulb to see who would notice. I recognized the trick because I once did it to my shop sign. I left a spare on his kitchen table.
agenda: To leave a working spare without exposing the owner's private test.
appearance: Lev is easy to recognize by a smooth side part with one rebellious curl and an aquiline nose and a square chin. Usually dressed in a moss-green cardigan with a copper-colored clasp that has been repaired by hand, Lev looks toward the door whenever a name is called when listening.
life: Lev tested signs for a shop chain until it replaced his team. He opened his repair business with one bulb over the door and kept a private count of drivers who slowed down on the first evening. Monday often includes a stop at the corner by Juniper Tailor, where Lev looks at the things people actually bring in for repair before looking in the display window.
personality: Lev can be lavish with time and quite careful with cash. A free afternoon is sometimes the biggest gift Lev can afford to give, and family knows to take it seriously.
family: Logan Calder is Lev’s second cousin. Lev brings a spare shopping bag. Logan chooses whether they walk home or sit a while. That small arrangement gives both a reason to see each other on weeks when asking for company outright feels difficult. Asked about *Five missing lunches*, Logan says, “I changed the roster to save wages. Now I eat alone next to five imaginary people.”
connections: Nabil Reed. They need to open the porch post without destroying the dates hidden behind the wiring.

reactions.situation: A buyer offers extra for the porch lamp
reactions.response: Lev asks the owner whether the lamp is even part of the sale before discussing the offer.
reactions.asWritten: A buyer offers extra for the porch lamp. Lev asks the owner whether the lamp is even part of the sale before discussing the offer.

reactions.response: Lev asks one close relative to check in privately instead of stopping the party for a public inquiry.
reactions.asWritten: A diner goes silent in the middle of a noisy family celebration. Lev asks one close relative to check in privately instead of stopping the party for a public inquiry.

reactions.response: Lev suggests meeting afterward and explains why without asking the others to abandon their plans.
reactions.asWritten: If invited to an expensive outing, Lev suggests meeting afterward and explains why without asking the others to abandon their plans.

name: Orla Till
voice: I used the lamp to know exactly how far I had left to walk. I'm giving him my old pedometer with the count from the gate to my door still taped on its back.
agenda: To let the owner know how far his lamp carried a stranger.
appearance: Out of work clothes, look for a boxy denim jacket and a braided bracelet with a single wooden bead. Orla has a flat bridge to the nose and a mobile brow, with a high puff tied with plain cord. Orla looks toward the door whenever a name is called during a conversation.
life: Orla measures the night shift in the distance between places where somebody knows she's walking home. She never thought the porch owner knew about her. Asking for the pedometer back would be easier than telling him what the light meant. Sunday often includes a stop at Juniper Street, where Orla knows which of the west-side porches has a seat in the shade.
personality: Orla carries anger into a conversation very slowly. Once it arrives, a quiet statement of facts can be considerably harder to sidestep than a shout.
family: Zara Barclay is Orla’s second cousin. Orla asks before bringing somebody along. Zara can always ask for five minutes alone. It keeps a conversation between two people from unexpectedly turning into a family committee. Asked about *A four o'clock kitchen*, Zara says, “I love feeding strangers. I don't want my children to think that's easier than feeding them.”
connections: Abel Weaver (porch owner). The night route and the porch lamp turn out to have been part of the same marriage without the nurse ever knowing it.

reactions.situation: A shift worker turns up after the porch goes dark
reactions.response: Orla keeps the worker company at the gate and lets the homeowner explain the dark.
reactions.asWritten: A shift worker turns up after the porch goes dark. Orla keeps the worker company at the gate and lets the homeowner explain the dark.

reactions.situation: A witness is embarrassed about remembering only a little
reactions.response: Orla writes down their exact words with room left for uncertainty and gives them back to check.
reactions.asWritten: A witness is embarrassed about remembering only a little. Orla writes down their exact words with room left for uncertainty and gives them back to check.

reactions.response: Orla offers to accompany them while they tell the truth.
reactions.asWritten: If a friend asks for a false alibi for an ordinary missed appointment, Orla offers to accompany them while they tell the truth.

name: Verity Long
voice: I can afford the house only with a lodger. The owner asked if that meant strangers all the time. I told him a stranger is how my children got the aunt who raised them.
agenda: To make a fair room offer to a prospective lodger.
appearance: Verity is easy to recognize by a dark undercut with a longer wave on top and fine brows over wide-set eyes. Usually dressed in a sand-colored linen shirt with a thin silver ring worn on a cord, Verity gathers both sleeves neatly before settling in when listening.
life: Verity became a school secretary because records showed her exactly which families needed another reminder before a deadline. In her own divorce she has been much worse at asking people for time. On Tuesday, near the window at Night Shift Donuts, Verity knows when the going-home crowd and the coming-to-work crowd will both be there.
personality: Verity has an appetite for a good argument about little things and works hard to keep a serious disagreement from being turned into entertainment.
family: Ruth Farah is Verity’s cousin raised in the same household. Verity makes room at the table. Ruth brings whatever was actually growing or affordable that week. The meal sometimes produces a solution. Even when it does not, everyone goes away knowing what the other household is up against. Asked about *Laundry for a stranger*, Ruth says, “I built her an iron rest from a broken tile.”
connections: Ruth Eade. The prospective buyer and agent must decide what a lodger means for the old owner's conditions.

reactions.asWritten: A buyer offers extra for the porch lamp. Verity asks the owner whether the lamp is even part of the sale before discussing the offer.

reactions.asWritten: A friend asks for a loan due back before payday. Verity agrees on a sum and a date with the friend in private, keeping the arrangement out of family gossip.

reactions.asWritten: When a private quarrel becomes a public joke, Verity says the plainest truthful thing possible and changes the subject.

name: Gus Lark
home: the streets inland from Pier Beach
voice: I sold the owner two bulbs every winter. He always wrote my name in a little book beside the price. I'd like to borrow the book for the shop's fiftieth birthday.
agenda: To display the bulb ledger alongside a photograph of the old shop sign.
appearance: Gus has tightly curled gray hair, a scattering of freckles across the bridge of the nose, and a favorite piece of clothing, a faded indigo overshirt. It usually goes with a fabric zip pull cut from a school scarf. When somebody else has the floor, Gus squares up pieces of paper while thinking.
life: Gus can remember the size of a light fitting from the way its owner cups both hands. The old ledger interests him because it records his shop under three successive names and never once misspells his. On Tuesday, near Studio Boulevard, Gus waits by the window where the whole crossing can be seen without leaning into the road.
personality: Gus treats a small promise with the gravity others reserve for a contract. This makes Gus lovely to rely on and surprisingly difficult to invite on a whim.
family: Reuben Sawyer is Gus’s cousin. Gus saves a place. Reuben chooses whether to use it. The invitation means something because declining it has never ended the friendship between their households. Asked about *The widow's dividend*, Reuben says, “I want one share for my grandson so somebody younger will keep asking how the rent is set.”
connections: Della Keys. The hardware ledger gives the committee a less costly way to commemorate the lamp than buying it.

reactions.situation: A shift worker turns up after the porch goes dark
reactions.response: Gus keeps the worker company at the gate and lets the homeowner explain the dark.
reactions.asWritten: A shift worker turns up after the porch goes dark. Gus keeps the worker company at the gate and lets the homeowner explain the dark.

reactions.situation: A family supper turns into an argument about old debt
reactions.response: Gus separates the money question from the broken promise and asks which one the family wants to discuss first.
reactions.asWritten: A family supper turns into an argument about old debt. Gus separates the money question from the broken promise and asks which one the family wants to discuss first.

reactions.asWritten: When offered a favor with ambiguous terms, Gus says what can be returned and asks whether that will do.

name: Nabil Reed
voice: We rebuilt the post around that live lamp during a blackout anniversary. I can take it down without losing the pencil dates inside. I want the daughters there when I open it.
agenda: To save the pencil dates when dismantling the porch post.
appearance: Nabil is easy to recognize by black hair twisted into a small knot and a round face with a pronounced chin. Usually dressed in an olive canvas jacket with a folded shopping list secured by a miniature clip, Nabil starts to lift a hand, then waits to be invited to speak when listening.
life: Nabil used to hide dates on roof timbers to prove he'd had a part in a house. Since his daughter started asking about his jobs he has preferred marks that future owners can actually find. People around Ferris Deli know Nabil by a small Saturday habit. Nabil asks for the end slice and listens to the names the counter workers use for regulars.
personality: Nabil is good at starting things, dreadful at waiting for them to take effect. Close family can tell how worried Nabil is by the number of tiny errands suddenly being done.
family: Lou Diaz is Nabil’s cousin raised in the same household. Nabil picks the meeting place. Lou sets the time to leave. It lets them stay close without turning a family visit into the loss of an entire day. They have both had stretches when that distinction mattered. Asked about *A prize nobody entered*, Lou says, “I promised the prize money to a printer before the author answered.”
connections: Lev Adair. They need to open the porch post without destroying the dates hidden behind the wiring.

reactions.situation: A buyer offers extra for the porch lamp
reactions.response: Nabil asks the owner whether the lamp is even part of the sale before discussing the offer.
reactions.asWritten: A buyer offers extra for the porch lamp. Nabil asks the owner whether the lamp is even part of the sale before discussing the offer.

reactions.situation: A colleague says somebody used the wrong name in public
reactions.response: Nabil asks which name they want to hear next time and uses it in the next ordinary introduction.
reactions.asWritten: A colleague says somebody used the wrong name in public. Nabil asks which name they want to hear next time and uses it in the next ordinary introduction.

reactions.asWritten: When asked to wait without intervening, Nabil agrees on a check-in time and keeps busy somewhere out of sight.

name: June Wicks
voice: I thought the dark porch meant he'd died. I left six papers to make sure people would stop. Now he wants me to come in for coffee and explain the headlines to him.
agenda: To read the headlines with the man behind the dark porch.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a mustard canvas overshirt and a partly rubbed-away embroidered initial. June has a broad nose and a deep dimple on one cheek, with a center part and straight chestnut hair. June starts to lift a hand, then waits to be invited to speak during a conversation.
life: June is saving paper-route wages for a secondhand keyboard. She stopped to look at the dark porch on a morning when lateness would cost her the whole route's tip. Thursday often includes a stop at the corner outside Coastal Barber, where June usually checks the board before the regulars give a more colorful account of the news.
personality: June tells a better story in a kitchen than at a microphone. Family members sometimes underestimate how far June will go to back a quiet opinion once it is actually challenged.
family: Eden Sun is June’s older cousin. June keeps the photographs. Eden knows which ones can be shared. voice: I used that lit window in a slide about waste. The night nurse was in the audience and stayed behind. I've asked her to record what the walk sounds like in darkness.

life: Ari's job rewards the number of wasted kilowatts identified in a district. An elderly nurse kept asking where his figures accounted for safe journeys home. On Sunday, near the corner by Juniper Tailor, Ari looks at the things people actually bring in for repair before looking in the display window.
personality: Ari is fond of ambitious ideas and deeply suspicious of grand openings. The question Ari asks at any launch is who has the keys for cleaning up a month later.

name: Della Keys

voice: We offered to buy the lamp as a landmark. He reminded me his wife's sister is still alive. I changed the vote to a travel allowance so he can deliver it himself.
agenda: To pay for the owner's visit to his wife's sister.
appearance: Della has a blunt cut just below the ears, a crooked front tooth visible when laughing, and a favorite piece of clothing, a faded indigo overshirt. It usually goes with a fabric zip pull cut from a school scarf. When somebody else has the floor, Della rubs a thumb along the edge of the nearest pocket.
life: Della is very good at raising money for things a committee can own. Paying for a journey whose only result is seeing a sister again feels uncomfortably difficult to photograph for the annual report. On Friday, near Lighthouse Cove, Della takes a few minutes by the low rocks, where conversation sounds different as the tide turns.
personality: Della is firm about boundaries and unusually forgiving of somebody who admits to crossing one. Demands to act grateful for unwanted help can end a friendship.
family: Ariel Pinto is Della’s half-sibling. Della leaves the first voice message. Ariel calls back when there is finally a little privacy. In their family a missed ring can mean a bus, a customer, a sleeping child or a bad hour. Neither treats it as an answer in itself. Asked about *The new language at dinner*, Ariel says, “I translated our first visit and cried in the lift because he sounded exactly like my late father.”

name: Joss Farin
voice: I made the first one with lemon because my husband hated lemon and wouldn't eat it on the way. Now people leave me notes telling me what their night tasted like. I want to bake one of those notes.
agenda: To turn one customer's description of a hard night into a breakfast flavor.
appearance: Joss has close-cropped dark curls, a long face and high cheekbones, and a favorite piece of clothing, a black overshirt with pearl buttons. It usually goes with one cuff folded back twice. When somebody else has the floor, Joss folds a paper napkin into quarters without noticing.
life: Joss's husband can taste lemon in a room where nobody else smells it. Their marriage runs on such very local bits of expert knowledge. He wants the bakery to know its late customers half as well. Wednesday often includes a stop at the approach to Seabright Court, where Joss likes to watch the beach traffic thin enough for workers going the other way.
personality: Joss keeps other people's confidences so well that friends sometimes mistake discretion for taking sides. Joss wants to be trusted and resents being asked for proof of it.
family: Bianca Breen is Joss’s stepsibling. Joss puts the kettle on. Bianca chooses the music. The cups come out before either brings up the reason for the visit. They trust a difficult conversation more if it has had an ordinary beginning. Asked about *The worker who couldn't read the joke*, Bianca says, “I run the break room. name: Lane Clegg
voice: I cut the gift into four and gave three pieces away. Somebody wrote that I disliked it. I came back with the knife my grandmother used for celebrations and explained what a little can mean.
agenda: To introduce a tasting portion customers can easily divide.
appearance: Lane has auburn hair cut square at the nape, a straight nose and deep-set eyes, and a favorite piece of clothing, a pale blue work shirt. It usually goes with a fabric zip pull cut from a school scarf. When somebody else has the floor, Lane touches a knuckle to the chin when searching for a word.
life: Lane reviews pastries by keeping separate notes on first bite and last bite. Portion sizes took on new meaning after the diabetes diagnosis. Sharing a cake is part pleasure, part calculation, and entirely Lane's business. Monday often includes a stop at the steps at Pier Beach, where Lane watches the working part of the waterfront before turning toward the open water.
personality: Lane always notices who paid for the last round. In a group that can be a kindness or a small tyranny, and Lane is trying to tell the difference before the bill arrives.
family: Miles Sato is Lane’s older relative by marriage. Lane chooses an ordinary story to tell. Miles asks the question the rest of the family avoided. They tend to get further with an important subject when it arrives in the middle of talk about dinner or work. Asked about *School after sixty*, Miles says, “I brought the fountain pen I saved for finishing school.”

name: Drew Milo
voice: I got the first free one and ate it sitting on the loading step. I'd just learned my son was moving out. I've paid for the next man's breakfast every Friday since.
agenda: To keep the Friday breakfast paid ahead for the next tired worker.
appearance: Drew is easy to recognize by black hair twisted into a small knot and heavy brows and an unusually delicate jaw. Usually dressed in a cream pullover with a pen clipped inside the neckline, Drew looks down for a moment before saying something difficult when listening.
life: Drew found the guard work after a restaurant closure and is tired of people describing the empty night as restful. He knows how much company a lighted bakery can provide somebody walking a long round. Monday often includes a stop at the window at Night Shift Donuts, where Drew knows when the going-home crowd and the coming-to-work crowd will both be there.
personality: Drew has a talent for getting adversaries to laugh at exactly the same thing. Drew knows better than to expect the laugh to settle what they are arguing about.
family: Terry Morse is Drew’s second cousin. Drew checks the date twice. Terry brings something that can still be enjoyed tomorrow. Arrangements do change in their family. Taking a delay seriously without treating it as an insult took both of them years. Asked about *The uniform money*, Terry says, “I thought my daughter was being vain about the right shade of skirt until I remembered my first day here.”
connections: Joss Farin. A lemon doughnut passed between their shifts before either knew why the other was awake.

life: Teri still has the envelope containing the first rejection from a packaging firm. She'd printed sample boxes that wasted a strip of card. What an accountant calls waste has often been the part people remember. Tuesday often includes a stop at the public end of the South Shore boardwalk, where Teri checks the shade on the benches before deciding how long to stay.
personality: Teri enjoys bargaining, including over things already settled. It is partly a joke and partly a test of whether the other person feels able to say no.
family: Owen Green is Teri’s cousin. Teri brings a spare shopping bag. Owen chooses whether they walk home or sit a while. That small arrangement gives both a reason to see each other on weeks when asking for company outright feels difficult. Asked about *A summer marriage*, Owen says, “I am their oldest friend. My speech is mostly about the groom's ex and I'm rewriting every line.”

life: Sera spent years recording decisions people never saw because they were working while the meeting took place. The meal sometimes produces a solution. Even when it does not, everyone goes away knowing what the other household is up against. Asked about *The button card*, Tali says, “I recognized the button from my first school blazer and came back with its twin.”

name: Vic Cho
voice: I recorded the crunch for a midnight program and accidentally caught two men making up in the background. I asked them which part I could keep. They chose the silence after it.
agenda: To give the recorded couple a final choice about the broadcast.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a gray fisher's sweater and a folded shopping list secured by a miniature clip. Vic has a deep crease beside the mouth when smiling, with a loose dark braid. Vic folds a paper napkin into quarters without noticing during a conversation.
life: Vic collects sounds at a volume that lets the people producing them hear each other. Some of the best recordings in the cupboard have no permission form. They will stay in the cupboard. personality: Vic admires skill and distrusts the idea that skill gives anyone permission to be rude. Vic learns fastest from somebody willing to show how they made a mistake.
family: Franklin Sun is Vic’s second cousin. Vic saves a place. Franklin chooses whether to use it. The invitation means something because declining it has never ended the friendship between their households. Asked about *The ladder crossing*, Franklin says, “I saw the ladder's shadow stretch across my old playground and asked for a photograph.”

agenda: To bring the baker to a show paid for by the flour route.
appearance: Eli is easy to recognize by a swept fringe and a closely clipped nape and heavy brows and an unusually delicate jaw. life: Eli inherited a flour route and spent six months telling friends it was temporary. Sunday often includes a stop at the entrance to the Wash House, where Eli stops for local notices even on a day without a load to wash.

voice: I get there after every good thing is gone. One morning they wrote my shift time on the lid. I want to learn the name of the person who knew it without asking.
agenda: To thank the person who held breakfast until the street was swept.
appearance: Dina has heavy brows and an unusually delicate jaw. Look for close-cropped dark curls. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is an old plum windbreaker with a small enamel bird on the lapel. In conversation Dina presses the lips together to keep a smile in.
life: Dina sweeps four blocks before dawn and can tell who works late by the things they throw away. Being recognized by a bakery employee without her cart startled her more than being recognized with it. People around the market by Market Flats know Dina by a small Thursday habit. Dina often waits until the delivery baskets are stacked before going in.
personality: Dina reads little signals of discomfort very accurately and has an unfortunate habit of overruling people for their own good. The friends who say stop are the ones Dina trusts most.
family: Ruben Ali is Dina’s younger cousin. Dina keeps the photographs. Ruben knows which ones can be shared. They enjoy remembering people in public and also know what it feels like to have a private afternoon turned into an anecdote for strangers. Asked about *The million-dollar flat*, Ruben says, “I came for a property feature. She introduced me to the fitter who can make the bath usable for another ten years.”

name: Nora Reiss
voice: The bank wants a sales forecast for the spare slot. I've sat through three dawns trying to find a number for it. I'm lending against the dozen and leaving the extra one out.
agenda: To get the loan approved on what a dozen actually earns.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a soft blue checked shirt and a train token tied to a zipper pull. Nora has a softly rounded chin under sharp cheekbones, with short copper curls. Nora steadies a cup with both hands while listening during a conversation.
life: Nora once refused credit to a café that fed late workers for free. The café closed and the workers' lateness rose across the street. She is still working out what a lender should have seen in that sequence. Sunday often includes a stop at the courtyard by Ferry Street Rooms, where Nora prefers the bench where the sound of the shop door reaches before the visitor does.
personality: Nora has a quick wit and an equally quick sense of shame. A joke is often Nora's way of finding out whether a room is friendly enough for a serious question.
family: Geraldine Quintero is Nora’s parent’s cousin. Nora makes the call. Geraldine is free to hang up first. Some of their best calls last less than a minute. A change of tone is sometimes all the news either one needs. Asked about *The spare spectacles*, Geraldine says, “I got my old glasses back and finally read the note I found in their case.”

reactions.asWritten: If the joke lands badly, Nora seeks out the person it hurt before telling anybody why it was supposed to be funny.

name: Suki Mossman
home: the western blocks near Ferry Street Rooms
voice: I knew her husband by the hand he held out for her on our front step. This is her first birthday without him. I saved the untidiest finger for the shade he bought her by mistake.
agenda: To keep the birthday appointment a celebration the client directs.
appearance: Suki has a narrow face with an expressive upper lip. Look for a dark undercut with a longer wave on top. After the last appointment, the familiar outfit is a plum-colored cardigan with a folded shopping list secured by a miniature clip. In conversation Suki looks toward the door whenever a name is called.
life: Suki learned nails on her grandmother's hands, knuckles bent from long hospital shifts. She offers her wrist for clients to lean on and lets them decide when to take their own hand back. People around the courtyard by Ferry Street Rooms know Suki by a small Saturday habit. Suki prefers the bench where the sound of the shop door reaches before the visitor does.
personality: Suki never tires of being shown how somebody makes a living. Suki can ask an expert question of a craftsperson and still mishandle a simple emotional cue from a friend.
family: Layla March is Suki’s second cousin. Suki offers the first invitation. Layla gets to change the plan. They learned that a promise to visit is easier to keep when changing a time does not count as letting down the whole family. Asked about *A dance for two fathers*, Layla says, “I am the other father who didn't get invited.”
connections: Fay March (birthday customer). The birthday woman has trusted these hands with every difficult appointment since her husband died.

reactions.situation: A birthday guest starts rearranging other people's colors

reactions.asWritten: A birthday guest starts rearranging other people's colors. Suki asks the birthday client whether she wants the colors moved.

name: Fay March
voice: I am the birthday girl. Everybody has taken to speaking softly around me. I asked for ten colors because I wanted to hear them quarrel over something cheerful.
agenda: To hear her friends argue and laugh over the ten colors.
appearance: Fay has a softly rounded chin under sharp cheekbones. Look for silver temples and a dark fringe. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a mustard canvas overshirt with a printed handkerchief folded into the pocket. In conversation Fay looks at people's hands before looking at what they carry.
life: Fay sewed wedding dresses for women who had opinions and mothers who had more. She trained herself to hear the quietest voice in the fitting room. Now that family speaks softly around her she would rather they raise a cheerful racket. People around the window at Night Shift Donuts know Fay by a small Monday habit. Fay knows when the going-home crowd and the coming-to-work crowd will both be there.
personality: Fay often says yes too quickly out of pride in being useful. The people closest to Fay have learned to ask again the next morning, when the answer is more likely to account for sleep.
family: Ivy Perreault is Fay’s younger relative by marriage. Fay puts the kettle on. Ivy chooses the music. The cups come out before either brings up the reason for the visit. They trust a difficult conversation more if it has had an ordinary beginning. Asked about *The second dog*, Ivy says, “I took the first report and wrote brown. The little girl gave me nine different browns to choose from.”
connections: Suki Mossman (longtime nail technician). The birthday woman has trusted these hands with every difficult appointment since her husband died.

reactions.asWritten: A witness is embarrassed about remembering only a little. Fay writes down their exact words with room left for uncertainty and gives them back to check.

reactions.asWritten: When two people ask for the same hour, Fay rings both of them before quietly counting on somebody else to fill in.

name: Imri Black
voice: I chose clear and got laughed at until I showed them the gold thread underneath. It came off my first uniform. I'd like her to see I'm ready for a chair of my own.
agenda: To win an independent chair with a design the birthday client likes.
appearance: After the last appointment, look for a sand-colored linen shirt and a pressed flower kept in the clear back of a phone case. Imri has a small notch in the left eyebrow, with thick, tightly coiled hair. Imri presses the lips together to keep a smile in during a conversation.
life: Imri has superb steady hands and still has trouble telling a customer that an idea won't work. Clear varnish over a gold thread is an argument made with the hands before having to make it aloud. Thursday often includes a stop at Ferris Deli, where Imri asks for the end slice and listens to the names the counter workers use for regulars.
personality: Imri thinks best while walking. Sitting beneath someone's office clock makes Imri sound more certain than they feel, an effect close friends have learned to distrust.
family: Harley Hooper is Imri’s cousin. Imri chooses an ordinary story to tell. Harley asks the question the rest of the family avoided. They tend to get further with an important subject when it arrives in the middle of talk about dinner or work. Asked about *The tide clock*, Harley says, “I want two clocks on the wall so workers with ferry connections can actually make them.”
connections: Pari Zed. Clear varnish and a wrongly mixed red give them an unexpected argument about who gets to name a color.

reactions.situation: A birthday guest starts rearranging other people's colors
reactions.response: Imri asks the birthday client whether she wants the colors moved.
reactions.asWritten: A birthday guest starts rearranging other people's colors. Imri asks the birthday client whether she wants the colors moved.

reactions.situation: A coworker arrives late after a night at the hospital
reactions.response: Imri asks them privately what can be shared about the delay and respects the answer.
reactions.asWritten: A coworker arrives late after a night at the hospital. Imri asks them privately what can be shared about the delay and respects the answer.

reactions.situation: When family demands an immediate answer
reactions.response: Imri asks them to walk to the corner together and listen until the corner comes.
reactions.asWritten: When family demands an immediate answer, Imri asks them to walk to the corner together and listen until the corner comes.

name: Pari Zed
home: the blocks north of the port
voice: I made the wrong red three summers ago. She wore it to her anniversary dinner anyway. I'm bringing the original sample and letting her name it.
agenda: To let the customer give the difficult red its permanent salon name.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a long navy raincoat and a folded shopping list secured by a miniature clip. Pari has a long face and high cheekbones, with thick, tightly coiled hair. Pari starts to lift a hand, then waits to be invited to speak during a conversation.
life: Pari mixes shade samples by the salon window because half the colors fashionable under the lamp look dead outdoors. An odd red taught her to let a client name what went wrong before trying to repair it. Sunday often includes a stop at Tideline Market, where Pari picks out the bruised fruit first and asks the seller what will ripen by supper.
personality: Pari gets protective of anybody who comes into a meeting unprepared. Pari privately wishes people would notice the amount of preparation behind this apparent ease.
family: Teresa Ellis is Pari’s second cousin. Pari checks the date twice. Teresa brings something that can still be enjoyed tomorrow. Arrangements do change in their family. Taking a delay seriously without treating it as an insult took both of them years. Asked about *Salt in the pockets*, Teresa says, “I wanted to return every coat to the right worker.”
connections: Imri Black. Clear varnish and a wrongly mixed red give them an unexpected argument about who gets to name a color.

reactions.situation: The birthday woman asks for five minutes by herself

reactions.asWritten: The birthday woman asks for five minutes by herself. Pari lets the room empty and puts the next invitation in her hands.

reactions.response: Pari writes down the shift time accurately, then helps them explain the circumstances without having to tell the whole room.
reactions.asWritten: A coworker arrives late after a night at the hospital. Pari writes down the shift time accurately, then helps them explain the circumstances without having to tell the whole room.

reactions.situation: If a colleague lies to save face
reactions.response: Pari offers one private chance to correct it before the next conversation.

name: Greta Falk
voice: I was halfway through arranging the colors into a gradient when she caught me. My own wedding is in two months. I'm letting my sisters pick their dresses.
agenda: To get through her own wedding without arranging everyone's clothes.
appearance: Greta has full cheeks and a mouth that pulls slightly to one side. Look for a long plait tucked inside the collar. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a cropped bottle-green coat with one cuff folded back twice. In conversation Greta folds a paper napkin into quarters without noticing.
life: Greta has put on more elaborate weddings than she can afford for herself. Her sisters have seen her change a table plan during dessert. Letting them surprise her about clothes is a considerable gamble. Thursday often includes a stop at the blocks below Foundry Lofts, where Greta checks the little hand-lettered notices around Harbour Supply.
personality: Greta uses precise names for tools and very approximate names for feelings. People who know Greta well listen to what gets repaired after a difficult conversation.
family: Denise Zhou is Greta’s older cousin. Greta brings a spare shopping bag. Denise chooses whether they walk home or sit a while. That small arrangement gives both a reason to see each other on weeks when asking for company outright feels difficult. Asked about *Two names on the chart*, Denise says, “I built the paper index and recognized my teenage handwriting.”
connections: Remi Ash. One wants an elegant arrangement. The other wants the birthday guest to enjoy a wonderfully rude shade name.

reactions.situation: A birthday guest starts rearranging other people's colors
reactions.response: Greta asks the birthday client whether she wants the colors moved.
reactions.asWritten: A birthday guest starts rearranging other people's colors. Greta asks the birthday client whether she wants the colors moved.

reactions.response: Greta moves the onlookers' bags out of the way, asks the rider what hurts, and asks one named bystander to call for help.
reactions.asWritten: A cyclist goes down in a crowded crossing. Greta moves the onlookers' bags out of the way, asks the rider what hurts, and asks one named bystander to call for help.

reactions.situation: After a family quarrel
reactions.response: Greta brings back the borrowed thing in good condition and tries the conversation again without an audience.
reactions.asWritten: After a family quarrel, Greta brings back the borrowed thing in good condition and tries the conversation again without an audience.
