name: Lark Kane
voice: I picked a green that flashes under stage light because I watch hands for a living. I've invited her to stand in the front row and conduct the warmup with those fingers.
agenda: To give the birthday client control of the warmup at one dance class.
appearance: Lark is easy to recognize by a cropped cut that shows the shape of the ears and a straight nose and deep-set eyes. Usually dressed in a cream pullover with a fabric zip pull cut from a school scarf, Lark gives a little nod before asking a hard question when listening.
life: Lark ran a children's dance class with the music turned off so the pupils would watch each other breathe. Parents called it silence. The children remember how noisy ten pairs of socks could be on a clean floor. Thursday often includes a stop at the window at Night Shift Donuts, where Lark knows when the going-home crowd and the coming-to-work crowd will both be there.
personality: Lark feels a room through sound. A door slammed in high spirits can produce the same instant startle as an angry one, and it takes a little while to hear what actually follows.
family: Beatrice Su is Lark’s older cousin. Lark asks before bringing somebody along. Beatrice can always ask for five minutes alone. It keeps a conversation between two people from unexpectedly turning into a family committee. Asked about *The boy on the corner*, Beatrice says, “I used to buy from the boy's dad. I'm offering childcare and he has good reason to check on me first.”
connections: Liv Oren. Conducting with ten bright fingers gives the photographer a way of taking the picture without posing the hands.

reactions.situation: The birthday woman asks for five minutes by herself
reactions.response: Lark lets the room empty and puts the next invitation in her hands.
reactions.asWritten: The birthday woman asks for five minutes by herself. Lark lets the room empty and puts the next invitation in her hands.

reactions.situation: Somebody finds a lost wallet outside the bank
reactions.response: Lark asks the counter staff for a receipt so its return can be traced even after their shift changes.
reactions.asWritten: Somebody finds a lost wallet outside the bank. Lark asks the counter staff for a receipt so its return can be traced even after their shift changes.

reactions.situation: If an argument gets loud at home
reactions.response: Lark lowers their own voice and asks for one thought at a time.
reactions.asWritten: If an argument gets loud at home, Lark lowers their own voice and asks for one thought at a time.

name: Remi Ash
voice: Our yellow has a vulgar stock name. My grandmother hated being told what words she could say. I whispered it to the birthday girl and she made me say it louder.
agenda: To let the woman enjoy the yellow's outrageous name in company.
appearance: Remi has a smooth side part with one rebellious curl, a straight nose and deep-set eyes, and a favorite piece of clothing, a long navy raincoat. It usually goes with a printed handkerchief folded into the pocket. When somebody else has the floor, Remi gives a little nod before asking a hard question.
life: Remi learned color names in a trade catalogue and swear words from the customers misreading them. Sending the birthday woman into helpless laughter was the first sales demonstration that made the whole shop sit down. Sunday often includes a stop at Harbour Bakery, where Remi buys one familiar thing and asks who chose the unfamiliar thing in the window.
personality: Remi treats keeping somebody waiting as a serious discourtesy. This can turn a helpful person into an impatient one when everybody else needs a slower conversation.
family: Salma Hayward is Remi’s older relative by marriage. Remi makes room at the table. Salma brings whatever was actually growing or affordable that week. The meal sometimes produces a solution. Even when it does not, everyone goes away knowing what the other household is up against. Asked about *The crash anniversary*, Salma says, “I lost a brother somewhere else. I sent one note to the family and left my phone number off it.”
connections: Greta Falk. One wants an elegant arrangement. The other wants the birthday guest to enjoy a wonderfully rude shade name.

reactions.situation: A birthday guest starts rearranging other people's colors
reactions.response: Remi asks the birthday client whether she wants the colors moved.
reactions.asWritten: A birthday guest starts rearranging other people's colors. Remi asks the birthday client whether she wants the colors moved.

reactions.situation: Someone offers a cash reward for naming a rumored culprit
reactions.response: Remi checks privately on the person being talked about and offers to accompany a real witness who wants to speak.
reactions.asWritten: Someone offers a cash reward for naming a rumored culprit. Remi checks privately on the person being talked about and offers to accompany a real witness who wants to speak.

reactions.situation: If a frightened person needs longer
reactions.response: Remi changes the plan openly and takes responsibility for the delay.
reactions.asWritten: If a frightened person needs longer, Remi changes the plan openly and takes responsibility for the delay.

name: Galen Howe
voice: We used to compete for the same corner lease. I chose the blue that is still on my shopfront. I'll lend her the folding chair my first customers sat in for the group picture.
agenda: To bring the original barber chair over for the birthday portrait.
appearance: After the last appointment, look for a washed violet jersey and one loose pocket corner secured with green thread. Galen has two dimples that appear only with a full smile, with a blunt cut just below the ears. Galen touches a knuckle to the chin when searching for a word during a conversation.
life: Galen's father had one barber chair and a cash tin that also paid the household bills. Losing the corner lease hurt more than he has admitted to the salon next door. Lending the first chair is a manageable beginning. People around the public end of the South Shore boardwalk know Galen by a small Thursday habit. Galen checks the shade on the benches before deciding how long to stay.
personality: Galen is patient with a person learning and fiercely impatient with somebody pretending to know. A half-finished job left where a beginner can see it is an invitation, as far as Galen is concerned.
family: Jean Shen is Galen’s cousin raised in the same household. Galen saves a place. Jean chooses whether to use it. The invitation means something because declining it has never ended the friendship between their households. Asked about *Salt in the pockets*, Jean says, “I took a photograph because it looked like our street under the one snowfall I remember.”
connections: Marta Ely. The borrowed barber chair goes into a room whose rent will have to be negotiated tomorrow.

reactions.situation: The birthday woman asks for five minutes by herself
reactions.response: Galen lets the room empty and puts the next invitation in her hands.
reactions.asWritten: The birthday woman asks for five minutes by herself. Galen lets the room empty and puts the next invitation in her hands.

reactions.response: Galen asks who can manage the stairs and who would rather wait by the landing, without attempting a move on their behalf.
reactions.asWritten: A power cut leaves two neighbors waiting on the stairs. Galen asks who can manage the stairs and who would rather wait by the landing, without attempting a move on their behalf.

reactions.situation: When someone invents an answer
reactions.response: Galen asks them to try it in front of the person who will have to live with it.
reactions.asWritten: When someone invents an answer, Galen asks them to try it in front of the person who will have to live with it.

name: Liv Oren
voice: I kept trying to pose the hands until she grabbed the kettle. That's the picture I'm giving her. You can see all ten colors and exactly who still pours the tea.
agenda: To deliver the candid kettle picture with the clients' agreement.
appearance: Liv is easy to recognize by close-cropped dark curls and a softly rounded chin under sharp cheekbones. Usually dressed in a washed violet jersey with a train token tied to a zipper pull, Liv leans a shoulder against the wall during long conversations when listening.
life: Liv learned photography at events where bridesmaids spent hours arranging pictures the guests had already taken. She has developed a liking for hands that are carrying, pouring, buttoning or busy enough to forget her. People around the steps at Pier Beach know Liv by a small Saturday habit. Liv watches the working part of the waterfront before turning toward the open water.
personality: Liv loves an audience until a private hurt enters the room. Then the performer disappears and someone very good at getting other people through a door takes over.
family: Frankie Armas is Liv’s younger cousin. After a relative came home with a walker, everyone offered errands and nobody remembered the threshold. The two of them still measure doors before offering a room to anyone. Liv notices the physical difficulty first. Asked about *A dance for two fathers*, Frankie says, “I used to think my family was embarrassing.”
connections: Lark Kane. Conducting with ten bright fingers gives the photographer a way of taking the picture without posing the hands.

reactions.situation: A birthday guest starts rearranging other people's colors
reactions.response: Liv asks the birthday client whether she wants the colors moved.
reactions.asWritten: A birthday guest starts rearranging other people's colors. Liv asks the birthday client whether she wants the colors moved.

reactions.response: Liv lets the child choose whether to stand by the door or sit beside the window while another adult gets help.
reactions.asWritten: A frightened child is waiting outside a shuttered shop. Liv lets the child choose whether to stand by the door or sit beside the window while another adult gets help.

reactions.situation: If a stranger asks to hear a private story
reactions.response: Liv offers one about their own embarrassment instead.
reactions.asWritten: If a stranger asks to hear a private story, Liv offers one about their own embarrassment instead.

name: Marta Ely
voice: I came to talk about the rent and found myself holding a tiny bottle of mauve. I came back the next morning with the figures. She deserved one evening without them.
agenda: To bring the rent figures back on a day that belongs to business.
appearance: Marta has a softly rounded chin under sharp cheekbones. Look for silver temples and a dark fringe. After the last appointment, the familiar outfit is a striped cotton shirt with a copper-colored clasp that has been repaired by hand. In conversation Marta steadies a cup with both hands while listening.
life: Marta owns the salon walls after a long career maintaining other people's properties. She still sees a repair bill behind every pretty display. The birthday client is unusually good at making her see the display as well. Sunday often includes a stop at the blocks below Foundry Lofts, where Marta checks the little hand-lettered notices around Harbour Supply.
personality: Marta enjoys routines and will defend the right of someone else to break one. As a result, Marta is often everyone's favorite cover for a missed morning.
family: Terry March is Marta’s younger relative by marriage. Marta keeps the photographs. Terry knows which ones can be shared. They enjoy remembering people in public and also know what it feels like to have a private afternoon turned into an anecdote for strangers. Asked about *The driving lesson fund*, Terry says, “I have a wealthy dad. The teacher asked me how many free practice hours he gave me before I called my pass hard-earned.”
connections: Galen Howe. The borrowed barber chair goes into a room whose rent will have to be negotiated tomorrow.

reactions.situation: The birthday woman asks for five minutes by herself
reactions.response: Marta lets the room empty and puts the next invitation in her hands.
reactions.asWritten: The birthday woman asks for five minutes by herself. Marta lets the room empty and puts the next invitation in her hands.

reactions.situation: A customer is short at the till while a queue forms
reactions.response: Marta keeps the customer's place while they check the amount and gets the impatient people talking about something else.
reactions.asWritten: A customer is short at the till while a queue forms. Marta keeps the customer's place while they check the amount and gets the impatient people talking about something else.

reactions.situation: If a family plan changes at the door
reactions.response: Marta keeps a place for the late person without making the others postpone their meal.
reactions.asWritten: If a family plan changes at the door, Marta keeps a place for the late person without making the others postpone their meal.

name: Saul Rosner
home: the blocks north of the port
voice: I can name the color of each light with my eyes closed. My daughter says this is exactly the trouble. I want to be the one who hands the keys across.
agenda: To decide where and when to hand the car keys across.
appearance: Saul has a scattering of freckles across the bridge of the nose. Look for tightly curled gray hair. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is an olive canvas jacket with a seam let out by a narrow strip of contrasting fabric. In conversation Saul squares up pieces of paper while thinking. Saul still wears the soft peaked cap that kept sunlight off the cab mirror.
life: Saul gave up taking fares on stormy evenings long before he gave up driving. His family interpreted each little concession as a promise of a larger one. This time he wants the decision remembered as his own. Wednesday often includes a stop at the public road outside the Port of Asphalt, where Saul can recognize shift change by the lull between two groups of walkers.
personality: Saul is kind in very practical ways and prickly about being thanked in public. Saul loves being recognized by the people who notice what happens after the guests have left.
family: Hamish Baxter is Saul’s younger cousin. Saul remembers the birthdays. Hamish asks what the birthday guest would like this year. A present that was perfect at sixteen may be completely wrong at forty. They take the trouble of finding out. Asked about *A play in a pocket*, Hamish says, “I had ten lines. The listener cried after the first two and asked if we could wait.”
connections: Pam Ravel (former driving pupil). They change places in the cab for a final ride over a route both know by smell.

reactions.situation: A relative asks to keep the driver's keys in secret
reactions.response: Saul asks Saul when he wants to hand over the keys.
reactions.asWritten: A relative asks to keep the driver's keys in secret. Saul asks Saul when he wants to hand over the keys.

reactions.situation: An unfamiliar person asks for directions but cannot read the street signs
reactions.response: Saul draws the route by its turns and entrances and has the person show which turn comes first.
reactions.asWritten: An unfamiliar person asks for directions but cannot read the street signs. Saul draws the route by its turns and entrances and has the person show which turn comes first.

reactions.situation: If somebody calls for applause
reactions.response: Saul gives the credit to a specific helper and slips out before the photograph.
reactions.asWritten: If somebody calls for applause, Saul gives the credit to a specific helper and slips out before the photograph.

performance.situation: A relative asks to keep the driver's keys in secret

name: Andre Bell
occupation: Patrol officer with a traffic assignment
voice: He once drove my mother to hospital and refused a fare. I am the one who took the report on his last scrape. I offered to stand at the crossing in ordinary clothes when he goes by.
agenda: To give Saul the courtesy of an ordinary goodbye at the crossing.
appearance: Andre has a high puff tied with plain cord, a wide brow and a narrow jaw, and a favorite piece of clothing, a cream pullover. It usually goes with a pen clipped inside the neckline. When somebody else has the floor, Andre leans a shoulder against the wall during long conversations.
life: Andre knew half the city's cabs by their rear lights before he could spell dispatch. On a beat he still catches himself thinking of drivers as a boy grateful for a ride instead of an officer obliged to take their details. On Sunday, near Paper & Pine Books, Andre starts with the handwritten shelf cards and often leaves with a suggestion for somebody else.
personality: Likes beautiful, unnecessary things and gets cross with people who mistake poverty for a lack of taste. Andre takes longer choosing a cheap birthday card than an expensive coat.
family: Noel Gomes is Andre’s second cousin. Andre offers the first invitation. Noel gets to change the plan. They learned that a promise to visit is easier to keep when changing a time does not count as letting down the whole family. Asked about *The boy on the corner*, Noel says, “I watched the little brother for grocery money.”
connections: Hana Solberg. One remembers being given a lift in a crisis. The other wants this final lift to include the view at the bridge crest.

reactions.situation: The old driver wants to change the farewell route
reactions.response: Andre takes the changed route seriously and checks who needs to know the new return time.
reactions.asWritten: The old driver wants to change the farewell route. Andre takes the changed route seriously and checks who needs to know the new return time.

reactions.situation: A street musician can't finish a familiar song
reactions.response: Andre offers a little space from the crowd and waits for the player to indicate whether company is wanted.
reactions.asWritten: A street musician can't finish a familiar song. Andre offers a little space from the crowd and waits for the player to indicate whether company is wanted.

reactions.situation: When a relative dismisses a little luxury
reactions.response: Andre asks which ordinary pleasure the relative would give up first.
reactions.asWritten: When a relative dismisses a little luxury, Andre asks which ordinary pleasure the relative would give up first.

performance.situation: The old driver wants to change the farewell route
performance.response: Andre takes the changed route seriously and checks who needs to know the new return time.

name: Mara Tev
voice: His callsign has been on my board since I joined. I took it off and put it on the passenger booking. I want the younger drivers to hear how a farewell sounds on the radio.
agenda: To turn the old callsign into a final passenger booking.
appearance: Mara has a high puff tied with plain cord, a softly rounded chin under sharp cheekbones, and a favorite piece of clothing, a pale blue work shirt. It usually goes with a tiny red thread tied through the lowest buttonhole. When somebody else has the floor, Mara touches a knuckle to the chin when searching for a word.
life: Mara became a dispatcher after losing a thumb joint in a luggage door. She understands the small indignity of a job being taken away piece by piece. Retiring a callsign deserves more ceremony than clearing a screen. Saturday often includes a stop at the foot of Harbor Viaduct, where Mara pauses where the machinery overhead makes two people stand close enough to hear each other.
personality: Mara can be wonderfully decisive about an emergency and maddeningly undecided about a gift. This is because a person can say precisely what hurts and rarely says exactly what they want.
family: Leon White is Mara’s cousin. Mara puts the kettle on. Leon chooses the music. The cups come out before either brings up the reason for the visit. They trust a difficult conversation more if it has had an ordinary beginning. Asked about *The absent signature*, Leon says, “I used the berth for pocket money and never asked whose money repaired it.”
connections: Carmen Saye. The retired callsign gives the payroll worker a way to book a last trip before drawing routes for the bus.

name: Ole Finchley
voice: I watched him do everything right until two things happened together. He asked me to explain that to his grandson without using the word failing. We're making a map of journeys he can still choose.
agenda: To draw a useful travel map with the family.
appearance: Out of work clothes, look for a cropped bottle-green coat and a small enamel bird on the lapel. Ole has full cheeks and a mouth that pulls slightly to one side, with a high puff tied with plain cord. Ole presses the lips together to keep a smile in during a conversation.
life: Ole learned to ask what driving actually buys a patient. For this cabdriver it bought the pleasure of knowing a route better than the passenger. Choosing a journey is one part of that pleasure he can keep. Wednesday often includes a stop at Maré Coffee, where Ole likes the table where people coming off shift stop checking the time.
personality: Ole can be lavish with time and quite careful with cash. A free afternoon is sometimes the biggest gift Ole can afford to give, and family knows to take it seriously.
family: Desmond Baldwin is Ole’s half-sibling. Ole chooses an ordinary story to tell. Desmond asks the question the rest of the family avoided. They tend to get further with an important subject when it arrives in the middle of talk about dinner or work. Asked about *Salt in the pockets*, Desmond says, “I fix linings. Someone had stitched a tiny silk fish beneath the salt line.”
connections: Tait Wynn. They propose letting the former driver teach one lesson about what a license can and can't measure.

name: Pam Ravel
voice: He trained me and never once sat quietly. On the farewell run I made him give me directions right down to the bakery smell at the turn. I want that recording for my first trainee.
agenda: To take a trainee over the route using Saul's recorded directions.
appearance: Pam has heavy brows and an unusually delicate jaw. Look for a blunt cut just below the ears. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a gray fisher's sweater with a partly rubbed-away embroidered initial. In conversation Pam listens with the head tilted a little to the left.
life: Pam drove her first bus in work gloves that Saul had cut short for her fingers. She kept them in the spare-tire compartment after upgrading. Now even Saul wants to know why the gloves still ride along. On Sunday, near the approach to Seabright Court, Pam likes to watch the beach traffic thin enough for workers going the other way.
personality: Pam carries anger into a conversation very slowly. Once it arrives, a quiet statement of facts can be considerably harder to sidestep than a shout.
family: Cassandra Li is Pam’s cousin raised in the same household. Pam checks the date twice. Cassandra brings something that can still be enjoyed tomorrow. Arrangements do change in their family. Taking a delay seriously without treating it as an insult took both of them years. Asked about *Nine unpaid hours*, Cassandra says, “I was paid because I have a permanent badge.”
connections: Saul Rosner (former driving mentor). They change places in the cab for a final ride over a route both know by smell.

name: Len Brune
voice: His old route passes the crooked arrow I painted in my first week. He has teased me about it for years. I've left it until after Friday so he can get in the last word.
agenda: To give the retired cabdriver a last chance to tease about the arrow.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for an unlined tan jacket and a train token tied to a zipper pull. Len has a wide brow and a narrow jaw, with a loose dark braid. Len takes off the watch before a long conversation during a conversation.
life: Len painted the crooked arrow before he discovered how a driver's eye reads a bend. The complaints died down, but the driver who teased him became a customer for life. On Sunday, near the foot of Harbor Viaduct, Len pauses where the machinery overhead makes two people stand close enough to hear each other.
personality: Len has an appetite for a good argument about little things and works hard to keep a serious disagreement from being turned into entertainment.
family: Harley Dias is Len’s younger cousin. Len brings a spare shopping bag. Harley chooses whether they walk home or sit a while. That small arrangement gives both a reason to see each other on weeks when asking for company outright feels difficult. Asked about *A call heard twice*, Harley says, “I called the resident later about paperwork.”
connections: Nita Ellisby. The road arrow and the seat dip are two marks of the same career that these workers can preserve for a little longer.

name: Nita Ellisby
voice: The driver's seat has a dip the shape of his hip. He asked me to fix it for the next owner. I kept a square of the old cover to wrap his spare house key.
agenda: To send Saul home with a house key wrapped in his old seat cover.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a red windbreaker and a folded shopping list secured by a miniature clip. Nita has a straight nose and deep-set eyes, with short sandy hair and a marked widow's peak. Nita gathers both sleeves neatly before settling in during a conversation.
life: Nita's upholstery accounts record seats by chassis number. Her own drawings record them by who sat crooked, leaned forward or drove with a child perched beside them in the old days. People around the entrance to the Wash House know Nita by a small Friday habit. Nita stops for local notices even on a day without a load to wash.
personality: Nita treats a small promise with the gravity others reserve for a contract. This makes Nita lovely to rely on and surprisingly difficult to invite on a whim.
family: Billie Abbott is Nita’s cousin. Nita asks before bringing somebody along. Billie can always ask for five minutes alone. It keeps a conversation between two people from unexpectedly turning into a family committee. Asked about *The empty drum stool*, Billie says, “I booked a full band and got an audience member.”
connections: Len Brune. The road arrow and the seat dip are two marks of the same career that these workers can preserve for a little longer.

name: Carmen Saye
voice: I used to take his cab after my double shifts. Now he needs to know how to change buses with sore knees. I drew the route with every seat and shelter marked.
agenda: To test the marked rest stops with Saul on public transport.
appearance: Carmen has a flat bridge to the nose and a mobile brow. Look for a long plait tucked inside the collar. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a washed violet jersey with a partly rubbed-away embroidered initial. In conversation Carmen holds eye contact until the other person has finished.
life: Carmen's father drove everywhere and never learned the bus colors. After he gave up the car she found that being able to read didn't tell him which shelter got a seat first. She draws maps from the knees up. On Thursday, near the market by Market Flats, Carmen often waits until the delivery baskets are stacked before going in.
personality: Carmen is good at starting things, dreadful at waiting for them to take effect. Close family can tell how worried Carmen is by the number of tiny errands suddenly being done.
family: Gareth Roth is Carmen’s cousin. Carmen makes room at the table. Gareth brings whatever was actually growing or affordable that week. The meal sometimes produces a solution. Even when it does not, everyone goes away knowing what the other household is up against. Asked about *Spin cycle choir*, Gareth says, “My father whistled that song through our last argument.”
connections: Mara Tev. The retired callsign gives the payroll worker a way to book a last trip before drawing routes for the bus.

name: Tait Wynn
voice: He told me to get a proper job when I was a kid. I've asked him to speak to my new drivers about stopping in time. The topic includes careers.
agenda: To bring Saul into a beginner class as someone with knowledge to pass on.
appearance: Tait has a small notch in the left eyebrow. Look for auburn hair cut square at the nape. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a striped cotton shirt with a tiny red thread tied through the lowest buttonhole. In conversation Tait rubs a thumb along the edge of the nearest pocket.
life: Tait made a good driving pupil and a terrible driving examiner. He left examination work because he kept wanting to teach after the clock stopped. Bringing an old driver into the classroom lets him do exactly that. Tuesday often includes a stop at the public end of the South Shore boardwalk, where Tait checks the shade on the benches before deciding how long to stay.
personality: Tait tells a better story in a kitchen than at a microphone. Family members sometimes underestimate how far Tait will go to back a quiet opinion once it is actually challenged.
family: Ruth Spencer is Tait’s cousin raised in the same household. Tait saves a place. Ruth chooses whether to use it. The invitation means something because declining it has never ended the friendship between their households. Asked about *The missing Sunday*, Ruth says, “I saved his old radio when he moved. It still gets the away matches better than my phone.”
connections: Ole Finchley. They propose letting the former driver teach one lesson about what a license can and can't measure.

name: Hana Solberg
voice: The best view is from the passenger side at the crest. He had crossed it eight thousand times without seeing the lighthouse in the mirror. I asked the driver to give him that seat.
agenda: To show the retiring driver the lighthouse in the passenger mirror.
appearance: Hana has dark brown curls cut close behind the ears, a crooked front tooth visible when laughing, and a favorite piece of clothing, a pale blue work shirt. It usually goes with a seam let out by a narrow strip of contrasting fabric. When somebody else has the floor, Hana looks down for a moment before saying something difficult.
life: Hana sees the viaduct from ladders, inspection platforms and the driver's seat. She didn't see the lighthouse in the mirror herself until a maintenance passenger showed it to her on a perfectly uneventful crossing. People around Harbour Bakery know Hana by a small Saturday habit. Hana buys one familiar thing and asks who chose the unfamiliar thing in the window.
personality: Hana is fond of ambitious ideas and deeply suspicious of grand openings. The question Hana asks at any launch is who has the keys for cleaning up a month later.
family: Elizabeth Yoon is Hana’s second cousin. Hana picks the meeting place. Elizabeth sets the time to leave. It lets them stay close without turning a family visit into the loss of an entire day. They have both had stretches when that distinction mattered. Asked about *Saturday keys*, Elizabeth says, “I used to hide my key in a shoe. After losing my home I hate the idea somebody else carries it.”
connections: Andre Bell. One remembers being given a lift in a crisis. The other wants this final lift to include the view at the bridge crest.

name: Cory Halevi
voice: I heard that rattle every time I played the low E. I thought it was my timing. I'm missing the audition to walk the instrument back unless the owner lets me tell the band the whole story.
agenda: To return the bass honestly and still make the audition if possible.
appearance: Outside school, look for a gray fisher's sweater and a comb in a sleeve sewn into the lining. Cory has a broad nose and a deep dimple on one cheek, with a cropped cut that shows the shape of the ears. Cory squares up pieces of paper while thinking during a conversation.
life: Cory borrows instruments because the family's rent changes faster than anyone can save. Learning the sound of a loose screw gave him an accidental education in listening to a thing other people have used. People around the window at Night Shift Donuts know Cory by a small Monday habit. Cory knows when the going-home crowd and the coming-to-work crowd will both be there.
personality: Cory finds it easier to own up to a mistake than to accept praise. The worse the mistake, the more precise the account of exactly when it happened.
family: Gareth Rivera is Cory’s first cousin once removed. Cory calls about good news first. Gareth is allowed to ask about the bad news afterward. Neither wants every family conversation to begin with a bill, a diagnosis or an apology. Asked about *A clean coat for court*, Gareth says, “I cheated him. Borrowing his coat feels worse than borrowing money because I'm wearing his good opinion.”
connections: Stevie Dain (bandmate). The audition only stays open if the drummer can persuade the other musicians to change their order. Also in the story is Iris Cade (music teacher).

name: Iris Cade
home: the blocks north of the port
voice: I lent the bass because I remembered what it was like to be the kid with empty hands. I hadn't asked where the donor got it. I have to make that call in front of the student.
agenda: To identify the lender in front of the pupil who trusted the loan.
appearance: Iris is easy to recognize by a high puff tied with plain cord and a softly rounded chin under sharp cheekbones. Usually dressed in a black overshirt with pearl buttons with one loose pocket corner secured with green thread, Iris steadies a cup with both hands while listening when listening.
life: Iris teaches music to children who rarely control which room they can practice in. Her lending system depends on knowing when an overdue instrument signals a family emergency and when it signals a reluctant pupil. People around Harbour Bakery know Iris by a small Tuesday habit. Iris buys one familiar thing and asks who chose the unfamiliar thing in the window.
personality: Iris keeps other people's confidences so well that friends sometimes mistake discretion for taking sides. Iris wants to be trusted and resents being asked for proof of it.
family: Dana Harris is Iris’s older cousin. The family spent one holiday with the electricity off. They remember who found the candles, who kept the food cold and who cracked the joke that let the children stop being brave. Iris remembers the joke word for word. Asked about *Two names on the chart*, Dana says, “I am the divorced spouse whose surname still turns up.”
connections: Dev Ferris. The teacher and the pawnbroker make the call that establishes whether the old ticket was settled. Also in the story is Cory Halevi (music student).

name: Dev Ferris
home: the streets inland from Pier Beach
voice: Somebody paid the ticket years ago and never removed it. I can tell from the tear. I want the old owner to find that out from me because we parted on ugly terms.
agenda: To show the former owner when the ticket was actually paid.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for an unlined tan jacket and a stitched row of blue crosses along an old repair. Dev has an aquiline nose and a square chin, with thick, tightly coiled hair. Dev grins on one side while the eyes stay serious during a conversation.
life: Dev ran the pawn counter through years when half his customers didn't want to be recognized. Releasing a paid ticket is often easy. Getting someone to believe the account is settled can take another decade. People around the window at Night Shift Donuts know Dev by a small Friday habit. Dev knows when the going-home crowd and the coming-to-work crowd will both be there.
personality: Dev always notices who paid for the last round. In a group that can be a kindness or a small tyranny, and Dev is trying to tell the difference before the bill arrives.
family: Edmund Porter is Dev’s second cousin. Dev offers the first invitation. Edmund gets to change the plan. They learned that a promise to visit is easier to keep when changing a time does not count as letting down the whole family. Asked about *The crane shadow*, Edmund says, “I can no longer climb the cab ladder. I stood inside its shadow and taught a child the controls from memory.”
connections: Iris Cade. The teacher and the pawnbroker make the call that establishes whether the old ticket was settled.

name: Pax Orr
home: the western blocks near Ferry Street Rooms
voice: I recognized the wiring by a burned thumbprint in the solder. My father repaired it the week he left us. I want a photo of the wiring and no part of the ownership argument.
agenda: To take a wiring photograph without claiming the instrument.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a dark green knitted vest and a seam let out by a narrow strip of contrasting fabric. Pax has a scattering of freckles across the bridge of the nose, with auburn hair cut square at the nape. Pax steadies a cup with both hands while listening during a conversation.
life: Pax started doing sound work in order to learn what his absent father knew. The more successful he became, the less sure he was that a repaired instrument could answer any of his original questions. People around Maré Coffee know Pax by a small Tuesday habit. Pax likes the table where people coming off shift stop checking the time.
personality: Pax has a talent for getting adversaries to laugh at exactly the same thing. Pax knows better than to expect the laugh to settle what they are arguing about.
family: Rae Nelson is Pax’s cousin raised in the same household. Pax puts the kettle on. Rae chooses the music. The cups come out before either brings up the reason for the visit. They trust a difficult conversation more if it has had an ordinary beginning. Asked about *The painted footprint*, Rae says, “I wear an artificial foot. I want to trace mine beside it on paper and take the pair home.”
connections: Sid Idris. They discuss how a photograph of a repair could stay with the family while the instrument goes on earning its keep.

name: Stevie Dain
voice: My friend thinks an audition happens once. I got the other acts to agree to go first. Now I have to play quietly enough for the phone to ring.
agenda: To secure a later time in the audition order for the full band.
appearance: Stevie is easy to recognize by a smooth side part with one rebellious curl and a scattering of freckles across the bridge of the nose. Usually dressed in a boxy denim jacket with a comb in a sleeve sewn into the lining, Stevie looks toward the door whenever a name is called when listening.
life: Stevie plays loud enough to feel brave. The quiet measure while the group waits for a call is the one she has practiced least. She wants the other acts to know her for something beyond volume. On Friday, near Lighthouse Cove, Stevie takes a few minutes by the low rocks, where conversation sounds different as the tide turns.
personality: Stevie enjoys bargaining, including over things already settled. It is partly a joke and partly a test of whether the other person feels able to say no.
family: Amos Choi is Stevie’s older cousin. Stevie chooses an ordinary story to tell. Amos asks the question the rest of the family avoided. They tend to get further with an important subject when it arrives in the middle of talk about dinner or work. Asked about *The worker who couldn't read the joke*, Amos says, “I thought the joke was about me because of a word that means something else at home.”
connections: Cory Halevi (bandmate). The audition only stays open if the drummer can persuade the other musicians to change their order.

name: Otis Wolff

agenda: To hear a new player take the old bass through a first audition.

life: Otis toured on other people's buses. He can summon a hundred venues from the smell of varnish and only one wedding he did not attend. A teenager getting an ordinary first audition matters to him for that reason. On Wednesday, near the bank steps, Otis takes a few minutes to read the public notices, especially the ones written in a hurry.
personality: Otis has a long memory for unfair prices and a short one for small insults. Otis can get along perfectly well with an enemy provided the account between them is clear.

name: Nia Oak
home: the western blocks near Ferry Street Rooms
voice: I usually have to tell bands to turn down. I loaned this one the quiet side of the fountain for the phone call. Their drummer came back afterwards and asked how loud the ducks like it.

appearance: Nia is easy to recognize by short copper curls and a wide brow and a narrow jaw. Usually dressed in a plum-colored cardigan with a braided bracelet with a single wooden bead, Nia counts on the side of one finger where hardly anybody notices when listening.

name: Mae Linford
voice: I nearly canceled the extra dinner. Then I remembered the winter my father fed our neighbor off his own plate. I want our form to have a box for someone you'd like to eat with.
agenda: To keep the unregistered diner on the food round.
appearance: Mae has short black hair swept back, a deep crease beside the mouth when smiling, and a favorite piece of clothing, a pale blue work shirt. It usually goes with a stitched row of blue crosses along an old repair. When somebody else has the floor, Mae squares up pieces of paper while thinking. A stub of green shopping pencil lives in the hem of Mae’s apron.
life: Mae can shop for twenty people in less time than her brother takes buying for one. Her father taught her that skill and most of her best recipes. He also taught her how easily efficient shopping can obscure who will share the meal. Sunday often includes a stop at the public road outside the Port of Asphalt, where Mae can recognize shift change by the lull between two groups of walkers.
personality: Mae prefers exact instructions at work and pleasant surprises at home. The two standards occasionally collide, especially when a relative thinks dropping by counts as notice.
family: Miles Price is Mae’s cousin. Mae brings the paper and a pen. Miles decides what stays off the paper. They have helped each other make decisions that were far easier to discuss once the figures could be moved around. The decisions themselves still belong to the person asking. life: Jae's school records say mother absent beside almost every parents' night she remembers. She saw her mother in three homes doing indispensable work on each of those evenings. name: Dane Aubin

appearance: Dane has a flat bridge to the nose and a mobile brow. Look for a blunt cut just below the ears. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a dark green knitted vest with a pressed flower kept in the clear back of a phone case. In conversation Dane squares up pieces of paper while thinking.
life: Dane drives his food bank van by a map in which knocks, bells, side entrances and impatient dogs are more important than road numbers. Monday often includes a stop at the public road outside the Port of Asphalt, where Dane can recognize shift change by the lull between two groups of walkers.

name: Sylvia Moros

name: John Hong

voice: It fit my prosthetic thumb. For five minutes I remembered the weight of holding hands with a child.
agenda: To find a glove that feels as comfortable over the prosthetic thumb.
appearance: Peter has a soft fringe that falls across one eyebrow, a round face with a pronounced chin, and a favorite piece of clothing, a cream pullover. It usually goes with a little coil of soft measuring tape. When somebody else has the floor, Peter squares up pieces of paper while thinking.
life: “My workshop changed when I learned to hold a chisel with my other hand.” On Wednesday, near the crossing outside Verve Nail Studio, Peter notices whose chair is empty and who has stayed talking after an appointment.
personality: Peter talks very little about private fear and recognizes it quickly in strangers. Offering a choice of seats is one of Peter's ways of saying that it is all right to leave.
family: Bruno Gao is Peter’s cousin. Peter leaves the first voice message. Bruno calls back when there is finally a little privacy. In their family a missed ring can mean a bus, a customer, a sleeping child or a bad hour. Neither treats it as an answer in itself. Asked about *The button card*, Bruno says, “I've been sewing pockets shut since my mother began losing coins.”
connections: George Crawford. The property photograph catches the patient discovering that the mitten will fit.

name: Aria Colón
voice: I was sitting in that chair on the worst day of my life. I came back to sit in it on a good day.
agenda: To come back to sit in the chair on a day of good news.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a red windbreaker and a pocket notebook shaped by years of sitting on it. Aria has a heart-shaped face and prominent ears, with soft white hair brushed sideways. Aria turns fully toward the person speaking during a conversation.
life: “I delivered the hospital mail long before I needed a hospital bed.” Monday often includes a stop at the blocks below Foundry Lofts, where Aria checks the little hand-lettered notices around Harbour Supply.
personality: Aria prefers exact instructions at work and pleasant surprises at home. The two standards occasionally collide, especially when a relative thinks dropping by counts as notice.
family: Joanna Zhou is Aria’s younger cousin. Aria chooses the familiar route. Joanna can stop the walk at any corner. Walking side by side makes it easier to disagree without turning each disagreement into a contest. Asked about *A room above the dryers*, Joanna says, “I sat for the first drawing. I love it and absolutely do not want strangers to see it.”
connections: Casey Armas. They choose a time when returning to the chair will feel like an ordinary visit.

name: Astrid Reed
home: the streets inland from Pier Beach
voice: I sorted it into clothing twice. Twice a porter brought it upstairs. I asked whom we were keeping it for.
agenda: To ask the porter which patient is actually waiting for the mitten.
appearance: Astrid has black hair twisted into a small knot, a narrow face with an expressive upper lip, and a favorite piece of clothing, a washed violet jersey. It usually goes with a stitched row of blue crosses along an old repair. When somebody else has the floor, Astrid touches a knuckle to the chin when searching for a word.
life: “I learned the ward numbers by where the trolleys rattled.” People around the blocks below Foundry Lofts know Astrid by a small Sunday habit. Astrid checks the little hand-lettered notices around Harbour Supply.
personality: Astrid never tires of being shown how somebody makes a living. Astrid can ask an expert question of a craftsperson and still mishandle a simple emotional cue from a friend.
family: Sam Lucas is Astrid’s cousin raised in the same household. Astrid brings the paper and a pen. Sam decides what stays off the paper. They have helped each other make decisions that were far easier to discuss once the figures could be moved around. The decisions themselves still belong to the person asking. Asked about *A four o'clock kitchen*, Sam says, “I designed a breakfast box the cook can bring home intact.”
connections: Audrey Mason. They trace how the bit of warm wool reached the coldest waiting-room armrest. Also in the story is Dale Nielsen (ward visitor).

name: Casey Armas
voice: My sister and I disagreed about the color. Our mother called it tomato and settled a thirty-year argument.
agenda: To agree on a family name for the shade of red.
appearance: Casey is easy to recognize by close-cropped dark curls and two dimples that appear only with a full smile. Usually dressed in a cropped bottle-green coat with a train token tied to a zipper pull, Casey takes off the watch before a long conversation when listening.
life: “My first stage job was sewing two mittens into one enormous crab claw.” People around the entrance to the Wash House know Casey by a small Thursday habit. Casey stops for local notices even on a day without a load to wash.
personality: Casey often says yes too quickly out of pride in being useful. The people closest to Casey have learned to ask again the next morning, when the answer is more likely to account for sleep.
family: Remy Monroe is Casey’s half-sibling. Casey calls about good news first. Remy is allowed to ask about the bad news afterward. Neither wants every family conversation to begin with a bill, a diagnosis or an apology. Asked about *One unposted detour*, Remy says, “I stood by the turn and gave directions in three languages.”
connections: Aria Colón. They choose a time when returning to the chair will feel like an ordinary visit.

name: Katherine Lowe
voice: I found the other mitten in the lift. I've put the pair on a cord long enough to cover two chairs.
agenda: To put the two mittens on a cord long enough to share.
appearance: Katherine is easy to recognize by a swept fringe and a closely clipped nape and a strong profile and a little space between the front teeth. Usually dressed in a dark green knitted vest with a thin silver ring worn on a cord, Katherine starts to lift a hand, then waits to be invited to speak when listening.
life: “I repaired a stuck hospital lift on the morning my daughter was born upstairs.” Thursday often includes a stop at the brick passage off the shop row, where Katherine takes the longer way when the smell from the ovens reaches the pavement.
personality: Katherine thinks best while walking. Sitting beneath someone's office clock makes Katherine sound more certain than they feel, an effect close friends have learned to distrust.
family: Noel Holmes is Katherine’s older cousin. Katherine remembers the birthdays. Noel asks what the birthday guest would like this year. A present that was perfect at sixteen may be completely wrong at forty. They take the trouble of finding out. Asked about *The spare spectacles*, Noel says, “I sat beside her because my own witness statement had cost me a friend.”
connections: Allen Marin. They reunite the pair and choose the cord between them.

name: Bess Lai
voice: I wrote the first objection when I was seventeen. I returned to disagree with myself at fifty.
agenda: To answer a teenage argument from the viewpoint of later life.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a mustard canvas overshirt and a fabric zip pull cut from a school scarf. Bess has a broad nose and a deep dimple on one cheek, with a long plait tucked inside the collar. Bess presses the lips together to keep a smile in during a conversation.
life: “I used to defend terrible headlines just because my name was under them.” On Friday, near the approach to Seabright Court, Bess likes to watch the beach traffic thin enough for workers going the other way.
personality: Bess has a talent for getting adversaries to laugh at exactly the same thing. Bess knows better than to expect the laugh to settle what they are arguing about.
family: Eli Brady is Bess’s younger relative by marriage. Bess asks before bringing somebody along. Eli can always ask for five minutes alone. It keeps a conversation between two people from unexpectedly turning into a family committee. Asked about *The dead man's tab*, Eli says, “I forged my father's signature once. Seeing the real one in the book made me own up.”
connections: Miles Price. One writer's teenage opinion survived a divorce in somebody else's carton. Also in the story is Julian Oh (fellow margin writer).

name: Fiona Nord
home: the western blocks near Ferry Street Rooms
voice: I recognized my old teacher by the way she corrects a question mark. I want to answer the one she left me.
agenda: To ask the retired teacher one more question in the margin.
appearance: Fiona is easy to recognize by a blunt cut just below the ears and a deep crease beside the mouth when smiling. Usually dressed in an unlined tan jacket with a printed handkerchief folded into the pocket, Fiona turns fully toward the person speaking when listening.
life: “I learned to shelve books before I learned how late their readers stayed up.” Sunday often includes a stop at the foot of Harbor Viaduct, where Fiona pauses where the machinery overhead makes two people stand close enough to hear each other.
personality: Fiona enjoys bargaining, including over things already settled. It is partly a joke and partly a test of whether the other person feels able to say no.
family: Allen Clay is Fiona’s older cousin. Fiona makes room at the table. Allen brings whatever was actually growing or affordable that week. The meal sometimes produces a solution. Even when it does not, everyone goes away knowing what the other household is up against. Asked about *The gift nobody wants*, Allen says, “I found the father's first rent receipt. It is framed in the corner where he tells young people to start from nothing.”
connections: Carlo Ueda. They turn a long argument in pencil into something an older reader can hear aloud.

name: Malcolm Soto
voice: I thought the pencil insults were aimed at me. Now I'm meeting the reader who was arguing with a fictional husband.
agenda: To read the notes with the person who lived through the same disappointment.
appearance: Malcolm has a crooked front tooth visible when laughing. Look for brown hair pinned away from the temples. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a cream pullover with a pocket notebook shaped by years of sitting on it. In conversation Malcolm draws breath as if to speak and lets someone else go first.
life: “I set tables for strangers while my first marriage turned into notes on the fridge.” Friday often includes a stop at the courtyard by Ferry Street Rooms, where Malcolm prefers the bench where the sound of the shop door reaches before the visitor does.
personality: Malcolm has a long memory for unfair prices and a short one for small insults. Malcolm can get along perfectly well with an enemy provided the account between them is clear.
family: June Brady is Malcolm’s older cousin. Malcolm saves a place. June chooses whether to use it. The invitation means something because declining it has never ended the friendship between their households. Asked about *The crash anniversary*, June says, “I bought the cheapest flowers every Friday.”
connections: Nell Marks. A blunt translation establishes who the old insults actually addressed.

name: Keir Zhou
home: the western blocks near Ferry Street Rooms
voice: I erased three lines before I understood. I've written down the one I remember.
agenda: To restore a penciled sentence before memory loses it.
appearance: Keir has a crooked front tooth visible when laughing. Look for black hair twisted into a small knot. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a brown corduroy jacket with a thin silver ring worn on a cord. In conversation Keir draws small circles on a tabletop while waiting.
life: “Books arrive damp more often from dry flats than owners like to admit.” On Saturday, near the entrance to the Wash House, Keir stops for local notices even on a day without a load to wash.

family: Fernando Arendt is Keir’s older cousin. Keir picks the meeting place. Fernando sets the time to leave. It lets them stay close without turning a family visit into the loss of an entire day. They have both had stretches when that distinction mattered. Asked about *Two names on the chart*, Fernando says, “I kept a clinic letter because the doctor spelled our village correctly.”

name: Miles Price
home: the blocks north of the port
voice: I donated the books during a divorce. My ex kept replying after I'd already moved out.
agenda: To exchange the final set of notes with the former spouse.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a pale blue work shirt and a comb in a sleeve sewn into the lining. Miles has a narrow face with an expressive upper lip, with a soft fringe that falls across one eyebrow. Miles starts to lift a hand, then waits to be invited to speak during a conversation.
life: “My divorce came with six cartons we couldn't bear to divide.” On Monday, near the steps at Pier Beach, Miles watches the working part of the waterfront before turning toward the open water.
personality: Miles admires skill and distrusts the idea that skill gives anyone permission to be rude. Miles learns fastest from somebody willing to show how they made a mistake.
family: Mae Linford is Miles’s cousin. Miles decides what stays off the paper. Mae brings the paper and a pen. They have helped each other make decisions that were far easier to discuss once the figures could be moved around. The decisions themselves still belong to the person asking. Asked about *Two portions*, Mae says, “I nearly canceled the extra dinner. Then I remembered the winter my father fed our neighbor off his own plate.”
connections: Bess Lai. One writer's teenage opinion survived a divorce in somebody else's carton.

name: Carlo Ueda
voice: My dad hated the book but loved the notes. I'm recording just the margins for his walks.
agenda: To record a version for a father who walks while listening.
appearance: Carlo has brown hair pinned away from the temples, a crooked front tooth visible when laughing, and a favorite piece of clothing, a narrow-striped sweater. life: “I recorded my first book in a closet lined with winter coats.” Sunday often includes a stop at Studio Boulevard, where Carlo waits by the window where the whole crossing can be seen without leaning into the road.
personality: Carlo has a strong competitive streak and a very soft spot for the person finishing last. A prize tastes better when everybody had enough time to enter.
family: Daphne Perez is Carlo’s parent’s cousin. Carlo makes the call. Daphne is free to hang up first. Some of their best calls last less than a minute. A change of tone is sometimes all the news either one needs. Asked about *Two birthdays in one ward*, Daphne says, “I dealt the first hand and lost to a woman I used to supervise on night shift.”
connections: Fiona Nord. They turn a long argument in pencil into something an older reader can hear aloud.

personality: Lina reads little signals of discomfort very accurately and has an unfortunate habit of overruling people for their own good. The friends who say stop are the ones Lina trusts most.
family: Shay Stein is Lina’s half-sibling. Lina leaves the first voice message. Shay calls back when there is finally a little privacy. connections: Julian Oh. The missing chapter and the penciled mustache finally find their way into the same conversation.

life: “My least promising student became the adult who recommended my best book.” People around the corner by Juniper Tailor know Georgia by a small Monday habit. Georgia looks at the things people actually bring in for repair before looking in the display window.
personality: Georgia listens for the familiar version of a story and then for the one detail that changes it. Friends bring problems here when they want to be heard twice.
family: Darcy Lewis is Georgia’s stepsibling. In this family birthdays are measured by the breakfast somebody requests. A person choosing plain toast or an elaborate fried meal gets the same fuss for one morning. Georgia gets the guest away from the sink before the dishes need doing. name: Julian Oh
voice: I drew a moustache on the author. Decades later my granddaughter guessed it was me from the shape.
agenda: To give the granddaughter the original mustache drawing.
appearance: Julian is easy to recognize by tightly curled gray hair and a softly rounded chin under sharp cheekbones. Usually dressed in a dark green knitted vest with a partly rubbed-away embroidered initial, Julian raises one eyebrow long before saying yes when listening.
life: “I used to paint fake whiskers on packages with badly printed faces.” People around the downtown fountain know Julian by a small Tuesday habit. Julian keeps a little time free to hear who is playing at the far end of the park.
personality: Julian talks very little about private fear and recognizes it quickly in strangers. Offering a choice of seats is one of Julian's ways of saying that it is all right to leave.
family: Remy Knight is Julian’s first cousin once removed. When a family elder realized nobody could pronounce a friend's original name, she spent a whole evening teaching the table the three difficult sounds. Under pressure the family still says the names slowly. Julian will correct a mistake even if it makes a meal awkward. Asked about *The new language at dinner*, Remy says, “I hold the client's hand at meals. Yesterday he said my name correctly in a language I have never spoken.”
connections: Lina King. The missing chapter and the penciled mustache finally find their way into the same conversation. Also in the story is Bess Lai (fellow margin writer).

name: Teresa Nielsen
voice: My mother called it the kettle. I want to hear her recorded laugh alongside whatever name wins.
agenda: To put the family's kettle name into the choir's programme.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a mustard canvas overshirt and a copper-colored clasp that has been repaired by hand. Teresa has full cheeks and a mouth that pulls slightly to one side, with black hair twisted into a small knot. Teresa listens with the head tilted a little to the left during a conversation.
life: “I sang my first solo behind a curtain because my shoes were borrowed.” Wednesday often includes a stop at the downtown fountain, where Teresa keeps a little time free to hear who is playing at the far end of the park.
personality: Teresa thinks best while walking. Sitting beneath someone's office clock makes Teresa sound more certain than they feel, an effect close friends have learned to distrust.
family: Jasmine Boyd is Teresa’s second cousin. Teresa brings a spare shopping bag. Jasmine chooses whether they walk home or sit a while. That small arrangement gives both a reason to see each other on weeks when asking for company outright feels difficult. Asked about *Care with a clock*, Jasmine says, “I borrowed a stopwatch to prove a point and found our client has a wonderful laugh at minute thirteen.”
connections: Jules Moran. The child's corrected note can sit beside the singer's memory of a mother's laugh.

name: Percy Andrade
voice: I scraped my knee there and have called it a much ruder name since. The choir wants to use it.
agenda: To teach the choir the name adults only use in bad weather.
appearance: Percy has a long face and high cheekbones. Look for salt-and-pepper curls. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a narrow-striped sweater with a narrow brass watch set a little fast. In conversation Percy rubs a thumb along the edge of the nearest pocket.
life: “We worked the night the cove froze at its very edge.” People around the corner by Juniper Tailor know Percy by a small Friday habit. Percy looks at the things people actually bring in for repair before looking in the display window.
personality: Percy gets protective of anybody who comes into a meeting unprepared. Percy privately wishes people would notice the amount of preparation behind this apparent ease.
family: Lola Jeong is Percy’s younger cousin. Percy asks before bringing somebody along. Lola can always ask for five minutes alone. It keeps a conversation between two people from unexpectedly turning into a family committee. Asked about *The button card*, Lola says, “I came to return a button my wife thought unlucky.”
connections: Ruben Keller. They decide which decidedly unofficial name can appear on the choir sheet.

name: Joseph Randall
voice: I can only hear it through my bare heels. I'm asking the singers to take off their shoes.
agenda: To let listeners feel the rock's note through bare feet.
appearance: Joseph has short copper curls, a narrow face with an expressive upper lip, and a favorite piece of clothing, an olive canvas jacket. It usually goes with a pair of reading glasses in a cloth sleeve. When somebody else has the floor, Joseph turns fully toward the person speaking.
life: “I kept rhythm for dancers for years before wearing hearing aids.” On Sunday, near Juniper Street, Joseph knows which of the west-side porches has a seat in the shade.
personality: Joseph uses precise names for tools and very approximate names for feelings. People who know Joseph well listen to what gets repaired after a difficult conversation.
family: Ramon Lloyd is Joseph’s cousin. Joseph makes room at the table. Ramon brings whatever was actually growing or affordable that week. The meal sometimes produces a solution. Even when it does not, everyone goes away knowing what the other household is up against. Asked about *The hair after illness*, Ramon says, “I am a barber losing my own hair. Today the customer told me she could see the shape of my head too.”
connections: Eric Hassan. They compare a sound felt through feet with the old story about a fog bell.

name: Kathleen Lu
home: the western blocks near Ferry Street Rooms
voice: I wrote a tune around the note and discovered it changes when the rock is wet. I need two endings.
agenda: To write separate endings for wet rock and dry rock.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a moss-green cardigan and a pressed flower kept in the clear back of a phone case. Kathleen has two dimples that appear only with a full smile, with dark brown curls cut close behind the ears. Kathleen turns fully toward the person speaking during a conversation.
life: “The first tune I sold was commissioned to advertise a leaking fountain.” Tuesday often includes a stop at Studio Boulevard, where Kathleen waits by the window where the whole crossing can be seen without leaning into the road.
personality: Kathleen feels a room through sound. A door slammed in high spirits can produce the same instant startle as an angry one, and it takes a little while to hear what actually follows.
family: Cal Esmond is Kathleen’s second cousin. Kathleen can stop the walk at any corner. Cal chooses the familiar route. Walking side by side makes it easier to disagree without turning each disagreement into a contest. Asked about *An unfinished atlas*, Cal says, “My funding depends on mapping a vanished street.”
connections: Lina Carey. The changing wet note gives the marker painter another reason to leave the rock alone. Also in the story is Jules Moran (choir accompanist).

name: Ruben Keller
voice: Our boat club wants an official name. I brought nine unofficial ones on a damp receipt.
agenda: To publish the nine old names beside the club's proposal.
appearance: Ruben is easy to recognize by dark brown curls cut close behind the ears and a round face with a pronounced chin. Usually dressed in a washed violet jersey with a knotted piece of sail thread on a key ring, Ruben counts on the side of one finger where hardly anybody notices when listening.
life: “Our club borrowed its first ledger from a defunct fishworkers' society.” Monday often includes a stop at the steps at Pier Beach, where Ruben watches the working part of the waterfront before turning toward the open water.
personality: Ruben treats keeping somebody waiting as a serious discourtesy. This can turn a helpful person into an impatient one when everybody else needs a slower conversation.
family: Sasha Crane is Ruben’s half-sibling. Ruben picks the meeting place. Sasha sets the time to leave. It lets them stay close without turning a family visit into the loss of an entire day. They have both had stretches when that distinction mattered. Asked about *The broken till*, Sasha says, “I wasn't hungry. I joined the queue because it felt like the first real conversation since my divorce.”
connections: Percy Andrade. They decide which decidedly unofficial name can appear on the choir sheet.

name: Lina Carey
voice: I climbed down to paint a marker and saw a crab with eggs. I carried the paint back unopened.
agenda: To keep paint and visitors away from the crab eggs.
appearance: Lina has a blunt cut just below the ears, a round face with a pronounced chin, and a favorite piece of clothing, a mustard canvas overshirt. It usually goes with one loose pocket corner secured with green thread. When somebody else has the floor, Lina folds a paper napkin into quarters without noticing.
life: “I learned to follow crabs under the rocks before I knew the tide had a timetable.” On Friday, near the crossing outside Verve Nail Studio, Lina notices whose chair is empty and who has stayed talking after an appointment.
personality: Lina is patient with a person learning and fiercely impatient with somebody pretending to know. A half-finished job left where a beginner can see it is an invitation, as far as Lina is concerned.
family: Rae Kelly is Lina’s stepsibling. Lina keeps the photographs. Rae knows which ones can be shared. They enjoy remembering people in public and also know what it feels like to have a private afternoon turned into an anecdote for strangers. Asked about *The tide clock*, Rae says, “I left a note saying see you at high. My old friend understood and the receptionist didn't.”

name: Eric Hassan

agenda: To ask the brother how the fog-bell story started.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a brown corduroy jacket and one cuff folded back twice. Eric has one cheek that creases before the other, with black hair twisted into a small knot. Eric counts on the side of one finger where hardly anybody notices during a conversation.
life: “I left garage work for a year to look after my brother's little boys.” Saturday often includes a stop at the market by Market Flats, where Eric often waits until the delivery baskets are stacked before going in.

name: Shay Poole
voice: I sell postcards of a silent cove. I'm leaving a blank on the next edition for people to write what they heard.
agenda: To leave room on a postcard for a visitor's own sound.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a sand-colored linen shirt and a partly rubbed-away embroidered initial. Shay has a softly rounded chin under sharp cheekbones, with silver temples and a dark fringe. Shay listens with the head tilted a little to the left during a conversation.
life: “My first coastal postcard was printed with the lighthouse facing the wrong way.” On Sunday, near the crossing outside Verve Nail Studio, Shay notices whose chair is empty and who has stayed talking after an appointment.
personality: Shay enjoys routines and will defend the right of someone else to break one. As a result, Shay is often everyone's favorite cover for a missed morning.

In their family a missed ring can mean a bus, a customer, a sleeping child or a bad hour. Neither treats it as an answer in itself. Asked about *A borrowed name*, Josephine says, “I thought my mother had told the author our story.”

name: Sam Kaur
home: the blocks north of the port
voice: I miss my first language most when somebody asks me to name a thing. I've invited my aunt to answer.
agenda: To give the aunt the first word when the name goes public.
appearance: Sam has auburn hair cut square at the nape, a deep crease beside the mouth when smiling, and a favorite piece of clothing, a faded indigo overshirt. It usually goes with one cuff folded back twice. When somebody else has the floor, Sam starts to lift a hand, then waits to be invited to speak.
life: “My aunt taught me the inland word for the low-tide smell.” Monday often includes a stop at the bank steps, where Sam takes a few minutes to read the public notices, especially the ones written in a hurry.
personality: Sam is cheerful on a bad morning and unexpectedly melancholy after a success. Finishing a hard thing means losing the daily company of the people who worked on it.
family: Faye Tran is Sam’s older cousin. Sam chooses the familiar route. Faye can stop the walk at any corner. Walking side by side makes it easier to disagree without turning each disagreement into a contest. Asked about *A dance for two fathers*, Faye says, “I trained both men on separate nights. Neither wanted the other to know how scared he was.”

name: Jules Moran
voice: The choir got the note wrong on purpose so the children would correct them. My shy son sang out first.
agenda: To hear the shy child sing the corrected note again.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a cream pullover and a train token tied to a zipper pull. Jules has a broad nose and a deep dimple on one cheek, with thick, tightly coiled hair. Jules gathers both sleeves neatly before settling in during a conversation.
life: “I can coax a note from a child who refuses every ordinary singing exercise.” On Wednesday, near the brick passage off the shop row, Jules takes the longer way when the smell from the ovens reaches the pavement.
personality: Jules finds names easy and faces hard on a crowded street. People who assume they have been snubbed usually get a warmer greeting once they speak.
family: Noor Khan is Jules’s second cousin. Jules brings the paper and a pen. Noor decides what stays off the paper. They have helped each other make decisions that were far easier to discuss once the figures could be moved around. The decisions themselves still belong to the person asking. Asked about *First shift back*, Noor says, “I thought coming back meant picking up exactly where I left.”
connections: Teresa Nielsen. The child's corrected note can sit beside the singer's memory of a mother's laugh. Also in the story is Kathleen Lu (composer).

name: Victor Sun

agenda: To add one present-day height mark after treatment.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a faded indigo overshirt and a narrow brass watch set a little fast. Victor has two dimples that appear only with a full smile, with tightly curled gray hair. Victor leans a shoulder against the wall during long conversations during a conversation.
life: “I used to check other people's scales using a little weight in my pocket.” On Monday, near the brick passage off the shop row, Victor takes the longer way when the smell from the ovens reaches the pavement.

agenda: To give the surviving daughter back the marks she remembers.
appearance: Grey has full cheeks and a mouth that pulls slightly to one side. Look for a neat white crop. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a brown corduroy jacket with one cuff folded back twice. In conversation Grey counts on the side of one finger where hardly anybody notices.
life: “I ran shifts through a winter when the whole family lived in two rooms.” Sunday often includes a stop at the downtown fountain, where Grey keeps a little time free to hear who is playing at the far end of the park.
personality: Grey can be lavish with time and quite careful with cash. A free afternoon is sometimes the biggest gift Grey can afford to give, and family knows to take it seriously.
family: Keiko Ruiz is Grey’s half-sibling. Grey brings a spare shopping bag. Keiko chooses whether they walk home or sit a while. name: Nora Ford

agenda: To reconstruct how high the old shoes made the sister stand.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a mustard canvas overshirt and a pocket notebook shaped by years of sitting on it. Nora has two dimples that appear only with a full smile, with tightly curled gray hair. Nora touches a knuckle to the chin when searching for a word during a conversation.

name: Stefan Tate

family: Jay Montoya is Kira’s younger cousin. Kira offers the first invitation. Jay gets to change the plan. They learned that a promise to visit is easier to keep when changing a time does not count as letting down the whole family. Asked about *The trust with a typo*, Jay says, “I received this scholarship years ago. I returned the typo letter with one month's pay enclosed.”

name: Alicia Nielsen
voice: I stood at the old stop for three days. Each day a different person waited with me so I wouldn't look foolish.
agenda: To make the old stop a useful meeting point during the change.
appearance: Alicia is easy to recognize by brown hair pinned away from the temples and heavy brows and an unusually delicate jaw. Usually dressed in a washed violet jersey with a square of clean cloth for polishing smudges, Alicia folds a paper napkin into quarters without noticing when listening.
life: “I have opened a hotel before sunrise for fourteen winters.” People around the corner by Juniper Tailor know Alicia by a small Wednesday habit. Alicia looks at the things people actually bring in for repair before looking in the display window.
personality: Alicia can be wonderfully decisive about an emergency and maddeningly undecided about a gift. This is because a person can say precisely what hurts and rarely says exactly what they want.
family: Ellen Soto is Alicia’s cousin. Alicia puts the kettle on. Ellen chooses the music. The cups come out before either brings up the reason for the visit. They trust a difficult conversation more if it has had an ordinary beginning. Asked about *An empty dedication*, Ellen says, “I am a character in the book by accident. I want the dedication to leave my real name alone.”

name: Agnes Kahn
home: the western blocks near Ferry Street Rooms
voice: The new stop faces the sun. I can read the driver's lips for the first time.
agenda: To show the planner where the light helps passengers read lips.
appearance: Agnes has short copper curls, a long face and high cheekbones, and a favorite piece of clothing, a narrow-striped sweater. It usually goes with a braided bracelet with a single wooden bead. When somebody else has the floor, Agnes gives a little nod before asking a hard question.
life: “I tested caption screens because broadcasts got my mother's name wrong.” On Monday, near Breakwater Way, Agnes stops on the landward side of the cycle track to watch the first boats turn for home.
personality: Agnes can be lavish with time and quite careful with cash. A free afternoon is sometimes the biggest gift Agnes can afford to give, and family knows to take it seriously.

Asked about *The last home visit*, Geraldine says, “I hate being called darling and will miss the only person who could get away with it.”

name: Nelson Carbone
voice: I sell coffee on the old corner. My first customer is now a pensioner who only comes to talk.
agenda: To give the cart a new set of regulars without losing the old neighbor.
appearance: Nelson has a strong profile and a little space between the front teeth. Look for close-cropped dark curls. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a cream pullover with a braided bracelet with a single wooden bead. In conversation Nelson turns fully toward the person speaking.
life: “My first cart belonged to a sailor who made very weak coffee.” People around the steps at Pier Beach know Nelson by a small Saturday habit. Nelson watches the working part of the waterfront before turning toward the open water.
personality: Nelson carries anger into a conversation very slowly. Once it arrives, a quiet statement of facts can be considerably harder to sidestep than a shout.
family: Samuel Molina is Nelson’s cousin. Nelson checks the date twice. Samuel brings something that can still be enjoyed tomorrow. Arrangements do change in their family. Taking a delay seriously without treating it as an insult took both of them years. Asked about *One clean day*, Samuel says, “I only knew my partner's working voice. I heard his school nickname and he sounded fourteen.”
