name: Ronan Vidal
voice: I sew flag repairs by the piece. All the flags came in at once and I won't have enough for autumn.
agenda: To spread flag repairs far enough to bridge autumn.
appearance: Ronan has a broad nose and a deep dimple on one cheek. Look for a high puff tied with plain cord. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a charcoal zip cardigan with a copper-colored clasp that has been repaired by hand. In conversation Ronan counts on the side of one finger where hardly anybody notices.
life: “I still remember the last flag I mended by candlelight.” People around Paper & Pine Books know Ronan by a small Tuesday habit. Ronan starts with the handwritten shelf cards and often leaves with a suggestion for somebody else.
personality: Ronan is kind in very practical ways and prickly about being thanked in public. Ronan loves being recognized by the people who notice what happens after the guests have left.
family: Martin Arrieta is Ronan’s stepsibling. A relative came back from a stay in hospital to a house rearranged for convenience and walked straight into the new chair. The family learned to ask before making helpful changes. Ronan will change a whole arrangement back without arguing. Asked about *Overdue by a lifetime*, Martin says, “I can tell which classroom it came from by the paste we used in winter.”
connections: Catherine Easton. A traveling summer contract looks different from the viewpoint of the worker who mends its flags.

name: Terry Fong
voice: I took deposits for sunset lessons. I'll refund the ones I can't teach even if it means losing my room.
agenda: To refund buyers whose lessons cannot run.
appearance: Terry has a smooth side part with one rebellious curl, heavy brows and an unusually delicate jaw, and a favorite piece of clothing, a long navy raincoat. It usually goes with a seam let out by a narrow strip of contrasting fabric. When somebody else has the floor, Terry takes off the watch before a long conversation.
life: “I still remember emptying my refund purse for a frightened visitor.” People around the crossing outside Verve Nail Studio know Terry by a small Saturday habit. Terry notices whose chair is empty and who has stayed talking after an appointment.

They learned that a promise to visit is easier to keep when changing a time does not count as letting down the whole family. Asked about *The return of a witness*, Winifred says, “I am her daughter. I know why we moved and I still miss the tree outside my first bedroom.”

name: Tali Peters
voice: I never told my kid this was a seasonal job. I asked him to help me take the name off the hut.
agenda: To tell the child how seasonal work actually ends.
appearance: Tali has fine brows over wide-set eyes. Look for close-cropped dark curls. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is an unlined tan jacket with a copper-colored clasp that has been repaired by hand. In conversation Tali takes off the watch before a long conversation.
life: “I still remember packing equipment while my child counted the cork floats.” On Saturday, near Harbour Bakery, Tali buys one familiar thing and asks who chose the unfamiliar thing in the window.
personality: Tali can be wonderfully decisive about an emergency and maddeningly undecided about a gift. This is because a person can say precisely what hurts and rarely says exactly what they want.
family: Sofia Ghosh is Tali’s stepsibling. Tali puts the kettle on. Sofia chooses the music. The cups come out before either brings up the reason for the visit. They trust a difficult conversation more if it has had an ordinary beginning. Asked about *The release address*, Sofia says, “I got out first and know the shock of seeing new windows in old walls.”
connections: Ida Gupta. The younger workers get a direct explanation about the huts closing before school starts.

name: Ismael Fong

appearance: Ismael has a crooked front tooth visible when laughing. Look for close-cropped dark curls. name: Anita Abbott
voice: I forgave the man years ago. I am still furious about the rent he left and the teeth we couldn't afford to fix.
agenda: To name the old rent loss without forbidding the visit.
appearance: Anita has a high puff tied with plain cord, a narrow face with an expressive upper lip, and a favorite piece of clothing, a striped cotton shirt. life: “I still remember the winter we postponed three dental appointments.” Friday often includes a stop at the courtyard by Ferry Street Rooms, where Anita prefers the bench where the sound of the shop door reaches before the visitor does.
personality: Anita is good at starting things, dreadful at waiting for them to take effect. Close family can tell how worried Anita is by the number of tiny errands suddenly being done.
family: Gilbert Moss is Anita’s half-sibling. Anita picks the meeting place. Gilbert sets the time to leave. It lets them stay close without turning a family visit into the loss of an entire day. They have both had stretches when that distinction mattered. Asked about *One last dress rehearsal*, Gilbert says, “I sewed the costumes. agenda: To let the two branches of the family tell different truths.

life: “I still remember our family's worst quarrel told as a cheerful story elsewhere.” On Tuesday, near Maré Coffee, Lina likes the table where people coming off shift stop checking the time.

name: Charlie Starr
home: the blocks north of the port
voice: I painted the spare room blue. He called it a color for a nursery and I nearly sent him packing.
agenda: To finish the blue room on terms the returning parent can accept.
appearance: Charlie has two dimples that appear only with a full smile. Look for a long plait tucked inside the collar. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a pale blue work shirt with a watch on a cracked leather band. In conversation Charlie takes off the watch before a long conversation.
life: “I still remember painting a bedroom before I knew who its owner was.” People around the downtown fountain know Charlie by a small Monday habit. Charlie keeps a little time free to hear who is playing at the far end of the park.
personality: Charlie is fond of ambitious ideas and deeply suspicious of grand openings. The question Charlie asks at any launch is who has the keys for cleaning up a month later.
family: Rene Mott is Charlie’s cousin. Charlie can always ask for five minutes alone. Rene asks before bringing somebody along. It keeps a conversation between two people from unexpectedly turning into a family committee. Asked about *An unfinished atlas*, Rene says, “My hand shook the day I ruined a school register with too much water.”

name: Adriana Diaz
home: the western blocks near Ferry Street Rooms
voice: I want my grandfather to teach me one thing with his hands before anybody asks him to explain.
agenda: To learn one practical skill from the grandfather.
appearance: Outside school, look for a boxy denim jacket and a little coil of soft measuring tape. Adriana has a flat bridge to the nose and a mobile brow, with thick, tightly coiled hair. Adriana counts on the side of one finger where hardly anybody notices during a conversation.
life: “I still remember learning which grandfather left-handedness came from.” Thursday often includes a stop at the public road outside the Port of Asphalt, where Adriana can recognize shift change by the lull between two groups of walkers.
personality: Adriana is firm about boundaries and unusually forgiving of somebody who admits to crossing one. Demands to act grateful for unwanted help can end a friendship.
family: Oakley Carbone is Adriana’s older cousin. When the family split between two addresses, the good frying pan traveled with whoever cooked Sunday dinner. The pan has outlasted the quarrel and both kitchens. Adriana can see when a sensible rule has become an insult. Asked about *The skipper goes ashore*, Oakley says, “I was her first sailing student. I asked her to teach my child from the pier without pretending she was still on board.”
connections: Ismael Fong (parent). One family welcome has to make room for both an adult's anger and a child's curiosity.

A change of tone is sometimes all the news either one needs. Asked about *A red mitten*, George says, “I photograph everything we find. voice: I know where the teenage boy waited for his father to return. I sat beside him more than once.

appearance: Lorenzo has heavy brows and an unusually delicate jaw. Look for closely cropped salt-and-pepper hair. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a narrow-striped sweater with a little coil of soft measuring tape. In conversation Lorenzo presses the lips together to keep a smile in.

name: Maya Abreu

agenda: To get a real chance to learn the timed oven.
appearance: Maya is easy to recognize by brown hair pinned away from the temples and a heart-shaped face and prominent ears. life: “I still remember setting pastries with the clock taken off our kitchen wall.” On Tuesday, near the steps at Pier Beach, Maya watches the working part of the waterfront before turning toward the open water.
personality: Maya can be wonderfully decisive about an emergency and maddeningly undecided about a gift. This is because a person can say precisely what hurts and rarely says exactly what they want.

name: Kieran Colón
home: the streets inland from Pier Beach
voice: I called the boat by my ex's name. For the first time I would like to change it.
agenda: To choose a workable new boat name.
appearance: Kieran has a softly rounded chin under sharp cheekbones. Look for a soft fringe that falls across one eyebrow. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is an unlined tan jacket with a watch on a cracked leather band. In conversation Kieran holds eye contact until the other person has finished.
life: “I still remember painting over a spouse's nickname with two coats.” Tuesday often includes a stop at the entrance to the Wash House, where Kieran stops for local notices even on a day without a load to wash.
personality: Kieran loves an audience until a private hurt enters the room. Then the performer disappears and someone very good at getting other people through a door takes over.
family: Alexei Walsh is Kieran’s second cousin. Kieran keeps the photographs. Alexei knows which ones can be shared. They enjoy remembering people in public and also know what it feels like to have a private afternoon turned into an anecdote for strangers. Asked about *The return of a witness*, Alexei says, “I am the brother of the convicted man. I can pass her on the pavement without either of us apologizing for existing.”
connections: Dana Wong. A co-owner who refuses to relay messages still has to hear the proposal for a new boat name.

name: Alfred Ross
voice: I am the new partner everyone resents. I would like Sunday morning alone on shore anyway.
agenda: To protect a Sunday ashore.
appearance: Away from the heat of the kitchen, look for a red windbreaker and a pen clipped inside the neckline. Alfred has two dimples that appear only with a full smile, with a swept fringe and a closely clipped nape. Alfred looks down for a moment before saying something difficult during a conversation.
life: “I still remember having Sunday morning temporarily to myself.” People around the downtown fountain know Alfred by a small Thursday habit. Alfred keeps a little time free to hear who is playing at the far end of the park.
personality: Alfred enjoys routines and will defend the right of someone else to break one. As a result, Alfred is often everyone's favorite cover for a missed morning.
family: Daryl Maciel is Alfred’s second cousin. Alfred is free to hang up first. Daryl makes the call. Some of their best calls last less than a minute. A change of tone is sometimes all the news either one needs. Asked about *The fitting mirror*, Daryl says, “I promised to fix the wheel and gave the mirror my son's old skate bearing.”
connections: Lennon Sanders. The teacher and new partner have reasons to preserve a morning at the breakfast table ashore.

name: Kai Mercer
voice: I can translate the questions but not the answer my aunt wants to give. She asked to sit the exam on her own.
agenda: To let the aunt give her own answers.
appearance: Kai is easy to recognize by a swept fringe and a closely clipped nape and a round face with a pronounced chin. Usually dressed in a mustard canvas overshirt with a little coil of soft measuring tape, Kai looks down for a moment before saying something difficult when listening.
life: “I still remember my aunt taking my dictionary away before I could answer for her.” People around the corner by Juniper Tailor know Kai by a small Monday habit. Kai looks at the things people actually bring in for repair before looking in the display window.
personality: Kai has excellent recall for voices and a poor memory for official titles. Someone who waited patiently at a counter years ago is more likely to be remembered than the person in charge.
family: Chris Moss is Kai’s second cousin. Kai knows which ones can be shared. Chris keeps the photographs. They enjoy remembering people in public and also know what it feels like to have a private afternoon turned into an anecdote for strangers. Asked about *The salon on strike*, Chris says, “I make commission on the bottles. I brought my sales figures so the assistants can point to what their work earns.”
connections: Ramona Vargas. A clean practice copy lets an adult decide when a translating relative can help.

name: Rowan Davis
voice: I took the day off with a stomach ache. I don't want my boss at the bank to know I'm learning to read his notices.
agenda: To read workplace notices without disclosing the class.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a boxy denim jacket and a printed handkerchief folded into the pocket. Rowan has two dimples that appear only with a full smile, with a center part and straight chestnut hair. Rowan rubs a thumb along the edge of the nearest pocket during a conversation.
life: “I still remember reading shop notices with the help of the lunchtime cleaner.” Thursday often includes a stop at the crossing outside Verve Nail Studio, where Rowan notices whose chair is empty and who has stayed talking after an appointment.
personality: Rowan finds it easier to own up to a mistake than to accept praise. The worse the mistake, the more precise the account of exactly when it happened.
family: Fiona Mann is Rowan’s half-sibling. Rowan is free to hang up first. Fiona makes the call. Some of their best calls last less than a minute. A change of tone is sometimes all the news either one needs. Asked about *The bitter orange*, Fiona says, “I can't eat the memorial sandwich. I chose the paper it will be wrapped in.”
connections: Yvette Tsai. Two workers using different strategies for private reading try the same examination paper.

name: Maria Tanner
voice: I am the old class bully. The classmate I frightened has chosen the chair opposite me and asked me to keep quiet.
agenda: To respect the former classmate's choice of silence.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a mustard canvas overshirt and a pressed flower kept in the clear back of a phone case. Maria has two dimples that appear only with a full smile, with silvery hair gathered at the nape. Maria listens with the head tilted a little to the left during a conversation.
life: “I still remember a childhood insult surviving into a pension-age dining room.” People around the corner outside Coastal Barber know Maria by a small Sunday habit. Maria usually checks the board before the regulars give a more colorful account of the news.
personality: Maria keeps other people's confidences so well that friends sometimes mistake discretion for taking sides. Maria wants to be trusted and resents being asked for proof of it.
family: Iva Allard is Maria’s second cousin. Maria decides what stays off the paper. Iva brings the paper and a pen. They have helped each other make decisions that were far easier to discuss once the figures could be moved around. The decisions themselves still belong to the person asking. Asked about *The widow's dividend*, Iva says, “I countersigned every page. The one missing signature is from the day I walked out.”
connections: Una Curtis. The lecturer and former bully both return to a room where their previous authority has no special force.

name: Pascal Boone
voice: I brought sandwiches for after, regardless of marks. We all know what a celebration conditional on passing feels like.
agenda: To serve everyone the same lunch after the exam.
appearance: Away from the heat of the kitchen, look for a cream pullover and a pressed flower kept in the clear back of a phone case. Pascal has heavy brows and an unusually delicate jaw, with auburn hair cut square at the nape. Pascal draws small circles on a tabletop while waiting during a conversation.
life: “I still remember cutting sandwiches before anybody knew their marks.” People around Tideline Market know Pascal by a small Friday habit. Pascal picks out the bruised fruit first and asks the seller what will ripen by supper.
personality: Pascal always notices who paid for the last round. In a group that can be a kindness or a small tyranny, and Pascal is trying to tell the difference before the bill arrives.
family: Ismael Gross is Pascal’s cousin. Pascal can stop the walk at any corner. Ismael chooses the familiar route. Walking side by side makes it easier to disagree without turning each disagreement into a contest. Asked about *Level with the window*, Ismael says, “I kept my curtains closed for years. The final empty morning was when I missed strangers most.”
connections: Miles Sato. An old pen and an unconditional lunch make this examination day quite unlike school.

name: Aria Machado
voice: I was that cleaner. I'm still alive and I would like the seat low enough for me to stand up from.
agenda: To sit and stand comfortably at the new bench.
appearance: Aria is easy to recognize by a long silver braid and a broad nose and a deep dimple on one cheek. Usually dressed in a moss-green cardigan with a copper-colored clasp that has been repaired by hand, Aria gathers both sleeves neatly before settling in when listening.
episode: The other side of the cove
life: “I still remember cleaning a beach the day after a public honor nobody invited me to.” On Wednesday, near Paper & Pine Books, Aria starts with the handwritten shelf cards and often leaves with a suggestion for somebody else.
personality: Aria takes a rejection personally for a day and analytically on the second morning. Aria can be generous with a rival once the first night's sleep has intervened.
family: Belinda Lee is Aria’s stepsibling. Aria brings something that can still be enjoyed tomorrow. Belinda checks the date twice. Arrangements do change in their family. Taking a delay seriously without treating it as an insult took both of them years. Asked about *Home with stairs*, Belinda says, “I rented my old flat out too soon after my own illness.”
connections: Daphne Ng. A working cleaner and a millionaire decide what, besides two names, the bench will give its users. Also in the story is Walter Ray (adult child).

name: Daphne Ng
voice: I gave the money after selling my second company. I wanted anonymity until my late partner's name entered the discussion.
agenda: To agree whether the late partner's name should appear.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a washed violet jersey and a seam let out by a narrow strip of contrasting fabric. Daphne has fine brows over wide-set eyes, with silvery hair gathered at the nape. Daphne turns fully toward the person speaking during a conversation.
episode: The other side of the cove
life: “I still remember my first company changing hands under a borrowed umbrella.” On Saturday, near Ferris Deli, Daphne asks for the end slice and listens to the names the counter workers use for regulars.
personality: Daphne admires skill and distrusts the idea that skill gives anyone permission to be rude. Daphne learns fastest from somebody willing to show how they made a mistake.
family: Nathan Neal is Daphne’s cousin’s child. Daphne chooses the music. Nathan puts the kettle on. The cups come out before either brings up the reason for the visit. They trust a difficult conversation more if it has had an ordinary beginning. Asked about *The split visit*, Nathan says, “I stayed for breakfast because the woman always eats faster when she thinks we're in a hurry.”
connections: Aria Machado. A working cleaner and a millionaire decide what, besides two names, the bench will give its users.

name: Peyton Waters
home: the streets inland from Pier Beach
voice: I brought the cleaner a newspaper every summer. She let me use her bucket for the sea glass.
agenda: To return the beach bucket with a picture of its use.
appearance: Peyton has a scattering of freckles across the bridge of the nose. Look for silvery hair gathered at the nape. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a plum-colored cardigan with a square of clean cloth for polishing smudges. In conversation Peyton grins on one side while the eyes stay serious.
episode: The other side of the cove
life: “I still remember delivering a paper to a beach hut that had no number.” People around the courtyard by Ferry Street Rooms know Peyton by a small Sunday habit. Peyton prefers the bench where the sound of the shop door reaches before the visitor does.
personality: Peyton has a strong competitive streak and a very soft spot for the person finishing last. A prize tastes better when everybody had enough time to enter.
family: Hector Clay is Peyton’s stepsibling. Peyton asks what the birthday guest would like this year. Hector remembers the birthdays. A present that was perfect at sixteen may be completely wrong at forty. They take the trouble of finding out. Asked about *The dead man's tab*, Hector says, “He charged me rent for a room he didn't own.”
connections: Warren Ito. The person who used to carry newspapers finds the lettering artist space on the public proof.

name: Walter Ray
voice: I want my mother's work named with her proper job title. The city keeps calling her a volunteer.
agenda: To get the mother's paid work accurately acknowledged.
appearance: Walter has heavy brows and an unusually delicate jaw. Look for auburn hair cut square at the nape. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a faded indigo overshirt with a partly rubbed-away embroidered initial. In conversation Walter squares up pieces of paper while thinking.
episode: The other side of the cove
life: “I still remember hearing rented hands called willing volunteers.” Tuesday often includes a stop at the corner by Juniper Tailor, where Walter looks at the things people actually bring in for repair before looking in the display window.
personality: Walter reads little signals of discomfort very accurately and has an unfortunate habit of overruling people for their own good. The friends who say stop are the ones Walter trusts most.
family: Carlo Gil is Walter’s stepsibling. Walter brings whatever was actually growing or affordable that week. Carlo makes room at the table. The meal sometimes produces a solution. Even when it does not, everyone goes away knowing what the other household is up against. Asked about *Midnight cinnamon*, Carlo says, “I sell cinnamon by weight. I am trying to price the little packets customers buy just to carry home.”

name: Warren Ito
home: the streets inland from Pier Beach
voice: I work in metal lettering. Both names fit if we give up the decorative crest.
agenda: To fit both names clearly on the metal.
appearance: Warren is easy to recognize by thick, tightly coiled hair and a small notch in the left eyebrow. Usually dressed in an olive canvas jacket with a braided bracelet with a single wooden bead, Warren grins on one side while the eyes stay serious when listening.
episode: The other side of the cove
life: “I still remember cutting one long name in brass without losing its final letter.” People around the bank steps know Warren by a small Thursday habit. Warren takes a few minutes to read the public notices, especially the ones written in a hurry.
personality: Warren has a quick wit and an equally quick sense of shame. A joke is often Warren's way of finding out whether a room is friendly enough for a serious question.
family: Nelson Mercer is Warren’s younger cousin. Warren calls back when there is finally a little privacy. Nelson leaves the first voice message. In their family a missed ring can mean a bus, a customer, a sleeping child or a bad hour. Neither treats it as an answer in itself. Asked about *Care with a clock*, Nelson says, “I am the newest visitor. I asked for training time with the slow client rather than the tidy example house.”
connections: Peyton Waters. The person who used to carry newspapers finds the lettering artist space on the public proof.

reactions.asWritten: Someone offers a cash reward for naming a rumored culprit. Warren keeps the money and the rumor out of the conversation and shares only firsthand observations with the person taking the report.

name: Vincent Albright
voice: I object to putting people's names on benches. I changed my mind when I found a friend's name I could say aloud.
agenda: To make space for a friend's remembered name.
appearance: Vincent has iron-gray waves, full cheeks and a mouth that pulls slightly to one side, and a favorite piece of clothing, a washed violet jersey. It usually goes with a replacement button a shade darker than the others. When somebody else has the floor, Vincent listens with the head tilted a little to the left.
episode: The other side of the cove
life: “I still remember talking to a friend's bench after a hard week.” On Thursday, near Harbour Bakery, Vincent buys one familiar thing and asks who chose the unfamiliar thing in the window.
personality: Vincent listens for the familiar version of a story and then for the one detail that changes it. Friends bring problems here when they want to be heard twice.
family: Clyde Starr is Vincent’s younger relative by marriage. Vincent brings whatever was actually growing or affordable that week. Clyde makes room at the table. The meal sometimes produces a solution. Even when it does not, everyone goes away knowing what the other household is up against. Asked about *The boy on the corner*, Clyde says, “I bought the child a costume for the school play.”
connections: Opal Felix. A saved donor letter helps a reluctant walker see how a name could earn its place on the bench.

name: Opal Felix
voice: I saved the original donor letter. It specified a sea view and made no mention of who's looking.
agenda: To verify the original gift's view requirement.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a faded indigo overshirt and a braided bracelet with a single wooden bead. Opal has a narrow face with an expressive upper lip, with short, uneven waves that refuse to lie flat. Opal looks toward the door whenever a name is called during a conversation.
episode: The other side of the cove
life: “I still remember the donor who cared more about direction than inscription.” People around the courtyard by Ferry Street Rooms know Opal by a small Sunday habit. Opal prefers the bench where the sound of the shop door reaches before the visitor does.
personality: Opal talks very little about private fear and recognizes it quickly in strangers. Offering a choice of seats is one of Opal's ways of saying that it is all right to leave.
family: Lou Reed is Opal’s cousin raised in the same household. Their relatives kept a holiday fund in a boot that still had its mate. Even after the family acquired bank accounts, an envelope of change at supper meant somebody was planning a journey. Opal works out what it costs to bring everybody. Asked about *The release address*, Lou says, “I moved without giving him the new number because I needed one quiet Christmas.”
connections: Vincent Albright. A saved donor letter helps a reluctant walker see how a name could earn its place on the bench.

agenda: To raise actual cleaning wages alongside the dedication.

episode: The other side of the cove
life: “I still remember emptying bins before a photographer would take the picture.” On Friday, near the window at Night Shift Donuts, Yusuf knows when the going-home crowd and the coming-to-work crowd will both be there.
personality: Yusuf prefers exact instructions at work and pleasant surprises at home. The two standards occasionally collide, especially when a relative thinks dropping by counts as notice.
family: Reuben Marsh is Yusuf’s cousin. Yusuf chooses an ordinary story to tell. Reuben asks the question the rest of the family avoided. They tend to get further with an important subject when it arrives in the middle of talk about dinner or work. Asked about *An ordinary mirror*, Reuben says, “I used that mirror to adjust my first work coat.”

personality: Jody never tires of being shown how somebody makes a living. Jody can ask an expert question of a craftsperson and still mishandle a simple emotional cue from a friend.

Asked about *The sheltered corner*, Ada says, “I gave directions using the old stop. A stranger arrived late for a reunion and I want to write to the host.”

name: Adela Marin

appearance: Avery is easy to recognize by a neat white crop and a softly rounded chin under sharp cheekbones. Usually dressed in a red windbreaker with a folded shopping list secured by a miniature clip, Avery gathers both sleeves neatly before settling in when listening.

agenda: To arrange one private goodbye inside the crane cab.
appearance: Back on the street, look for a plum-colored cardigan and a cloth patch so neatly matched it only shows in strong light. Ariel has heavy brows and an unusually delicate jaw, with a long silver braid. Ariel listens with the head tilted a little to the left during a conversation.
life: “I still remember shutting a crane cab door after a hard goodbye.” On Thursday, near Breakwater Way, Ariel stops on the landward side of the cycle track to watch the first boats turn for home.
personality: Ariel is kind in very practical ways and prickly about being thanked in public. Ariel loves being recognized by the people who notice what happens after the guests have left.
family: Hollis Fong is Ariel’s younger relative by marriage. Ariel brings something that can still be enjoyed tomorrow. Hollis checks the date twice. Arrangements do change in their family. Taking a delay seriously without treating it as an insult took both of them years. Asked about *The empty drum stool*, Hollis says, “I only play on kitchen pots. The stool was higher than our worktop, so I stood up.”
connections: Mika Williams (longtime workmate). The two retiring workers have earned both a shared shift and a few private minutes at its end.

reactions.situation: A younger worker is asked to perform the final lift

name: Stanley Hull
voice: I am the foreman who cannot offer both options. I have put my own paid hour into the pot.
agenda: To offer an hour that lets both retirees choose.
appearance: Stanley is easy to recognize by auburn hair cut square at the nape and a crooked front tooth visible when laughing. Usually dressed in a cropped bottle-green coat with a braided bracelet with a single wooden bead, Stanley draws small circles on a tabletop while waiting when listening.
life: “I still remember using my paid hour to cover a colleague's daughter's birthday.” Wednesday often includes a stop at the crossing outside Verve Nail Studio, where Stanley notices whose chair is empty and who has stayed talking after an appointment.
personality: Likes beautiful, unnecessary things and gets cross with people who mistake poverty for a lack of taste. Stanley takes longer choosing a cheap birthday card than an expensive coat.
family: Tess Walker is Stanley’s half-sibling. Stanley asks what the birthday guest would like this year. Tess remembers the birthdays. A present that was perfect at sixteen may be completely wrong at forty. They take the trouble of finding out. Asked about *The Saturday swap*, Tess says, “I want to swap so I can meet the sister my father only mentioned in his will.”
connections: Clyde Schmidt. The foreman's hour gives the younger hand a real chance to work beside the departing crew.

reactions.situation: The two old workers are offered separate farewell days
reactions.response: Stanley asks each worker separately what kind of last day they want.
reactions.asWritten: The two old workers are offered separate farewell days. Stanley asks each worker separately what kind of last day they want.

reactions.situation: A coworker arrives late after a night at the hospital
reactions.response: Stanley asks them privately what can be shared about the delay and respects the answer.
reactions.asWritten: A coworker arrives late after a night at the hospital. Stanley asks them privately what can be shared about the delay and respects the answer.

reactions.situation: When a relative dismisses a little luxury
reactions.response: Stanley asks which ordinary pleasure the relative would give up first.
reactions.asWritten: When a relative dismisses a little luxury, Stanley asks which ordinary pleasure the relative would give up first.

performance.situation: The two old workers are offered separate farewell days

name: Vincent Trent
home: the western blocks near Ferry Street Rooms
voice: I used to be their apprentice. I want them to stand back and see a lift go right without either of them directing it.
agenda: To show the two mentors a lift their trainee can handle.
appearance: Vincent has a scattering of freckles across the bridge of the nose. Look for short black hair swept back. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a washed violet jersey with a partly rubbed-away embroidered initial. In conversation Vincent rubs a thumb along the edge of the nearest pocket.
life: “I still remember my trainers watching the first load I handled without them.” Sunday often includes a stop at the courtyard by Ferry Street Rooms, where Vincent prefers the bench where the sound of the shop door reaches before the visitor does.
personality: Vincent can be wonderfully decisive about an emergency and maddeningly undecided about a gift. This is because a person can say precisely what hurts and rarely says exactly what they want.
family: Amanda Roy is Vincent’s older cousin. Vincent asks what the birthday guest would like this year. Amanda remembers the birthdays. A present that was perfect at sixteen may be completely wrong at forty. They take the trouble of finding out. Asked about *The first delivery fee*, Amanda says, “I used to do those drops while my baby slept in the sling.”
connections: Maria Jackson. A parent's request to see the ship lets an apprentice demonstrate a clean lift where the family can see it.

reactions.situation: A younger worker is asked to perform the final lift
reactions.response: Vincent lets the trainee carry out the job they are qualified for and keeps space for the retirees to watch.
reactions.asWritten: A younger worker is asked to perform the final lift. Vincent lets the trainee carry out the job they are qualified for and keeps space for the retirees to watch.

reactions.asWritten: A driver splashes a market worker and tries to laugh it off. Vincent helps shift the damp stock and makes sure the worker gets to describe the loss without interruption.

reactions.asWritten: If a neighbor offers a costly present, Vincent asks for an afternoon to work out whether accepting it would put someone else in debt.

name: Jamie Hamilton
voice: I make the retirement plaques. One misspelling on the old time sheets has become a nickname they both want on the brass.
agenda: To put the familiar spellings on the plaques.
appearance: Jamie has short black hair swept back, one cheek that creases before the other, and a favorite piece of clothing, a red windbreaker. It usually goes with a folded shopping list secured by a miniature clip. When somebody else has the floor, Jamie turns fully toward the person speaking.
life: “I still remember spelling a nickname the way a man actually said it.” People around Maré Coffee know Jamie by a small Tuesday habit. Jamie likes the table where people coming off shift stop checking the time.
personality: Jamie can be lavish with time and quite careful with cash. A free afternoon is sometimes the biggest gift Jamie can afford to give, and family knows to take it seriously.
family: Parker Valdez is Jamie’s stepsibling. Jamie is free to hang up first. Parker makes the call. Some of their best calls last less than a minute. A change of tone is sometimes all the news either one needs. Asked about *The ladder crossing*, Parker says, “I was late for an interview. I described the crossing when they asked how I handle delays.”
connections: Marcel Easton. The person making the plaque brings it to the room where the kettle and the crew actually are.

reactions.situation: The two old workers are offered separate farewell days
reactions.response: Jamie asks each worker separately what kind of last day they want.
reactions.asWritten: The two old workers are offered separate farewell days. Jamie asks each worker separately what kind of last day they want.

reactions.situation: A frightened child is waiting outside a shuttered shop
reactions.response: Jamie stays where the child can see the shop door and asks the neighboring counter to help find the adult expected there.
reactions.asWritten: A frightened child is waiting outside a shuttered shop. Jamie stays where the child can see the shop door and asks the neighboring counter to help find the adult expected there.

reactions.situation: If invited to an expensive outing
reactions.response: Jamie suggests meeting afterward and explains why without asking the others to abandon their plans.
reactions.asWritten: If invited to an expensive outing, Jamie suggests meeting afterward and explains why without asking the others to abandon their plans.

name: Joel Arendt
voice: I spent forty years packing those two lunches. My partner asked what retirement will change for me.
agenda: To give the retiring worker's partner a real voice about home life.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a charcoal zip cardigan and a tiny red thread tied through the lowest buttonhole. Joel has a deep crease beside the mouth when smiling, with a thin scattering of white hair over the crown. Joel steadies a cup with both hands while listening during a conversation.
life: “I still remember packing lunches an hour before anyone else stirred.” On Tuesday, near Harbour Bakery, Joel buys one familiar thing and asks who chose the unfamiliar thing in the window.
personality: Joel carries anger into a conversation very slowly. Once it arrives, a quiet statement of facts can be considerably harder to sidestep than a shout.
family: Ely Kern is Joel’s younger cousin. Joel chooses whether to use it. Ely saves a place. The invitation means something because declining it has never ended the friendship between their households. Asked about *A tide at noon*, Ely says, “I sent guests down in polished shoes. One guest took hers off and stayed for hours.”
connections: Lionel Wu. Packed lunches and one last scorecard complicate the story that only two people are retiring.

reactions.situation: A younger worker is asked to perform the final lift
reactions.response: Joel lets the trainee carry out the job they are qualified for and keeps space for the retirees to watch.
reactions.asWritten: A younger worker is asked to perform the final lift. Joel lets the trainee carry out the job they are qualified for and keeps space for the retirees to watch.

name: Clyde Schmidt
voice: I am the younger hand who gets the vacancy. I am proud of it and have promised them their old table whenever they visit.
agenda: To keep visiting rights at the old table.
appearance: Clyde has auburn hair cut square at the nape, a deep crease beside the mouth when smiling, and a favorite piece of clothing, a narrow-striped sweater. It usually goes with a comb in a sleeve sewn into the lining. When somebody else has the floor, Clyde gathers both sleeves neatly before settling in.
life: “I still remember walking into a port office under somebody else's lucky number.” People around Paper & Pine Books know Clyde by a small Wednesday habit. Clyde starts with the handwritten shelf cards and often leaves with a suggestion for somebody else.
personality: Clyde has an appetite for a good argument about little things and works hard to keep a serious disagreement from being turned into entertainment.
family: Jasmine Miranda is Clyde’s second cousin. Clyde is allowed to ask about the bad news afterward. Jasmine calls about good news first. Neither wants every family conversation to begin with a bill, a diagnosis or an apology. Asked about *An address in pencil*, Jasmine says, “I wanted the house number on a necklace so my mother can tell a driver where she lives.”
connections: Stanley Hull. The foreman's hour gives the younger hand a real chance to work beside the departing crew.

reactions.situation: The two old workers are offered separate farewell days
reactions.response: Clyde asks each worker separately what kind of last day they want.
reactions.asWritten: The two old workers are offered separate farewell days. Clyde asks each worker separately what kind of last day they want.

reactions.situation: An envelope of wages is found under a café chair
reactions.response: Clyde finds a second person to witness its return so an honest mistake won't cost a worker their pay.
reactions.asWritten: An envelope of wages is found under a café chair. Clyde finds a second person to witness its return so an honest mistake won't cost a worker their pay.

reactions.situation: When a private quarrel becomes a public joke
reactions.response: Clyde says the plainest truthful thing possible and changes the subject.
reactions.asWritten: When a private quarrel becomes a public joke, Clyde says the plainest truthful thing possible and changes the subject.

name: Lionel Wu
voice: I beat them at dominoes as a teenager. I want one last game with both clocks still ticking on company time.
agenda: To play the last scored game before clocking out.
appearance: Lionel has brown hair pinned away from the temples, a straight nose and deep-set eyes, and a favorite piece of clothing, a rust-colored canvas coat. It usually goes with a train token tied to a zipper pull. When somebody else has the floor, Lionel touches a knuckle to the chin when searching for a word.
life: “I still remember scoring a domino match on the back of a payslip.” People around the downtown fountain know Lionel by a small Thursday habit. Lionel keeps a little time free to hear who is playing at the far end of the park.
personality: Lionel treats a small promise with the gravity others reserve for a contract. This makes Lionel lovely to rely on and surprisingly difficult to invite on a whim.
family: Lydia Ames is Lionel’s stepsibling. A relative let everybody believe a favorite tune was a folk song. Only later did the family find the melody in a book with a relative's real name under it. Lionel wants the person who made something to have a chance to claim it. Asked about *The pawned trumpet*, Lydia says, “I sold the trumpet with a practice mute. The mute is still on my shelf and so is the child's name.”
connections: Joel Arendt. Packed lunches and one last scorecard complicate the story that only two people are retiring.

reactions.situation: A younger worker is asked to perform the final lift
reactions.response: Lionel lets the trainee carry out the job they are qualified for and keeps space for the retirees to watch.
reactions.asWritten: A younger worker is asked to perform the final lift. Lionel lets the trainee carry out the job they are qualified for and keeps space for the retirees to watch.

reactions.asWritten: A stranger waves a phone camera in a crying person's face. Lionel asks the person crying whether they want to go somewhere quieter, leaving them control over the next step.

reactions.response: Lionel says what can be returned and asks whether that will do.
reactions.asWritten: When offered a favor with ambiguous terms, Lionel says what can be returned and asks whether that will do.

name: Maria Jackson
voice: I watched the ship berth from the road as a child. The two workers promised my daughter she can see it too.
agenda: To bring the daughter to a safe public view of the berth.
appearance: Maria is easy to recognize by short copper curls and a round face with a pronounced chin. Usually dressed in a cropped bottle-green coat with a copper-colored clasp that has been repaired by hand, Maria leans a shoulder against the wall during long conversations when listening.
life: “I still remember seeing two cranes in the space between a fence and my father's hat.” People around the steps at Pier Beach know Maria by a small Thursday habit. Maria watches the working part of the waterfront before turning toward the open water.
personality: Maria is good at starting things, dreadful at waiting for them to take effect. Close family can tell how worried Maria is by the number of tiny errands suddenly being done.
family: Rosemary Heller is Maria’s second cousin. Maria chooses whether they walk home or sit a while. Rosemary brings a spare shopping bag. That small arrangement gives both a reason to see each other on weeks when asking for company outright feels difficult. Asked about *The boy on the corner*, Rosemary says, “I rent the shop. I cleared a table for homework and asked the oldest brother to respect what happens at it.”
connections: Vincent Trent. A parent's request to see the ship lets an apprentice demonstrate a clean lift where the family can see it.

reactions.situation: The two old workers are offered separate farewell days
reactions.response: Maria asks each worker separately what kind of last day they want.
reactions.asWritten: The two old workers are offered separate farewell days. Maria asks each worker separately what kind of last day they want.

reactions.response: Maria puts distance between the frightened person and the argument and asks nearby staff for help.
reactions.asWritten: An argument on the pavement makes a bystander feel unsafe. Maria puts distance between the frightened person and the argument and asks nearby staff for help.

name: Marcel Easton
voice: I thought goodbye would sound like a whistle. The last thing they wanted to hear was the kettle boiling in the break room.
agenda: To put the kettle on for the last shared break.
appearance: Marcel has close-cropped dark curls, an aquiline nose and a square chin, and a favorite piece of clothing, a plum-colored cardigan. It usually goes with a knotted piece of sail thread on a key ring. When somebody else has the floor, Marcel starts to lift a hand, then waits to be invited to speak.
life: “I still remember hearing a kettle above the sound of a stopped ship.” On Monday, near Maré Coffee, Marcel likes the table where people coming off shift stop checking the time.
personality: Marcel tells a better story in a kitchen than at a microphone. Family members sometimes underestimate how far Marcel will go to back a quiet opinion once it is actually challenged.
family: Valentina Berry is Marcel’s cousin raised in the same household. Marcel brings something that can still be enjoyed tomorrow. Valentina checks the date twice. Arrangements do change in their family. Taking a delay seriously without treating it as an insult took both of them years. Asked about *The ladder crossing*, Valentina says, “I held up a bus and lost the driver's goodwill.”
connections: Jamie Hamilton. The person making the plaque brings it to the room where the kettle and the crew actually are.

reactions.situation: A younger worker is asked to perform the final lift
reactions.response: Marcel lets the trainee carry out the job they are qualified for and keeps space for the retirees to watch.
reactions.asWritten: A younger worker is asked to perform the final lift. Marcel lets the trainee carry out the job they are qualified for and keeps space for the retirees to watch.

reactions.situation: An unfamiliar person asks for directions but cannot read the street signs
reactions.response: Marcel finds out what the destination actually looks like to the traveler and gives directions in those terms.
reactions.asWritten: An unfamiliar person asks for directions but cannot read the street signs. Marcel finds out what the destination actually looks like to the traveler and gives directions in those terms.

reactions.situation: If a relative makes a joke at a child's expense
reactions.response: Marcel repeats the child's actual point and waits for a reply to that.
reactions.asWritten: If a relative makes a joke at a child's expense, Marcel repeats the child's actual point and waits for a reply to that.

name: Joseph Moran
voice: I made money selling buildings. I thought the finest gift I could give her was never having to ask a landlord for anything.
agenda: To offer the daughter security on terms she can decline.
appearance: Joseph is easy to recognize by gray hair trimmed very close behind the ears and a straight nose and deep-set eyes. Usually dressed in a boxy denim jacket with a thin silver ring worn on a cord, Joseph raises one eyebrow long before saying yes when listening.
life: “I still remember selling my first strip of land to a family with a van.” Friday often includes a stop at Studio Boulevard, where Joseph waits by the window where the whole crossing can be seen without leaning into the road.
personality: Joseph has excellent recall for voices and a poor memory for official titles. Someone who waited patiently at a counter years ago is more likely to be remembered than the person in charge.
family: Jo Bloom is Joseph’s younger cousin. Joseph is allowed to ask about the bad news afterward. Jo calls about good news first. Neither wants every family conversation to begin with a bill, a diagnosis or an apology. Asked about *The soft wharf chalk*, Jo says, “I thought it was a safety warning and stopped a delivery.”
connections: Cassandra Collins (daughter). A wealthy father and a young tailor disagree about whether owning a whole building constitutes freedom.

reactions.situation: The daughter declines the property gift
reactions.response: Joseph takes the daughter's preferred shop seriously before proposing another gift.
reactions.asWritten: The daughter declines the property gift. Joseph takes the daughter's preferred shop seriously before proposing another gift.

reactions.situation: A friend asks for a loan due back before payday
reactions.response: Joseph asks which other bill repayment would displace, then offers only what the household can afford to give.
reactions.asWritten: A friend asks for a loan due back before payday. Joseph asks which other bill repayment would displace, then offers only what the household can afford to give.

reactions.response: Joseph asks for the name of the person who will still be around tomorrow.
reactions.asWritten: When somebody trades on a title, Joseph asks for the name of the person who will still be around tomorrow.

name: Cassandra Collins
home: the blocks north of the port
voice: I am the daughter. Dad has offered me a valuable building with his office on the top floor.
agenda: To get a modest tailoring space under personal control.
appearance: On an ordinary day, look for a brown corduroy jacket and a comb in a sleeve sewn into the lining. Cassandra has fine brows over wide-set eyes, with a soft fringe that falls across one eyebrow. Cassandra folds a paper napkin into quarters without noticing during a conversation.
life: “I still remember pinning cloth in a shop barely wider than the mirror.” Monday often includes a stop at the corner by Juniper Tailor, where Cassandra looks at the things people actually bring in for repair before looking in the display window.
personality: Cassandra finds it easier to own up to a mistake than to accept praise. The worse the mistake, the more precise the account of exactly when it happened.
family: Freya King is Cassandra’s older cousin. Cassandra calls back when there is finally a little privacy. Freya leaves the first voice message. In their family a missed ring can mean a bus, a customer, a sleeping child or a bad hour. Neither treats it as an answer in itself. Asked about *The bitter orange*, Freya says, “I brought her son in expecting tears. He ordered something completely different and made everyone laugh.”
connections: Joseph Moran (father). A wealthy father and a young tailor disagree about whether owning a whole building constitutes freedom. Also in the story is Marin Brady (master tailor).

reactions.situation: A tenant hears about the building sale secondhand
reactions.response: Cassandra gives the tenant a reliable contact for the sale information and a real date to expect an answer.
reactions.asWritten: A tenant hears about the building sale secondhand. Cassandra gives the tenant a reliable contact for the sale information and a real date to expect an answer.

reactions.situation: Somebody finds a lost wallet outside the bank
reactions.response: Cassandra asks the counter staff for a receipt so its return can be traced even after their shift changes.
reactions.asWritten: Somebody finds a lost wallet outside the bank. Cassandra asks the counter staff for a receipt so its return can be traced even after their shift changes.

reactions.situation: When thanked for a shared success
reactions.response: Cassandra points to the person who noticed the original mistake.
reactions.asWritten: When thanked for a shared success, Cassandra points to the person who noticed the original mistake.

performance.response: Cassandra gives the tenant a reliable contact for the sale information and a real date to expect an answer.

name: Cassandra Knight
home: the western blocks near Ferry Street Rooms
voice: I was hired to value the gift. I asked whether the young woman wanted to be a landlord at all.
agenda: To ask the intended owner what responsibilities are welcome.
appearance: Cassandra has a dark undercut with a longer wave on top, a small notch in the left eyebrow, and a favorite piece of clothing, a rust-colored canvas coat. It usually goes with a square of clean cloth for polishing smudges. When somebody else has the floor, Cassandra listens with the head tilted a little to the left.
life: “I still remember pricing a view the prospective owner never wanted.” On Sunday, near the corner outside Coastal Barber, Cassandra usually checks the board before the regulars give a more colorful account of the news.
personality: Cassandra keeps other people's confidences so well that friends sometimes mistake discretion for taking sides. Cassandra wants to be trusted and resents being asked for proof of it.
family: Quinn Pereira is Cassandra’s younger cousin. Cassandra chooses whether they walk home or sit a while. Quinn brings a spare shopping bag. That small arrangement gives both a reason to see each other on weeks when asking for company outright feels difficult. Asked about *One sleeve short*, Quinn says, “I practiced my handshake with the unaltered arm.”
connections: Tom Crane. The valuation and the tenants' explanation give the daughter a realistic picture of ownership.

reactions.situation: The daughter declines the property gift

reactions.asWritten: The daughter declines the property gift. Cassandra takes the daughter's preferred shop seriously before proposing another gift.

reactions.response: Cassandra stays beside the bystander in a public place and reports only what happened in sight and earshot.
reactions.asWritten: An argument on the pavement makes a bystander feel unsafe. Cassandra stays beside the bystander in a public place and reports only what happened in sight and earshot.

reactions.asWritten: When somebody asks who said it first, Cassandra offers to introduce them to the person willing to put a name to it.

name: Grey Black
home: the western blocks near Ferry Street Rooms
voice: I rent the shop below. The family's generosity could decide where my family eats next year.
agenda: To obtain the proposed building's actual tenant terms.
appearance: Grey has a flat bridge to the nose and a mobile brow. Look for a center part and straight chestnut hair. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a black overshirt with pearl buttons with a fabric zip pull cut from a school scarf. In conversation Grey starts to lift a hand, then waits to be invited to speak.
life: “I still remember renewing a lease before my family knew we could stay.” On Saturday, near Juniper Street, Grey knows which of the west-side porches has a seat in the shade.
personality: Grey always notices who paid for the last round. In a group that can be a kindness or a small tyranny, and Grey is trying to tell the difference before the bill arrives.
family: Mo Gill is Grey’s half-sibling. Grey decides what stays off the paper. Mo brings the paper and a pen. They have helped each other make decisions that were far easier to discuss once the figures could be moved around. The decisions themselves still belong to the person asking. Asked about *The aquarium*, Mo says, “I gave them an old pump marked display only.”
connections: Marin Brady. A tenant's actual upstairs neighbor is one of the people measuring how little room a tailor needs.

reactions.response: Grey gives the tenant a reliable contact for the sale information and a real date to expect an answer.
reactions.asWritten: A tenant hears about the building sale secondhand. Grey gives the tenant a reliable contact for the sale information and a real date to expect an answer.

reactions.situation: A colleague says somebody used the wrong name in public
reactions.response: Grey asks which name they want to hear next time and uses it in the next ordinary introduction.
reactions.asWritten: A colleague says somebody used the wrong name in public. Grey asks which name they want to hear next time and uses it in the next ordinary introduction.

reactions.situation: If somebody tries to repay an old favor all at once

reactions.asWritten: If somebody tries to repay an old favor all at once, Grey suggests a smaller gesture they can repeat without hardship.

name: Ivan Ruiz
home: the western blocks near Ferry Street Rooms
voice: I would give my right arm to inherit a place. Listening to the daughter made me reconsider what a gift with no exit costs.
agenda: To listen to the heir without comparing family fortunes.
appearance: Ivan has black hair twisted into a small knot, a long face and high cheekbones, and a favorite piece of clothing, a sand-colored linen shirt. It usually goes with a tiny red thread tied through the lowest buttonhole. When somebody else has the floor, Ivan looks down for a moment before saying something difficult.
life: “I still remember meeting an heir who needed permission to disappoint a parent.” People around the market by Market Flats know Ivan by a small Friday habit. Ivan often waits until the delivery baskets are stacked before going in.
personality: Ivan has a talent for getting adversaries to laugh at exactly the same thing. Ivan knows better than to expect the laugh to settle what they are arguing about.

voice: I am the electrician who suggested timers. The owners asked me to leave the switches where human hands can get to them.
agenda: To retain the reachable human-operated switches.
appearance: Noel is easy to recognize by a cropped cut that shows the shape of the ears and a round face with a pronounced chin. Usually dressed in an olive canvas jacket with a pen clipped inside the neckline, Noel looks down for a moment before saying something difficult when listening.
episode: The last light at the harbor
life: “I still remember fitting a switch somebody could comfortably reach with wet hands.” People around the window at Night Shift Donuts know Noel by a small Saturday habit. Noel knows when the going-home crowd and the coming-to-work crowd will both be there.
personality: Noel has a strong competitive streak and a very soft spot for the person finishing last. A prize tastes better when everybody had enough time to enter.
family: Kai Ibrahim is Noel’s older relative by marriage. Noel can stop the walk at any corner. Kai chooses the familiar route. Walking side by side makes it easier to disagree without turning each disagreement into a contest. Asked about *The savings club*, Kai says, “I've won the draw twice and deferred it twice.”
connections: Samuel Mehta. The resident and electrician agree that an accessible switch can still belong in human hands.

name: Nico Lin
voice: I wait on the public benches for my wife's shift to end. I know which boat will blink first when the wind comes round.
agenda: To keep the bench invitation open through the wife's shift.
appearance: Nico has full cheeks and a mouth that pulls slightly to one side. Look for a soft fringe that falls across one eyebrow. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a long navy raincoat with a copper-colored clasp that has been repaired by hand. In conversation Nico gathers both sleeves neatly before settling in.
episode: The last light at the harbor
life: “I still remember holding a corner of the bench for my wife's coat.” Saturday often includes a stop at the courtyard by Ferry Street Rooms, where Nico prefers the bench where the sound of the shop door reaches before the visitor does.
personality: Nico reads little signals of discomfort very accurately and has an unfortunate habit of overruling people for their own good. The friends who say stop are the ones Nico trusts most.
family: Anthony Carey is Nico’s cousin raised in the same household. Nico brings whatever was actually growing or affordable that week. Anthony makes room at the table. The meal sometimes produces a solution. Even when it does not, everyone goes away knowing what the other household is up against. Asked about *The empty drum stool*, Anthony says, “I mended the cracked foot by wrapping it in cloth from my graduation gown.”
connections: Albert Wilson. A hospital shift and a waiting spouse use the same set of lights to mark opposite ends of the day.

name: Marcel Briggs
voice: I sat through all four lights with the sister I hadn't spoken to for a year. We agreed to come back next Sunday without settling everything tonight.
agenda: To return with the sister for another unfinished conversation.
appearance: Marcel is easy to recognize by close-cropped dark curls and a crooked front tooth visible when laughing. Usually dressed in a faded indigo overshirt with a narrow brass watch set a little fast, Marcel squares up pieces of paper while thinking when listening.
